en: The Sutra on the Great Expedient Means of the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness, Scroll One.
Translator’s name lost; included in the Later Han Record.
1. Prologue, Chapter One. Prologue. Chapter One.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twenty-eight thousand bhikṣus. All had done what was to be done, established the holy life, and were no longer subject to further existence;

they were like great elephants (mahānāga), having attained mastery over their minds. Their names were: Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Kauṇḍinya, Revata, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Pilindavatsa, Śāriputra, Mahākātyāyana, Ānanda, Rāhula, and others.

There were thirty-eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were well-known to the world; these bodhisattvas had long planted the roots of virtue, having constantly practiced the pure conduct under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas, fulfilling their great vows and attaining mastery over hundreds of thousands of dhyānas and dhāraṇīs.
They did not abandon great compassion, benefiting sentient beings according to their needs, and they upheld and glorified the Three Jewels so that they would never be severed.
They are able to erect the banner of the Dharma and act as uninvited friends to all sentient beings;
having reached the shore of great wisdom, their fame is heard everywhere. Their names are:
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Nityodyukta Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
Gadgadasvara Bodhisattva, Vidyutprabha Bodhisattva, Samantavyūha Bodhisattva,
Guṇarāja Bodhisattva, Merurāja Bodhisattva, Gandhahastin Bodhisattva, and Mahāgandhahastin Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Holding Power, Bodhisattva Transcending the Three Realms, Bodhisattva Constant Compassion, Bodhisattva Jewel Palm,
Bodhisattva Supreme Light Glory, Bodhisattva Blazing Wondrousness, Bodhisattva Jewel Moon, Bodhisattva Great Strength,
Bodhisattva Immeasurable Wisdom, Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, and Bodhisattva Lion’s Roar.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita, the Bodhisattva Pūrṇapraṇidhāna,
the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, and others, together with their retinues of hundreds of thousands.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras from the desire realm, each accompanied by their retinues, carrying various subtle and exquisite celestial incenses and flowers, performing divine music, and remaining in mid-air.

The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, each accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues, bowed at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata was surrounded by a great assembly who made offerings to him with reverence, respect, honor, and praise.
Then, Ānanda, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, entered the city of Rājagṛha at dawn to beg for alms in regular order.

At that time, there was a son of a brahmin in the city who had served his parents with filial piety. His family had fallen into ruin and his wealth was completely exhausted; thus, he carried his aged mother on his back and went from door to door begging for alms. If he obtained fine food or fragrant, delicious fruits and melons, he would offer them up to his mother;
if he obtained poor food, such as withered vegetables or dried fruit, he would eat them himself.
When Ānanda saw this, his heart was filled with joy, and he praised this person in verse:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Noble son! To provide for one's parents is a marvelous and peerless feat!

There was a brahmin who was a follower of the Six Teachers; he was clever and eloquent, fully proficient in the four Vedas, calendrical calculations, divination of good and bad fortune, the shifts of yin and yang, and able to anticipate the thoughts of others.
He was also a leading teacher for the great assembly, revered by many;
yet, clinging to heterodox doctrines, he destroyed the True Dharma for the sake of gain and offerings, harboring jealousy in his heart to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
He said to Ānanda:
"Your teacher Gautama, a scion of the Śākyas, claims for himself that he is virtuous and possesses great merit; yet he has only an empty reputation, while lacking any actual practice."
Your teacher Gautama is truly an evil man; having been born for only seven days, his mother passed away—is he not indeed an evil man?

Upon leaving the palace city, his father the King was overcome with bitter anguish; he fell to the ground in a state of delirium and confusion, and it took seven days for him to regain consciousness after water was sprinkled upon his face.
"How is it that today I have lost the one from whom I was born?
Raising her voice, she wept bitterly and said,
"The kingdom is yours."
"I have only you, my one son; why do you abandon me to enter the deep mountains?
Your teacher Gautama, unaware of the debt of gratitude and showing no concern for you, has gone on ahead; therefore, you should know that he is an unfilial person.

The father-king built a palace for him and took Gopī as his wife, yet he did not observe the rites due to a wife, causing her bitter grief; therefore, you should know that he is a person devoid of gratitude.
Having heard these words, Ānanda felt shame and remorse.
After finishing his almsround, he returned to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Within the Buddha-dharma,
is there perhaps no such thing as filial piety and the nurturing of one's parents?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Who taught you to ask such a question?
Were it the devas, or were they humans?"
"Are you a non-human being?
Or do you ask the Tathāgata this question by means of your own power of wisdom? Ānanda replied:
"Furthermore, no devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, or non-humans came to see me or instruct me.
Just now, while begging for alms, I encountered Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha and his followers, the six teachers, who insulted and reviled me."
Ānanda immediately related these matters to the Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled with a serene countenance, and from his face he emitted light of five colors that passed beyond immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-lands in the eastern direction.

There is a world named Uttara-vijaya; its Buddha is named Priyarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The country is named Resplendent (Śrīmat), its terrain level and even. Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, with golden cords delineating the borders along the roadsides.

There are rows of trees made of the seven treasures; each tree reaches a height of one arrow-shot. Their flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves are arranged in successive layers of adornment. When a gentle breeze stirs them, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds that all sentient beings delight in hearing, never tiring of it.
Everywhere there were flowing springs and bathing pools; these pools were pure, with golden sand spread across their bottoms and filled with water possessing the eight virtues.
On the four sides of the pools were exquisite fragrant flowers—padmas, puṇḍarīkas, and vārṣikas—in blue, yellow, red, and white, as large as chariot wheels, covering the surface.
Within the waters of these pools, various kinds of birds sang together in harmony, producing subtle and wondrous sounds that were most delightful.
There were also ships made of the seven treasures within it, wherein all sentient beings sported at will.

Within those groves of trees, lion thrones were spread, one yojana in height, likewise adorned with the seven treasures; furthermore, celestial robes were layered upon them, celestial precious incense was burned, and various celestial jewel flowers were strewn across the ground.
The Tathāgata Prītirāja sat upon it, seated in the full lotus posture.
Countless billions of bodhisattvas from that land surrounded him on all sides, standing to one side with palms joined toward the Tathāgata, speaking with one voice in unison:
"We pray that the World-Honored One, out of his compassionate pity, will tell us by what causes and conditions this radiance has appeared."

Blue, yellow, red, and white—its colors were brilliant and magnificent, beyond easy comparison. Coming from the west, it illuminated this great assembly; those who encountered this light found their minds and thoughts to be serene and at ease.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will sever the net of my doubts.
The Buddha said,
"O sons of good family!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
I shall now explain this to you in detail.

To the west of here, beyond immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds, there is a world named Sahā. In it dwells a Buddha called Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, surrounded by a great assembly. He now wishes to preach the *Mahopāya-mahāpratyupakāra-sūtra* for the sake of the great assembly; for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings;
and for the purpose of extracting the poisonous arrows of false doubt from all sentient beings.
It is for the purpose of making bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds firm in their bodhi so that they do not regress;
for the purpose of causing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to ultimately reach the path of the One Vehicle;
and for the purpose of enabling the great bodhisattvas to swiftly accomplish bodhi in order to repay the Buddha's kindness.
It is because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to mind their heavy debt of gratitude;
because he wishes to cause sentient beings to cross over the ocean of suffering;
and because he wishes to cause sentient beings to practice filial piety and support their parents.
"It is for this reason that we emit this light.

At that time, within the great assembly, there were ten thousand bodhisattvas; each of these bodhisattvas was a leading teacher of the multitude. They immediately rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We pray that the World-Honored One will exert his majestic spiritual power so that we may go to the Sahā world to personally attend upon and make offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and furthermore, to hear the subtle and wondrous scripture, the *Mahā-upāya-buddha-pratyupakāra-sūtra*."
At that time, that Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
When you go to the Sahā world, if you see that Buddha, you should give rise to thoughts of making offerings, of reverence, and of his being difficult to encounter."

Why is this? Because during immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, Śākyamuni Tathāgata practiced difficult and painful austerities and made this Great Compassionate Vow:

"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall do so within a defiled land filled with mountains, hills, mounds, rubble, and thorns; therein, among sentient beings who are fully possessed of afflictions and commit the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, I shall achieve Buddhahood to benefit them, causing them to sever all suffering, obtain all happiness, and perfect the Dharma-body until nothing remains."
"Such was the original vow of that Buddha.
You should now go as the Buddha went, and abide as the Buddha abides.
The assembly of bodhisattvas all spoke with one voice:

“As the World-Honored One has commanded,” each of the bodhisattvas took with them as their retinue immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of other bodhisattvas, surrounding them before and behind, and proceeded toward the Sahā world.
The lands he traversed shook in six ways, and a great light shone everywhere;
the devas of the void rained down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, emitting a vast radiance;
and through his supernormal powers, he moved worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music that resounded spontaneously in the void without being struck.
These bodhisattvas went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, approached the Tathāgata, prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata again emitted a ray of light that shone directly toward the south, passing through eighty trillion Buddha-lands until it reached a world named Prabhāśrī.
In that world-system there is a Buddha named Cintyākāra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The land is named Good Purity; its terrain is level and even, with lapis lazuli for its ground. Golden cords demarcate the sides of the roads.

Rows of trees made of the seven treasures stand there, each reaching a height of one arrow-shot. Their flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves are adorned in orderly succession; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds that all sentient beings delight in hearing, never tiring of them.
Everywhere there were flowing springs and bathing ponds; these ponds were pure, with golden sand spread across their bottoms and filled with water possessing the eight virtues.
Along the four sides of the ponds were exquisite fragrant flowers—padmas, puṇḍarīkas, and vārṣikas—in blue, yellow, red, and white, as large as chariot wheels, covering the surface.
Within the waters of these ponds, various kinds of birds sang together in harmony, producing subtle and wondrous sounds that were most delightful.
There were also ships made of the seven treasures within it, wherein all sentient beings sported at will.

Within the groves of trees, lion thrones were spread out, one yojana in height, adorned with the seven treasures; furthermore, celestial garments were layered upon them, celestial precious incense was burned, and various celestial precious flowers were strewn across the ground.
The Tathāgata Siṃhavikrāntagāmin sat upon it, seated in the full lotus posture.
Countless billions of bodhisattvas from that land surrounded him on all sides, standing to one side with palms joined toward the Tathāgata, speaking with one voice in unison:
"We pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion and pity."
By what causes and conditions does this radiance exist?
Its colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—are brilliant and magnificent, beyond easy comparison.
Coming from the north, it illuminates this great assembly; those who encounter this light find their minds serene and at ease.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will sever the net of my doubts.

Reflect upon it well.
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

To the north, beyond immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds from here, there is a world named Sahā. In it dwells a Buddha called Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who is currently surrounded by a great assembly. He now wishes to preach the *Mahopāya-mahāpratyupakāra-sūtra* for the sake of the great assembly, in order to benefit all sentient beings;
in order to extract the poisonous arrows of false doubt from all sentient beings.
It is for the purpose of causing bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds to be firm in their bodhi and not regress;
for the purpose of causing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to ultimately reach the path of the One Vehicle;
and for the purpose of enabling the great bodhisattvas to swiftly attain bodhi and repay the Buddha's kindness.
It is because he wishes to cause all sentient beings to remember their heavy debt of gratitude;
because he wishes to cause sentient beings to cross over the ocean of suffering;
and because he wishes to cause sentient beings to practice filial piety and support their parents.
"It is for this reason that this radiance is emitted.

At that time, within the great assembly, there were ten thousand bodhisattvas, each of whom was a leading teacher among the multitude. They immediately rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We pray that the World-Honored One will exert his majestic spiritual power so that we may go to the Sahā world to personally approach, serve, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and furthermore, to hear the subtle and wondrous scripture, the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means*."
At that time, that Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
Go to the Sahā world; if you see that Buddha there, you should conceive thoughts of making offerings, of reverence, and of the rarity of such an encounter."

Why is this? Because Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, performed difficult practices and austerities, and made this great compassionate vow:

"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall do so in a defiled land filled with mountains, hills, mounds, rubble, and thorns; therein, for the sake of sentient beings who are fully possessed of afflictions and commit the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, I shall attain enlightenment and benefit them, causing them to sever all suffering and obtain all happiness, and to achieve the Dharma-body, forever exhausting [suffering] without remainder."
"Such was the original vow of that Buddha.
You should now go as the Buddha went, and abide as the Buddha abides.
The assembly of bodhisattvas spoke in unison:
"As the World-Honored One has commanded," each of the bodhisattvas,
taking with them as their retinue immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, surrounded them before and behind as they proceeded toward the Sahā world.
All the lands he passed through shook in six ways, and a great light shone everywhere;

the celestial deities of space rained down *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, emitting a vast radiance, while their supernormal powers caused worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to tremble.
Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music played spontaneously in the void without being struck.

These bodhisattvas went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, approached the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the Tathāgata again emitted a great light that shone directly toward the west, passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-lands. There was a world named Pure Abode (*Vimalāvāsa*), where the Buddha was named Candrasūryapradīpa-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
The land is named Abhirati; its terrain is level and even, with lapis lazuli for its ground. Golden cords demarcate the sides of the roads.

Rows of trees made of the seven treasures stand there, each reaching the height of a full arrow-shot. Their flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves are arranged in successive layers of adornment; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds that all sentient beings delight in hearing, never growing weary of them.
Everywhere there are flowing springs and bathing pools; these pools are pure, with golden sand spread across their bottoms and filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
On the four sides of the pools are exquisite fragrant flowers—padmas, puṇḍarīkas, and vārṣikas—in blue, yellow, red, and white, as large as chariot wheels, covering the surface.
Within the waters of these pools dwell various kinds of birds that warble in harmony, producing subtle and wondrous sounds that are most delightful.
There were also ships made of the seven treasures within it, where all sentient beings sported at will.

Amidst the groves of trees, lion thrones were spread out, one yojana in height, adorned with the seven treasures; furthermore, celestial garments were layered upon them, celestial precious incense was burned, and various celestial jewel flowers were strewn across the ground.
The Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa sat upon it, seated in the full lotus posture.

To the east, beyond immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddha-worlds from here, there is a world named Sahā. In it dwells a Buddha titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, surrounded by a great assembly.
Now, I wish to preach the *Mahā-upāya-mahā-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* for the sake of the great assembly; it is because I desire to bring benefit and joy to all sentient beings;
it is because I desire to extract the poisonous arrows of false doubt from all sentient beings;
and it is because I desire to cause bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds to be firm in their bodhi and never to regress.
It is for the sake of causing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to ultimately attain the path of the One Vehicle;
it is for the sake of enabling all great bodhisattvas to swiftly achieve bodhi and repay the Buddha’s kindness;
and it is because one desires to cause all sentient beings to be mindful of this profound debt of gratitude.
It is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to cross over the ocean of suffering;
it is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to practice filial piety and support their parents. For these reasons, he emits this radiance.

At that time, there were ten thousand bodhisattvas within the great assembly; each of these bodhisattvas was a preeminent teacher who led the multitude. They rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We pray that the World-Honored One will exert his majestic spiritual power so that we may go to the Sahā world to approach and make offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and furthermore, to hear the subtle and wondrous scripture, the *Sūtra on the Requital of Gratitude by the Buddha through Great Expedient Means*."
At that time, that Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
Go to the Sahā world; if you see that Buddha there, you should give rise to thoughts of making offerings, of reverence, and of the rarity of such an encounter."

"Such was that Buddha’s original vow.
You should now go as the Buddha went, and abide as the Buddha abides.

the celestial deities of the void rained down *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, emitting a vast radiance that moved worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges through its supernormal power.

At that time, the five-colored light of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni shone toward the north, passing through five hundred myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands. There was a world named Sovereign King of Renown, wherein dwelt a Buddha named Red Lotus Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At that time, that Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
When you go to the Sahā world, if you see that Buddha, you should give rise to thoughts of making offerings, of reverence, and of the rarity of such an encounter."

Why is this? Because for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, Śākyamuni Tathāgata practiced difficult and painful austerities and made this great compassionate vow:

"When I attain Buddhahood, I shall do so within a defiled and evil land—filled with mountains, hills, mounds, rubble, and thorns—wherein sentient beings are possessed of afflictions and commit the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds; therein I shall attain Buddhahood to benefit them, causing them to sever all suffering and obtain all happiness, and to achieve the Dharma-body, forever exhausting [suffering] without remainder."
"Such was the original vow of that Buddha.
You should now go as the Buddha went, and abide as the Buddha abides.
The assembly of bodhisattvas spoke in unison:
"As the World-Honored One has commanded," each of the bodhisattvas,
taking with them as their retinue immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other bodhisattvas, surrounded by them before and behind, proceeded toward the Sahā world.
All the lands he passed through shook in six ways, and a great light shone everywhere;
the celestial beings of the void rained down *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, emitting a great radiance;
and by his supernormal power, he moved worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of celestial music played spontaneously in the void without being struck.

These bodhisattvas and others proceeded to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; having arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Furthermore, the great assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who had come from the four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir throughout the ten directions—each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers—arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was. They made offerings, paid homage, showed reverence, and offered praise; with one voice and in unison, they each spoke hundreds of thousands of verses in praise of the Buddha.
Having praised the Buddha, they withdrew to stand to one side.
At that moment, the Sahā world was transformed into purity, becoming free of all mountain thickets, large and small mountains, rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, brooks, gullies, and ravines.

The sentient beings therein, having seen the Buddha following the light, rejoiced with palms joined; they prostrated themselves in reverence, their hearts filled with longing and devotion, never for a moment averting their gaze.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his radiance, which circled his body seven times before returning and entering through the crown of his head.
Venerable Ānanda observed the minds of the assembly and saw that they were all likewise filled with doubt.
He wished to reveal the Tathāgata’s skillful means and secret conduct; he also wished to open the eye of wisdom for all sentient beings of the future;
and he wished to enable all sentient beings to cross the ocean of craving and reach the other shore, attaining eternal peace and happiness.

Desiring to cause sentient beings to mindfully remember the profound kindness of their parents and teachers, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since Ānanda has served the Buddha, he has never before seen the Buddha smile.
A smile must surely have its meaning.
We pray that the Buddha will reveal it; we pray that the Buddha will explain it, so as to sever the net of doubt within this great assembly.

2. Chapter on Filial Support: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means, Chapter Two: Filial Support. At that time, from within the great assembly, seven-jeweled lotus flowers manifested spontaneously from the earth; they had stems of white silver, leaves of gold, and pedestals made of *cintāmaṇi* (jambūnada) jewels, adorned in succession with nets of pearls.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata rose from his seat, ascended the flower dais, and sat cross-legged, immediately manifesting his pure body.

Within that body he manifested the bodies of the five destinies; within each of these bodies there were eighteen thousand varieties of forms; within each variety of form there appeared one hundred thousand kinds of bodies; and within each of those bodies there were further immeasurable bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Within each of these bodies, which were as numerous as the sands of four Ganges Rivers, he further manifested bodies equal in number to the atoms of dust in the great earth of the four continents.
Within a single body as small as a mote of dust, he further manifests bodies equal in number to the motes of dust in a trichiliocosm;

within each of those dust-like bodies, he further manifests in the ten directions, in each and every quarter, bodies equal in number to the motes of dust in hundreds of billions of Buddha-worlds, even up to bodies equal in number to the inconceivable sentient beings of the space-pervading Dharma-realm.

At that time, having manifested such bodies as these, the Tathāgata addressed Ānanda, as well as the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who had come from the ten directions, and all the members of the great assembly, including the sons of good family:
"The Tathāgata, by means of his correct and universal knowledge, now proclaims words of truth."
The Dharma is beyond verbal expression; yet, through sublime skillful means, the Tathāgata is able to express the nameless and signless Dharma by means of names and signs.

In the past, while within the cycle of birth and death, the Tathāgata fully assumed bodies among all sentient beings—whose forms and types are as numerous as motes of dust and inconceivable in their variety.
Because they have received a body, all sentient beings have also once been the parents of the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata has likewise once been the parent of all sentient beings.

For the sake of all parents, he constantly practiced difficult and arduous austerities; he was able to relinquish what is hard to give, bestowing his head, eyes, marrow, and brain, as well as kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, the seven treasures, palanquins, carriages, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—giving all these things away.

Diligently cultivating diligence, precepts, generosity, extensive learning, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they fulfill all myriad practices without ceasing or resting, their minds free from weariness.
Because they practice filial piety and support their parents, and because they recognize and repay kindness, they are now able to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, all sentient beings can cause the Tathāgata to fulfill his original vows.
Therefore, one should know that all sentient beings have rendered great kindness to the Buddha; because they have rendered such great kindness, the Tathāgata does not abandon sentient beings.

Out of a heart of great compassion, he constantly cultivates skillful means and practices impartial loving-kindness for all sentient beings within the twenty-five states of existence across the three realms, never considering his own merit, and always practicing the skillful means of equanimity.

Furthermore, they clearly discern that all sentient beings are empty, phenomena are empty, and the five aggregates are empty; thus, they do not regress or sink, nor do they become submerged in emptiness or existence. Because they cultivate the skillful means of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), they do not abandon the two vehicles, but instead cultivate the skillful means of universal study (*sarvaśikṣā*).
Because they have cultivated such profound and subtle skillful means, they attain clear discernment of the characteristics of dharmas.

Although the beginning, middle, and end of the Buddha-dharma are not one and the same, sentient beings are clouded and deluded, acting with wild abandon in three ways; shrouded by craving, they sink into the sea of suffering.

They are inverted by the four perversions, perceiving through false conceptualization within tainted phenomena: seeing a self where there is no self, permanence where there is impermanence, bliss where there is no bliss, and purity where there is impurity.
Subject to the transitions and destructions of birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is impermanent from moment to moment;
shrouded by the five hindrances and the ten entanglements, one transmigrates through the three realms of existence, fully undergoing birth and death without beginning or end, like a revolving wheel.

Therefore, the Tathāgata’s traces of teaching accord with what is appropriate; through the three piṭakas and nine divisions, up to the twelve divisions of the sūtras, he disseminates the path of transformation and preaches various scriptures according to the depth of one's faith.
Those who discriminate between phenomena and cling to words consider themselves to have reached their goal, believing they have already attained nirvana.
Therefore, out of the compassionate original vow of the Tathāgata, he manifests great skillful means to summon all those with karmic affinity throughout the ten directions.

Since those with the karmic affinity have gathered, I shall expound and disseminate this wondrous sutra within this great assembly, providing instruction for a thousand years, circulating it during the Semblance Dharma Age, so that all sentient beings may constantly attain great peace.
Therefore, the Tathāgata guides sentient beings according to their capacities and transforms them through his activity; he appears at the appropriate time and passes away at the appropriate time.
In other lands, he is called Vairocana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān;
or he ascends to the Tuṣita Heaven to serve as the teacher of the devas.
Or descending from Tuṣita Heaven, he manifests in Jambudvīpa, manifesting a lifespan of eighty years.

One should know that the Tathāgata is inconceivable, the world is inconceivable, karmic retribution is inconceivable, sentient beings are inconceivable, meditative concentration is inconceivable, and the dragon kings are inconceivable; these are the inconceivabilities of the Buddha.

If the Buddha wishes for all sentient beings to know the Buddha’s mind, even those of the lowest stream and dull faculties shall be made to know it; if he wishes for all sentient beings to be able to see him, they shall immediately see him.

If he wishes for them not to see him, even if they were face-to-face with his eyes, they would be unable to see him; even if Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possessed the supernormal power of the divine eye, they still could not see him.

Furthermore, the Buddha emits a great radiance that extends downward to the Avīci Hell and upward to the Peak of Existence; those who are ready for deliverance all behold it, while those not yet ready for deliverance do not see it even before their own eyes.
At times the Tathāgata grants permission, and at times he remains silent.
One should know that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are inconceivable, immeasurable, and difficult to comprehend.
How is it that you are now able to question the Tathāgata regarding such profound, subtle, and difficult-to-practice asceticism?
That you have raised this question is truly due to great compassion and pity for sentient beings; it shall close the paths to the three evil realms and open the way to the human and celestial worlds.
"Ānanda, listen well!
I shall briefly explain for you the causes and conditions of the ascetic practices performed in filial support of one's parents.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, all the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and the entire assembly, speaking these words:
"In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a land named Vārāṇasī.

Therein appeared a Buddha in the world, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
That Buddha’s lifespan was twelve minor kalpas; the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remained for twenty minor kalpas.
During the period of the Semblance Dharma, a king appeared in the world named King Rāja.
The King of Vārāṇasī had twenty thousand consorts, four thousand ministers, and five hundred mighty elephant kings.
He ruled over sixty small kingdoms and eight hundred villages.
The king had three crown princes, all of whom served as kings of minor frontier states.
At that time, the Great King of Vārāṇasī was wise, benevolent, and virtuous; he always governed the country with the True Dharma and never oppressed the people.
"By the power of the King's merit and virtue, the winds and rains fall in their proper seasons, the five grains ripen in abundance, and the people enjoy prosperity and well-being.
At that time, the Great King of Vārāṇasī had a chief minister named Rāhu.

The minister Rāhu conceived a rebellious intent and raised a fourfold army—namely, elephant troops, chariot troops, cavalry, and infantry—to attack the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and take the life of the Great King.
Having finished killing the king, he again dispatched the fourfold army to a bordering state to kill the eldest prince, and subsequently went to seize the second prince.
"The youngest brother became a minor king of a frontier state.
This minor king was of handsome and imposing stature, with features that were exceptionally beautiful and refined;
he was benevolent and well-disciplined by nature, and his speech was always accompanied by a smile."
His speech was beneficial and never offended others' feelings.

He always governed the state according to the True Dharma and never treated the people with injustice or partiality; consequently, the land was prosperous and joyful, the population flourished, wealth and treasures were abundant, and the household provisions were overflowing.
The people of the kingdom praised their king, extolling his virtues beyond measure; even the devas in the void and all the spirits likewise revered and loved him.

At that time, the king gave birth to a crown prince named Sujāta (in the original, *Sujātā*, with the first character being *Chǎn* and the subsequent characters being identical to *Tí*). He was intelligent, compassionate, and benevolent, and he delighted in the practice of giving.
Prince Sujāti’s body was the color of gold, with the seven parts of his body level and full, and he was endowed with all the marks of a superior person.
At the age of only seven years, his father loved him so dearly that his heart could not bear to be parted from him for even a moment.
At that time, the deity who guards the palace addressed the Great King, saying:
“Does Your Majesty know?

The minister Rāhu has recently conceived a rebellious intent and plotted to seize the throne. Having already killed the Father King, he has now raised a fourfold army to hunt down your two elder brothers; he has already cut off their life-roots, and his troops will arrive here before long.”
"Great King!
Why do you not flee for your life now?
At that time, having heard these words, the Great King’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; his body trembled so violently that he could not support himself.

Filled with grief, resentment, and distress, sighing and sighing in frustration, his heart and liver burned with anguish; he rolled and fell to the ground, remaining unconscious for a long while before regaining consciousness.
In a low voice, he addressed the void, saying: "Who are you?"
"I hear only their voices, but do not see their forms.
Is what you have just proclaimed truly so?
He then replied to the king:
"I am the deity who guards this palace.
Because Your Majesty is wise and possesses merit, you do not oppress the people and govern the kingdom with the True Dharma; for this reason, I have come first to inform you."
"Great King!
It is now time for you to depart with all haste.
Suffering, affliction, and calamity will soon arrive; your enemies are drawing near."
At that time, the great king entered his palace and thought to himself:
"I should now seek refuge in another kingdom.
He then reflected further:
"Regarding the neighboring country, there are two routes:
one route takes seven full days to reach the other country, while the other route requires fourteen days."
He immediately packed provisions for seven days’ journey and set out in humble attire.

Upon reaching the outskirts of the city, he returned once more to the palace, called Prince Sujāti to his side, and cradled him in his lap, his gaze never wavering for a moment; yet, startled as if by a sudden shock, he rose up and then sat down again.
At that time, the queen saw that the Great King was not at ease and appeared to be in a state of terror; she immediately stepped forward and asked, "Great King!
Why do you now appear to be in a state of terror?"

For what reason and by what cause do you sit uneasily, your body covered in dust and dirt, your hair disheveled, your gaze uneven, and your breath unsteady—bearing such inauspicious signs as if a kingdom has been lost, a loved one has departed, or an enemy is about to arrive?
"I pray that you will inform me.
The king said, "The matters I have are not for you to know."
The lady then addressed the king, saying:
"My body and yours, O King, are one entity with two forms, like the two wings of a bird, the two feet of a body, or the two eyes of a head."
"Great King, why do you now say that it has no concern for us?
The King said to the lady: "Do you not know?"
The minister Rāhu has recently committed a heinous rebellion; having murdered the father-king, he has now sought out and captured my two elder brothers, severing their life-faculties as well.
Now, his troops and horses have arrived in succession to seize me.
"Now I wish to escape for my life.
He then took up Prince Siṃhaketu in his arms and immediately set out on the road.
At that time, the Queen also followed behind them.

At that time, the king was distraught and his mind was bewildered; he mistakenly entered the path for the fourteenth day—a path that was perilous and difficult, where there was neither water nor grass.
After traveling forward for several days, his provisions were completely exhausted.
"Originally, we intended for one person's portion of grain to suffice for a journey of seven days; now that three people share it, we have mistakenly entered upon a fourteen-day journey.
After several days, our provisions were exhausted, yet the road ahead remains far."
At that time, the Great King and his consort raised their voices and wept bitterly:
"How strange! How strange!"
Alas! Alas! Since birth, I have never heard of such suffering; how is it that today my own body must experience it?
"Today we are in dire straits; misfortune and calamity have already arrived.
Raising his hands, he struck his head until dust covered him; casting his whole body to the ground, he reproached himself, saying:
"What evil deeds did we commit in our past lives?"
Did you kill your father, mother, a true person, or an arhat?
Did you slander the True Dharma or destroy the Sangha of harmony?
Or did you engage in hunting and fishing, using light scales and small measures to rob and plunder sentient beings?
"Was it used for the property of the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters?
Why have I encountered this retribution today?
He wished to stop for a moment, yet he feared the arrival of his enemies; if they were to capture him, his death would be certain beyond doubt.
Just as he was about to move forward, he was overcome by hunger and thirst, his life hanging by a thread.
At that time, the Great King and his consort, having contemplated this suffering, broke into a loud, wailing cry.
The king, overcome with grief and fainting, threw his whole body to the ground; after a long while he regained consciousness and reflected again:
"If no skillful means are employed, these three will perish together; they cannot escape death here."
"What if I were now to kill the lady so that I might save my own life and continue the life of my son?
Having thought this, he immediately drew his sword, intending to kill the lady.

When the son, Sujāti, saw the king’s unusual appearance, he drew a sword with his right hand, intending to kill his mother; however, he stepped forward, seized the king’s hand, and said to his father:
"What do you intend to do?"
At that time, the father king, his eyes filled with tears of grief, spoke to his son in a low voice:
"I wish to kill your mother, take her flesh and blood, to sustain my own body and continue your life."
"If I do not kill her, I too shall die; what difference, then, is there between life and death for my own person?
Now, for the sake of my son's life, I wish to kill your mother."
At that time, Śūḍānti addressed his father, saying:
"If Your Majesty kills my mother, I shall not eat either.
Where is there a son who would devour the flesh of his own mother?"
"If you do not eat meat, both of us, father and son, shall die.
Your father, the King, why does he not now kill his son to save the lives of his parents?
When the King heard his son's words, he immediately fainted and fell to the ground, rolling about; in a faint voice, he spoke to his son:
"My son is like my own eyes; what person could pluck out their own eyes and then eat them?
I would rather lose my life than ever kill you and devour your flesh."
At that time, Śūḍathī admonished his father, the king, saying:
"Father King, if you were to take my life now, my flesh and blood would rot and fester before many days have passed."
"I only pray that my parents will not kill this son's body; I wish to ask for one boon. If you should refuse me, you would no longer be compassionate parents.
At that time, the father king spoke to the prince, saying, "We shall not oppose your wishes. Whatever boon you desire, speak it forthwith."

Suṣadha said: "Father and Mother, out of compassion for your son, you should go to my body every day with a knife and cut three *jin* of flesh; divide it into three portions, offer two portions to your parents, and eat one portion yourself to sustain your lives."

At that time, the parents followed their son’s words; they cut three *jin* of flesh and divided it into three portions. Two portions were for the parents, and one portion was for himself to eat so as to sustain his life until he reached the road ahead.

Before two days had passed, his flesh was completely consumed until only his limbs, joints, and marrow remained joined together; with his life-force not yet severed, he suddenly collapsed to the ground.
At that moment, his parents rushed forward to embrace him and wailed aloud, crying out:
"We have acted recklessly, devouring your flesh at will and causing you such agony!"
"The road ahead is still long and we have not yet reached our destination, yet your flesh is already exhausted.
Now we shall perish together, and let our corpses be gathered in one place.
At that time, Śūḍānti spoke with a faint voice, offering this plea:
"Having already devoured my son's flesh and traveled this far, calculating the distance covered, there is but one day's journey remaining.
My son’s body can no longer move; he shall give up his life right here."
"Father and Mother, it would not be right for you to perish together with an ordinary person.
I beg you to grant me one word out of compassion; do not reject or oppose me.
You may scrape away the remaining flesh from the joints of my body to provide sustenance for yourselves, so that you may reach your destination."

At that time, the parents followed their words; they took a small amount of flesh from their own limbs and joints, divided it into three portions, gave one portion to the child, and ate two portions themselves.
Having finished eating, the parents departed.
Susīma rose and stood, gazing after his parents.
At that time, the parents raised their voices and wept bitterly as they followed the road away.

His parents had gone far away and could not be seen; Prince Viśvantara, out of longing and devotion for them, did not turn his eyes away for even a moment, until after a long while he collapsed to the ground.

At that time, the fresh blood and flesh of his body were fragrant; mosquitoes and gadflies from the ten directions, smelling the scent of the blood and flesh, came to swarm over his body and bit and fed upon him everywhere, such that the piercing and agonizing pain was beyond description.
"At that time, while the Prince's remaining life-force was not yet severed, he raised his voice and made this vow:
'May the calamities and evils of my past lives be completely eradicated from this moment on; henceforth, I shall never again dare to commit them.'"
Now, with this body of mine, I provide for my parents and relieve their greatest concern; may my parents always obtain the eleven remaining blessings:

peace in sleep, peace upon waking, no seeing of evil dreams, protection by devas, being loved by people, the elimination of harm from officials, thieves, and conspiracies, and auspiciousness in all undertakings.
I offer my own flesh and blood to these mosquitoes and gadflies, so that they may all be fully satiated.

May this cause me to attain Buddhahood in a future life; and when I have become a Buddha, I vow to eliminate your hunger, thirst, and the grave illness of birth and death by means of the food of the Dharma.

When this vow was made, the earth and heavens shook in six ways; the sun lost its brilliance; birds and beasts were startled and fled in all directions; the great ocean surged with waves; Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, leaped up and sank down, rising and falling; and even the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were greatly shaken.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, leading the various devas of the desire realm, descended to Jambudvīpa out of fear for Prince Sujāti; he manifested himself as lions, tigers, wolves, and other such beasts, with eyes wide open and pupils glaring, roaring loudly upon the earth, leaping and bounding about, coming forward with the intent to seize and devour him.
At that time, Śūḍānti, seeing the various birds and beasts displaying great ferocity, spoke in a low voice:
"If you wish to devour me, take me as you please; why do you act with such terror?"
At that time, Śakra, King of Devas, said:
"I am not a lion, tiger, or wolf; I am Śakra, Lord of Devas, and have come here to test you.
When the prince saw Śakra, King of Devas, he was filled with immeasurable joy.
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, asked the prince:
"You are one who can relinquish what is difficult to give, offering your own body's flesh and blood as an offering to your parents.
By virtue of such merit, do you pray to be reborn in heaven as a Māra king, a Brahmā king, a celestial king, a human king, or a Cakravartin?"
Suṣadri replied to Śakra, the Heavenly King, saying:
"I do not wish to be born in the heavens as a Māra king, a Brahmā king, a heavenly king, a human king, or a Cakravartin wheel-turning sage king."
"I seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path in order to deliver all sentient beings.
Śakra, King of Devas, said:
"You are greatly deluded."
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is achieved only after enduring arduous suffering for a long time.
How can you possibly endure such suffering?
Suṣadhu replied to Śakra, King of Devas, saying:
"Even if a glowing iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of my head, I would never, because of this suffering, retreat from the Unsurpassed Way.
King Śakra said: "These are but empty words; who would believe you?"
Suṣadhi then immediately made this vow:
"If I have deceived the Heavenly King Śakra, may the sores on my body never heal from beginning to end;
if it is not so, may my body be restored to its original state, and may my blood turn back to white and become milk."

Immediately his body was restored to its former state; the blood turned back into white milk, and his physical appearance became more upright and handsome than ever before. He rose and prostrated himself at the feet of Śakra, King of Devas.
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, immediately exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
I am not your equal.
You are diligent and courageous; you shall surely attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before long.
When you have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I pray that you will deliver me first.
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, immediately vanished from mid-air and was no longer seen.
Then, the king and his consort arrived at a neighboring kingdom.
At that time, the king of that country came out from afar to welcome them, providing all their necessities and giving them whatever they desired.

At that time, the Great King recounted the preceding circumstances to the other king, saying: "The manner in which my son nourished his parents with the flesh from his own body was exactly like this."

At that time, the neighboring king, having heard these words, was moved by Prince Sujāta’s ability to give what is so difficult to give—offering his own body, flesh, and blood as sustenance for his parents—such was the filial piety he displayed.
Moved by his filial piety and compassion, the king immediately assembled his fourfold army and returned with that monarch to attack Rāhula.
At that time, the Great King led his fourfold army and returned along the same route.
Upon arriving at the place where he was separated from Prince Sujāti, he thought to himself:
"My son must also have died!
I shall now collect his remains and return to my own country."
Raising his voice, he wept piteously and searched along the road.

Seeing from afar that his son’s body had been restored and was more handsome than ever before, he immediately went forward to embrace him; with grief and joy mingling within him, he said to the prince, "You are still alive!"
At that time, Śūradatta related all these matters in detail to his parents. His parents rejoiced, and they traveled together on a great elephant, returning to their own country.
"By the power of Śūradatta’s merit, he recovered his original kingdom and immediately installed Prince Śūradatta as king.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The father-king at that time was none other than my current father, King Śuddhodana."
The mother at that time is now my own mother, Lady Māyā;
the Prince Sujāti at that time is now I myself, Śākyamuni Tathāgata;
and the Heavenly King Śakra at that time was Ājñātakauṇḍinya.

When this "Chapter on Filial Support for Parents" was being preached, there were twenty billion bodhisattvas in the assembly who all attained the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*) to benefit all beings;
furthermore, there were twelve trillion bodhisattvas who all attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and there were others from the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of dust, who all attained the gates of dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, there were śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as numerous as the atoms in the sands of the Ganges, who abandoned the minds of the two vehicles and perfected the One Vehicle;
additionally, there were upāsakas and upāsikās, as numerous as atoms, some of whom attained the first fruit and others the second fruit;
and furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of people who resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, there were devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, some of whom resolved upon the mind of bodhi, while others resolved upon the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In this way, for the sake of all sentient beings, the bodhisattva performs difficult practices and ascetic austerities, filially supporting his parents, and even offers his own body’s flesh and blood as sustenance for them."
Such were the events.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the entire great assembly each attained benefit; filled with joy, they paid homage, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
The Sutra on the Great Expedient Means of the Buddha’s Requital of Gratitude, Volume One.
The Sutra on the Great Expedient Means of the Buddha’s Requital of Gratitude, Volume Two.
Translator unknown; included in the Later Han Records.
Chapter Three: The Chapter on Antidotes.
At that time, the World-Honored One was seated amidst the great assembly, like the orb of the sun, its brilliant radiance eclipsing the multitude of stars;

he was like a great dragon coiled upon Mount Lan-chun, its magnificent colors dazzling and resplendent, such that beholding him caused the eyes to reel and the mind to be confounded by his awe-inspiring majesty, his splendor so radiant that no metaphor could equal it.
It is like the light of a firefly that does not appear when the sun rises;
though the sun and moon possess hundreds of thousands of rays of light, compared to Śakra they are like a heap of ink.
Though Śakra possesses pure and wondrous white light, compared to the radiance possessed by Mahābrahmā, it is like potsherds and rubble compared to a *maṇi* jewel that glows in the night.
Although the Great Brahmā King possesses hundreds of thousands of pure and wondrous rays of light, compared to the radiance possessed by the Tathāgata, they are like a mass of ink. Why is this?
The Tathāgata’s halo extends seven feet, reaching far to illuminate the worlds of the ten directions.

Any sentient beings who encounter this light—those who are blind regain their sight, those with hunched backs regain their extension, and those who are crippled or paralyzed immediately regain their hands and feet; deluded beings come to perceive the True Word. In short:
all that is not to their liking shall be fulfilled according to their wishes.

At that time, there were seventy great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the assembly who rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and then withdrew to stand to one side. With one voice and in different mouths, they spoke a hundred thousand verses in praise of the Tathāgata.
Their names were: the Bodhisattva Acintya, the Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭaśabda, the Bodhisattva Smṛtivibhūti, the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti,
the Bodhisattva Anantaghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Mahāyaśas, and the Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhi.
The Bodhisattva Satyanāman, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhasiṃha, the Bodhisattva Ekacārin,
the Bodhisattva Muktasmṛti, as well as the Bodhisattva Jñānakośa, the Bodhisattva Susthitamati, the Bodhisattva Anantanimitta,
the Bodhisattva Prajñāprabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Vinarditamanas, the Bodhisattva Paritrātṛ, and the Bodhisattva Satyavikrama.
The Bodhisattva Sāgara, the Bodhisattva Padmavikrāmin, the Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati,
the Bodhisattva Puṇyaketu, the Bodhisattva Acintya, the Bodhisattva Śubhabrahmadatta, the Bodhisattva Ratnakarman,
the Bodhisattva Mahāpuṣpadhara, the Bodhisattva Sucintita, and the Bodhisattva Anantadharma...
The Bodhisattva Saṃjñāśravaṇamati, the Bodhisattva Vibhaktasaṃcaya, the Bodhisattva Vaiśvaramukha,
the Bodhisattva Daśabalaka, the Bodhisattva Daśabala, the Bodhisattva Mahāmahaḥkaruṇā, the Bodhisattva Anatikramaṇa,
the Bodhisattva Pravicarapraśānta, the Bodhisattva Tatra-sthita, and the Bodhisattva Asaṃkhyeya-deva...
The Bodhisattva Sāgaraprabha, the Bodhisattva Meruprabha, the Bodhisattva Ghanagarbha, the Bodhisattva Hetuvyativṛtti,
the Bodhisattva Ekacārin, the Bodhisattva Tejovikrāmin, the Bodhisattva Mahālokadhātu, the Bodhisattva Parvatarakṣita,
the Bodhisattva Tryadhvadhara, the Bodhisattva Guṇavikrama, and the Bodhisattva Yaśaḥkīrti.
Satsa, Suryaprabha Bodhisattva, Simhasena Bodhisattva, Rturaja Bodhisattva,
Simhagarbha Bodhisattva, Samdarśanāvatī Bodhisattva, Dūraprabha Bodhisattva, Parvatasimha Bodhisattva,
Upādānadatta Bodhisattva, Anabhibhūta Bodhisattva, and Varadhvaja Bodhisattva.
Sādhuprīti Bodhisattva, Dṛḍhavīrya Bodhisattva, Anupahata Bodhisattva, Yaśasvin Bodhisattva, Abhaya Bodhisattva, Asaṅgadeva Bodhisattva, Mahāpradīpa Bodhisattva,
Lokaprabhāsa Bodhisattva, Sūkṣmasvara Bodhisattva, and Guṇadhara Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sarva-vidyā-viśuddha, the Bodhisattva Tamonuda,
and the Bodhisattva Asama-pratima each made a vow before the Buddha,

saying: "After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, we shall protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, causing it to spread widely throughout the worlds of the ten directions so that it shall never be interrupted."
For what reason?

We now behold the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and wondrous physical form and its radiance; within that radiance, we have all been able to hear the inconceivable Buddha-dharma. Having heard the Dharma, we are freed from mental obstructions, our accumulated fetters are forever extinguished, and our bodies and minds are purified—resplendent like celestial gold, illuminating the myriad things.
Because we contemplate such merits and benefits as these, we conceive the thought of the Tathāgata as our Great Teacher and the thought of him as our compassionate father.
We shall constantly be mindful of the Buddha’s kindness and repay that kindness.

Why is this? Because having heard the True Dharma, they shall before long sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), turn the wheel of the True Dharma, and deliver all sentient beings; by virtue of all of them having heard the Dharma, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata addressed the entire great assembly, saying:

"These seventy bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *paramāṇu*-dust-like *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the distant past, have already made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the dust motes in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of worlds equal to the sands of the Ganges River. In the presence of these Buddhas, they have constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), making offerings to the Buddhas with minds untiring;
they have purified their bodies through loving-kindness and skillfully protected the Buddha-dharma."
Without abandoning great compassion, they constantly benefit all beings throughout the ten directions.

If there are sentient beings who, at the time of their death, hear the name of one bodhisattva, or two, three, four, or even up to seventy, and call upon these names with single-minded devotion, they shall, upon the end of life, attain rebirth in a buddha-field where they will be born by transformation from a lotus flower, far removed from lustful desire;
they shall not dwell within a womb and shall be free from all foulness and impurity.
His body is pure and possesses a wondrous fragrance;
he is respected by the multitude and cherished by all people.
Because he is respected and cherished by others, his mind is filled with joy.
Because of a joyful mind, one is able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
because one gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one is able to give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings;
having given rise to a compassionate mind, one subsequently also generates the mind to benefit sentient beings.

Having already developed the mind that benefits sentient beings, one further develops the mind that does not forsake sentient beings, the mind that benefits sentient beings, the mind that benefits both oneself and others, the mind that eliminates obstacles, the mind that pacifies afflictions, the mind that approaches virtuous friends with constant reverence, the mind that listens to the Dharma with single-minded focus, the mind that remembers, maintains, and contemplates the sublime meaning without forgetting, the mind that aspires to understand the meaning deeply from hearing little rather than aspiring to hear much without understanding the meaning;
next, one gives rise to the mind of faith in suchness and the mind of faith in the meaning of reality;
having given rise to the mind of the meaning of reality, one next gives rise to the mind of practicing according to what has been taught.
Having generated the mind that practices according to what has been taught, one next generates the mind of non-retrogression;
having generated the mind of non-retrogression, one then generates toward all sentient beings a mind of equal counteraction:

"Just as I do not delight in death, so it is for all those within the twenty-five states of existence in the three realms—whether with form or without form, four-legged or many-legged, down to the smallest ant and all classes of living beings."
For this reason, even at the cost of losing their own lives,
Bodhisattvas will never unjustly seize the lives of others.

"Just as I possess wealth, grain, silk, clothing, food and drink, elephants, horses, carriages, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, my body, hands, and feet, and I provide for and protect them while disliking it when others come uninvited to harm them, so it is with all sentient beings."
Therefore, a bodhisattva, even at the cost of losing their own body and life, will never give rise to the thought of plundering the clothing, wealth, food, or drink of sentient beings.
"Just as I do not delight in others' mistreatment of me—such as the deprivation of my beautiful sisters, wives, or concubines—all sentient beings are likewise.

For this reason, a bodhisattva, even at the cost of losing body and life, does not give rise to improper thoughts or defiled minds regarding the beautiful forms of others, much less engage in lewd or evil acts."
"Just as I do not delight in face-to-face disparagement, double-tongued speech, or harsh words, so it is for all sentient beings.
Therefore, even at the cost of losing their own bodies and lives, Bodhisattvas will never speak falsely, engage in double-tongued speech, or cause strife and discord between others."
"Just as I do not delight in being struck with sticks, stones, whips, canes, or subjected to flogging and torture, so it is for all sentient beings.
Therefore, even at the cost of losing his own life, a bodhisattva will never strike, stone, inflict bitter suffering upon, or torture sentient beings."
"Just as I do not delight in handcuffs, fetters, stocks, shackles, imprisonment, confinement, and binding—these various afflictions—all sentient beings are likewise."
Therefore, even at the cost of losing their own bodies and lives, Bodhisattvas will never place sentient beings in shackles, chains, or confinement, nor bind them with cangues and fetters.

Just as I do not delight in being oppressed by others, coerced by force, intimidated by threats or favors, or suppressed by those relying on their power and position—being held down and stifled so that I am not permitted to speak clearly before others to manifest my own innocence—all sentient beings are likewise.
Therefore, even at the cost of losing his own body and life, a bodhisattva shall never act unrighteously toward sentient beings.

"Just as I have been provided with offerings, honored, and praised by others, bringing me joy, so too shall I constantly bestow upon sentient beings clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all articles of comfort."

"If I undertake a great task—whether it be a matter concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha—and my power of wisdom is limited such that I cannot bring it to completion, I shall fall into sorrow and distress."
If there were a wise person who saw me thus grieving, resentful, and distressed, and realized that these states could not accomplish the task, they would say to me:
"Good son, do not be sorrowful."
"I shall provide whatever you require to fulfill your needs and enable you to accomplish your task.
Hearing these words, joy arose in my heart; therefore, I too shall constantly exhort and transform sentient beings for their benefit.
"Suppose I, as a king, were oppressed by thieves, water, fire, or government officials—whether imprisoned or confined—and my mind were filled with the poison of sorrow.
Then, there might be a wise person who, seeing me thus beset by such manifold sufferings and difficulties, would come to me and, with kind words of persuasion and exhortation, say:
'Do not grieve or suffer.'"

I shall intercede on your behalf with the king or the various ministers, or provide you with wealth and provisions, or employ other skillful means, so that you may be liberated and freed from all decline and affliction.
Upon hearing these words, my heart was filled with joy.
"Therefore, a Bodhisattva should always diligently cultivate the arts and master many skills:

music and performance, calendrical calculation and arithmetic, incantations and elixirs, riding elephants and horses, wielding halberds, spears, and arrows, and engaging in great martial prowess when advancing into or withdrawing from battle."
I possess such diverse and wondrous skills that no one among the common people, nor even kings or great ministers, dares to oppose my will.

Furthermore, I have clothing, wealth, food, and drink; pearl rings, hairpins, and bracelets; gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, agate, pearls, rubies, and mani-jewels; elephants, horses, palanquins, and carriages; male and female servants and attendants; palace ladies and beautiful women; flowing springs and bathing pools; and towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures—such various, exquisite, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of things as these.

Although the Bodhisattva possesses such majestic power and mastery, hundreds of thousands of arts and crafts, immeasurable treasuries of jewels, elephants, horses, and carriages, exquisite and beautiful women, as well as towers, pavilions, flowing springs, and bathing pools—all such implements for the five desires—his mind is free from greedy attachment. He always has few desires and is content, delighting in seclusion and tranquility;
he dwells in peaceful meditation and silent stillness beneath the trees of mountain forests.
Even when among great assemblies engaged in conversation and debate, his mind constantly enters the gates of remedial practice (*pratipakṣa*).
Although he harmonizes his light with that of ordinary beings amidst the mundane world, managing their assets, livelihoods, and profits, he never commits evil, but always benefits sentient beings.

If there are those who are impoverished or afflicted by various sufferings who come to the Bodhisattva seeking what they require, the Bodhisattva gives to them according to their wishes and to their hearts' content.

“If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who love and delight in the Buddha-dharma coming to draw near, make offerings, serve, and attend upon him—washing his feet, massaging him, laundering and drying his robes, providing tooth-sticks and water for rinsing, wiping down his bedding and seats, and folding away his blankets and pillows.

During the first and last watches of the night, they provided lamps and candles, as well as food before the meal, food after the meal, *tambala* (refreshments), *pūṣāṇīya* food, and *khādaniya* food, along with various drinks—namely, *ariṣṭa* liquor, *phalasa* fruit juice, grape juice, and black honey syrup.
Attending to him in this manner for as long as one week up to ninety days, they sought to entreat the Bodhisattva to listen to the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, although the Bodhisattva saw this person making such offerings, his heart felt no joy.
Why is this? Because for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Bodhisattva has sought the Buddha-dharma;
and because my mind toward all sentient beings is without increase or decrease.
By virtue of a heart of compassion;
because he abides in a mind of equanimity, he occasionally becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King, constantly guiding and transforming all sentient beings through the ten wholesome paths of action.

Out of devotion to my intention, they joyfully practice accordingly; after their lives end, they attain rebirth among humans or devas, experiencing the exquisite pleasures of the five desires, with dignity and noble status, all according to their hearts' content.
As they lie down or rise, enter the palace, mount horses, sport in gardens, delight themselves with music, and enjoy food and drink with joy, death suddenly arrives.

They grow old, fall ill, and pass away; their family members, both men and women, are consumed by grief and anguish, wailing aloud, beating their breasts with their hands, sometimes tearing out their hair, eating ashes and dust, fainting and collapsing to the ground, and carrying banners on carriages as they weep while escorting them away.

Once the funeral rites were completed, the men and women of the household supported one another with their hands as they returned to their home. Overwhelmed by grief and anguish, they collapsed to the ground for a long time; some fell ill, some became insane or delirious, and some even died.
"It brings great harm to those who live and offers no benefit to those who die.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, escorted by his attendants before and behind, traveled throughout the realm and saw all sentient beings undergoing such suffering and affliction; moved by compassion and sorrow, he spoke these words:
"As one who is a king, I rule over the land and govern all sentient beings."

"Although I have guided and transformed others through the ten wholesome actions, resulting in such subtle and exquisite fivefold desires, I cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, impermanence, and decay.
You should know that although I govern the country with the True Dharma, it has brought no benefit to sentient beings."
If you do not benefit sentient beings, how can you be called a Great Wheel-Turning King?
How can you be called a Great Compassionate Father?
And how can you be called a Great King of Physicians?
Why, furthermore, is he called the Great Guide?
A Great Guide leads by the correct path and shows the way to Nirvana, enabling others to attain the unconditioned and to enjoy constant peace and happiness.
At present, our names do not accord with our conduct.
It is like a person on the verge of death from thirst who runs hither and thither seeking cool water.
Seeing an empty well in the distance, his heart is filled with joy, and he thinks to himself:
"Now this body of mine has been restored to life. Why is this?
For had I not obtained water, my life would have departed before long."
"Now that I see this fine well, I shall surely obtain its pure, cool water to quench my parched thirst and save my life, which is in such urgent peril.
Having formed this thought, he ran swiftly toward it; upon reaching the well, he stripped off the clothes he was wearing and placed them all in one spot.
He entered the well to fetch water but found no water; he saw only venomous snakes, lizards, vipers, scorpions, centipedes, and their like, as well as shards, thorns, and various weeds and filth.
At that time, because the thirsty man had lost his original aspiration, he failed to obtain water; moreover, various venomous insects stung his body, and he immediately sought to exit the well.
However, the well was dilapidated and old, and as he fell, he tumbled into a steep and treacherous abyss.
That dilapidated well was as deep as the range of an arrow-shot, and it had neither ladders, steps, ropes, nor wooden poles.

Although he might leap upward, his momentum could not carry him high; his strength being exhausted and his breath failing, he would fall back to the bottom of the well to be devoured by various venomous snakes.
Before his life was cut short, he spoke these words:
"If I had known beforehand that this well contained no water, I would not have even looked at it, let alone gone to fetch from it.
Today’s bitter suffering is due to being deceived by the well."
At that time, when the Wheel-Turning Sage King saw the people—men and women of every household—separated from those they loved and suffering in distress, he spoke these words:
"Now, my own body is like an empty well; though it has the name of a 'well,' there is no water within."
Though there is a destination toward which I am proceeding, I have gained nothing; my life and body are lost, and my suffering is thus.

Although I now occupy the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, possessing the seven treasures and guiding and transforming others through the ten wholesome paths, governing the nation by means of the True Dharma.

Although they cause all sentient beings to be born among humans and devas to enjoy the exquisite pleasures of the five desires, they have not yet enabled them to escape birth, old age, sickness, and death; nor separation from those one loves, union with those one hates, or the sorrows, lamentations, suffering, and afflictions of mutual weeping.
However, this is my fault, not the fault of sentient beings.

Why is this? Because I lack the supramundane Dharma to benefit all sentient beings—though they follow me to inquire about and receive the wholesome Dharma, hoping to attain peace and happiness, they are in fact unable to cross over the ocean of suffering.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King again had this thought:
"My own person now is like a foolish and ignorant donor.
At that time, the donor encountered a great drought; for seven years there was no rain, and the trees withered and dried up.

At that time, there was a famine in the world; grain and rice were extremely scarce and expensive. The people were starving and devoured one another, drinking blood and eating flesh, harming and killing each other indiscriminately and without cause. Some fathers ate their sons, and some sons ate their fathers; parents, brothers, wives, children, and men and women all devoured one another.

"At that time, the great donor was traveling about for sightseeing when he saw various sentient beings who were emaciated by hunger, haggard, gaunt, and trembling; their strength was depleted and feeble, their countenances were withered, their hair was disheveled, and their bodies were thin and dark."

Upon their shoulders, one may see them carrying or hoisting nothing but the heads, hands, wrists, forearms, elbows, ribs, shoulders, kneecaps, thighs, and toes of the dead, or perhaps their livers, gallbladders, intestines, and stomachs.
At that time, the great donor asked in a low voice,
"What is this thing you are carrying on your shoulder? He replied:
"I am carrying the head, hands, elbows, joints, and wrists of a dead man. He asked, "What will you do with these arms,
elbows, joints, and wrists of a dead man that you are carrying?"
He replied: "Do you not know?
The weather is currently parched with drought, and the world suffers from famine. Grain is exceedingly expensive, and the people are so hungry that they devour one another."
"What I am carrying is my food and drink.
At that time, having heard these words, the donor’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; he fainted and fell to the ground.
He sprinkled cold water on his face, and after a long while he revived.
He asked again:
"Although this was your food, whose flesh was it?"
