At that time, having heard these words, the starving man raised his voice and wept bitterly; overcome with grief and despair, he replied to the donor, "It is beyond description."
How painful! How painful!
How strange!
"How extraordinary! Great donor!
I shall now speak to you with absolute sincerity."
As for what I carry, some say it is my father, some say it is my mother, some say it is my wife or children, and some say it is my brothers or close relatives and kinsmen.
At that time, each of those starving people spoke of their circumstances with complete sincerity:
"O Great Benefactor!
There is nothing else."
"Because of the conditions of hunger, we have come to devour one another.
When the Great Benefactor heard these words, he sighed with suppressed breath and addressed the multitude, saying:
"From this day forward, you must no longer eat each other's flesh."
"If you have any requirements for clothing, food and drink, various medicinal decoctions, or any other necessary items, gather all of you, the great assembly, at my house one week from now;
I shall provide you with whatever you require—clothing, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions for illness and weakness—giving to each according to your wishes."
Upon hearing this, the multitude felt joy in their hearts and exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is truly marvelous!
At that time, the donor returned to his home and summoned his wife, his children, his servants, and his laborers, until they had all assembled.
Amidst the multitude, with a serene and joyful countenance and gentle speech, he addressed his wife, children, and all his servants, saying:
"You should listen to what I say with a sincere heart."
"Do you know, sirs?
The weather is parched with drought and the world is suffering from famine; countless people are dying of hunger.
Yet our household has its storehouses overflowing and our grain and rice are in limitless supply."
"We can together take this opportunity to sow seeds in the field of merit.
Having heard this, his wife and children said, "Excellent!"
Excellent! How wonderful and immeasurably good!
Our very lives and bodies shall follow the donor’s, let alone the great storehouse of wealth, money, food, and drink.
At that time, the donor felt great joy in his heart and said:
"You all are now truly my unsurpassed companions on the path.
Excellent!"
Excellent! You all, each of you, should take charge of yourselves.
According to what ought to be done and according to what ought to be performed—do that which is to be done, and quickly perform that which is to be performed.
"After seven days have passed, I shall certainly ensure its completion.

At that time, having finished assigning each task, the patron himself went outside to observe everywhere, looking for a place with level and expansive ground where he might establish and arrange the sacrificial altar.
Immediately, he established it in a pure location, removing the saline soil, stumps, and thorns.
Once the ground was purified, he arranged upon it couches, mats, woolen rugs, and fine carpets.
Having immediately provided seating for the great assembly, he prepared five hundred magnificent elephants laden with food and drink, which were transported to the site of the offering altar.
The food and drink were as vast as mountains; the milk and curds were like lakes; and there were oils, cakes, dried meats, and all manner of delicacies, complete with a hundred flavors.
Furthermore, there were various garments, pearl rings, ornate bracelets, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures, all fully provided and having been completely arrayed.

After one week had passed, at the rising of the dawn—specifically on the morning of the seventh day—the bells were struck, the drums were beaten, and the great conch shells were blown, as they proclaimed in a loud voice:
"O Great Assembly!..."
"Everyone has gathered at the altar of the Great Benefactor.
At that time, when the multitude heard this proclamation, joy arose in their hearts as if they had received the grace of a worthy sage.

Having heard these words, they followed the sound toward the great assembly’s site of almsgiving. There, they took whatever they desired: clothing and robes, food and drink, pearl rings, hairpins and bracelets, a hundred kinds of medicinal decoctions, elephants and horses, and the seven treasures—selecting at will and taking as much as their hearts delighted in.
At that time, once the multitude had taken away all the goods given by the donor,
the donor, having felt joy in his heart, immediately returned home.
The members of his household, including his wife and children, lived in joy and happiness, delighting themselves with the five desires.
After seven days had passed, he heard people outside say:
"Those who previously received the robes, food, and drink offered by him have all died from the effects of the medicine."
Or those who had not yet died all uttered these words:
"How strange! How strange!"

Although this great donor possesses compassion and pity, providing them with all necessary clothing, bedding, food, and drink, these may indeed satisfy hunger and quench thirst at the time, thereby sustaining their life; yet after several days, the medicine will take effect and cause their death.
At that time, the great donor was filled with grief, anger, and distress, and he asked his wife and children:
"How did you prepare the food and drink, such that this foul poison caused it to fall into the meal?"
His wife, children, servants, and all his attendants replied,
"It is not so. [The man asked,] "If it is not so, from where did the poison come?"
He replied, "I do not know.
At that time, the donor again examined the matter for himself; he entered his home and proceeded to inspect it in order, where he saw a well whose opening was covered over with earth.
He asked the people, "What well is this?
and the family members replied:
"This donor, when he was a young child, raised three venomous snakes and dug this well to place them within it.
This well is the dwelling place of these venomous snakes; the water is also poisonous, and whoever drinks it will die."
When the donor saw this, he asked the laborers,
"When you were preparing the food earlier, did you not take water from this well to use for the meal?
The laborers replied:
"The food and drink were so abundant that at that time our resources were urgently needed; we drew this water to use for food and drink.
The great donor said, "How strange!
How extraordinary!"
"How strange!
That I, being now so foolish and lacking wisdom, should nourish this venomous snake and create this well of poison!
He then spoke to his wife and children:
"Go quickly and block them!
As for the three venomous snakes within, burn them to death!
At that time, the messenger went swiftly to eliminate them.

"At that time, after the donor had cleared away the poisoned well, he went outside to observe and saw those who had accepted his offerings dying from the onset of the medicine. With one voice and in unison, they all said:
'It is because of this donor who gave us poisoned food that we have so early lost our lives.'"
"If I had known beforehand that this food was poisoned, I would never have eaten it.
When the donor heard these words, his heart was filled with remorse.

Just as that Wheel-Turning Sage King, although he guides and transforms beings through the ten wholesome paths, causing all sentient beings to be reborn among humans and devas, and although they enjoy such subtle fivefold desires and exquisite happiness, is still unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, and death.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King immediately made this vow:

"I should now seek the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma and the supramundane dharma, so that all sentient beings may read, recite, and study them, thereby distancing themselves from birth and death and attaining nirvana."
“At that time, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, the Wheel-Turning Sage King issued a proclamation throughout Jambudvīpa:
‘Who understands the Buddha-dharma?
The Great Wheel-Turning King wishes to study and practice it.’”
Proclamations were issued everywhere, all stating that he was not there.
[The messengers] arrived at a small kingdom on the border, where there was a brahmin who understood the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the messengers went straight to him; having reached the brahmin’s location, they asked:
"Venerable sir, do you understand the Buddha-dharma? He replied, "I do."
At that time, the messenger prostrated with his head at [the king's] feet and reported:
"Great Master! The Great Wheel-Turning King wishes to entrust you with a final charge."
"I only pray that the Great Master will deign to extend his divine virtue and go to the place of that Wheel-Turning King.

Then the Wheel-Turning King went out from afar to welcome him, prostrating with his head at the Master's feet, and inquiring after his well-being: "I trust you have not been fatigued by the journey across these roads?"
He immediately invited him into the palace; in the main hall, he spread out the royal throne and requested the Great Master, saying, "I pray that you will sit upon this seat.
Thereupon, the Brahmin ascended the sublime throne and sat with his legs crossed in the full lotus posture.

At that time, when the Great King saw that the Great Master was firmly seated, he provided him with all necessities; having completed the offering of comfort, he joined his palms toward the Brahmin and said:
"Great Master!..."
"Do you understand the Buddha-dharma?
At that time, the brahmin replied,
"I understand the Buddha-dharma."
At that time, the Great King replied,
"O Great Teacher!
Please explain this for me."
The brahmin said, "The king is truly foolish!
I studied this Buddha-dharma for a long time, enduring diligent hardship before finally succeeding."
"Now, Great King, how is it that you wish to hear [this] directly?
At that time, the Great King said to the Master,
"What things do you require?"
The brahmin said, "Give me the offerings. The king said:
"What are these requisites for offering?
Are they clothing and food and drink?
Or are they gold, silver, and precious jewels?"
The Brahmin said, "I have no need for such offerings. The King said:
"If you do not require such offerings as these, would it be elephants, horses, and carriages?
Or a kingdom, a city, wife, and children?
Or music, singing, and dancing?"
The Brahmin said: "I have no use at all for such offerings as these.
If you can cut a thousand sores upon your own body, fill them with oil and fat, insert wicks, and light them as an offering, then I shall explain the Buddha-dharma to you."
"If you cannot do so, I wish to rise and depart.
Before the King had replied, [the man] immediately descended from his high seat.
At that moment, the Great King stepped forward, embraced him, and said in reply:
“Great Master! Please wait a moment longer.
At present, my wisdom is slight and shallow, and my merit is meager; allow me a short while to reflect within myself, and then I shall offer my service.”
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King reflected within himself and thought:
"Since beginningless worlds, I have lost my body countless times, yet never for the sake of the Dharma."
"Now this body of mine shall surely fall into decay and ruin, serving no purpose at all.
Today is precisely the time for that.
He then looked up and addressed the Great Master, saying:
"Whatever offerings are required, you must prepare them quickly.
At that time, the Great King entered the palace and announced to his consorts:
"I shall now part from you all."

When the ladies heard the king’s words, their hearts were startled and their hair stood on end; not knowing the reason for this, they asked the king in a low voice, "Where does Your Majesty wish to go?"
The King said, "Now I wish to carve out my own flesh to create a thousand lamps as an offering to the Great Teacher.

When the queens heard the King's words, they rolled about and fell to the ground, wailing aloud with loud cries; they fainted and vomited, and after a long while they regained their breath and addressed the Great King, saying:
"Among all things valued in the world, none is more precious than one's own body; it is revered and honored, nurtured according to the seasons, and guarded against any discomfort.
How is it that you now seek to destroy, harm, and cast it away?"
"The King is a man of wisdom; why is it that today he seems as if he has gone mad, possessed by a demon?
The King replied, "No."
"If it is not so, for what reason do you undergo such hardship to make this offering to this Brahmin, and what is your purpose?
The King replied to the Queen:
"I wish to seek the Buddha-dharma for the sake of all sentient beings."
"If you have done so for the sake of all sentient beings, why do you now abandon me?
The King replied to his consorts, "All affectionate attachments in this world must eventually end in separation; therefore, I now offer my own body as an act of供养 (dāna)."

I desire, for your sake and for the sake of all sentient beings, to kindle the lamp of great wisdom within this great chamber of darkness, to illuminate the black gloom of ignorance regarding birth and death, to sever the various fetters and afflictions of saṃsāra, to transcend all hardships, and to enable you to reach nirvāṇa.
"You all, why do you now act in opposition to my heart?

When the ladies heard the king's words, they remained silent and offered no reply; with hearts filled with grief, they sobbed and wailed aloud, tearing out their hair and clawing at their faces, crying out once more:
"We are of such meager fortune that we have lost our lord while he was still alive."
"The Heavenly King has five hundred princes, all of whom are handsome, intelligent, wise, and endowed with the marks of excellence.
Their father loves and cherishes them as he does his own eyes."
At that time, the Great King said to his sons:
"Today I wish to perform an offering; fearing that my life may not be sustained, I shall part from you."
"In the kingdom and among its people, all matters of royal law are governed by the eldest.
When the princes heard these words, their bodies, limbs, tendons, and veins were wracked with acute pain.
It was as if a man were choking, unable to swallow and yet unable to spit out;
with a faint voice, he asked his father the King,
"Why today do you forever abandon and turn your back on me, an orphan?"
Then the princes came forward, some embracing the king’s neck and others seizing his hands and feet, wailing aloud with voices of grief:
“How strange! How strange!”
"How is it that today we have forever lost our protection?
At that time, the Great King admonished and enlightened his sons, proclaiming for them that all worldly affection is subject to separation.
The sons replied, "Although it is as our father the king has said, our hearts are filled with longing and we cannot bear to part from you.
Your Majesty, today you should grant us one wish: that we, with these very bodies and lives, may offer ourselves to your majesty to serve as offerings for the Brahmin teacher."
The king said, "My sons are young and have not yet attained any understanding;
they are not yet capable of preparing such an offering."
"Just as I have now invited the Great Master from afar and he has consented to receive our offerings, you must not fail or err in this.
As a filial son, one does not contravene his father's intent; why do you now oppose my heart?"
When the princes heard these words, they raised their voices in a roar that startled the gods and spirits; they threw themselves to the ground with their whole bodies, like the collapse of Mount Tai.
At that time, the Great King again took his leave of all the minor kings and returned to the palace.

He went to the place where the Great Master was, removed the necklaces and exquisite garments from his body, set them aside to one side, and sat upright with a composed body. He then addressed the ministers, the minor kings, the five hundred princes, and the twenty thousand ladies:
"Among you now, who is able to gouge a thousand sores into my own body for my sake?"
The queen, the crown prince, and all the ministers, with one accord, spoke these words:
"We would rather gouge out both our own eyes with sharp knives than ever use our hands to gouge the King’s body."
At that time, the Great King felt sorrow and distress in his heart, thinking:
"I am now left alone and exposed;
among this great assembly, there is not a single person to assist me."
"At that time, the great king had a *caṇḍāla* who was by nature wicked and feared by all people.
Hearing the sound, he went toward them and said to the princes:
'Do not grieve or suffer for now.'"
"I have a skillful means by which I can ensure that the Great King's undertaking does not succeed.
If the undertaking fails, you shall return to rule your kingdom as before, no different from how it was.
Upon hearing these words, the princes felt great joy in their hearts.
At that time, the candāla went before the king and said to the Great King:
"Great King, what are you doing now, carving out lamps from your own body to make offerings to the Great Teacher?"
Then the caṇḍāla said, "As for the desire to gouge out my own body, I am able to do it.
When the king heard these words, joy arose in his heart, and he replied to the caṇḍāla:
"You are now truly my peerless companion on the Path.
At that time, the caṇḍāla stood before the king, gnashing his teeth and opening his mouth wide, crying out in a loud voice:

"Great King, you should know the law of killing: the head is severed, the neck is cut, the hands and feet are sliced off, the tendons are pulled and the ribs are extracted—the suffering is like this."
"Great King, can you endure this now?
When the king heard these words, his heart was filled with joy.
Then the caṇḍāla took up a knife shaped like a cow's tongue and, in the blink of an eye, carved a full thousand wounds all over the king's body.
At that time, the caṇḍāla thought that the king’s resolve had faltered; yet, finding it did not waver, he threw his sword to the ground and fled.
Then the Great King, having poured medicinal oil into all the sores on his body, took a piece of the finest, most exquisite cotton and wound it around them to serve as a wick.
At that time, when the great brahmin teacher saw the Great King performing these deeds, he thought to himself:
"I should now first proclaim the Buddha-dharma for the sake of the Great King."
Why is this? Great King, you must now kindle the lamps of your own body; I fear your life will not be sustained.
If your life is not sustained, who shall hear the Dharma?
Having reflected thus, he addressed the Great King, saying:
"Such is his diligence; he performs what is difficult to perform, practicing these ascetic austerities for the sake of hearing the Buddha-dharma."
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
"I shall proclaim the Buddha-dharma for the sake of the King.

Upon hearing these words, the King’s heart was filled with great joy, just as when a filial son has recently lost his parents and his grief is unspeakable, yet he rejoices immensely when those parents return to life.
When the king heard these words, he was likewise moved.
Thereupon, the brahmin immediately recited half a verse for the king concerning the law of arising and decaying:
"Whatever is born must inevitably die; The cessation of this is bliss."
"Having heard the Dharma, the king’s heart was filled with joy, and he addressed his princes and ministers, saying:
'If you all possess a heart of compassion for me, you should remember and uphold this Dharma for my sake.'"
Throughout all the lands, in every village, wherever there were people—whether in cities, towns, or along the streets—he proclaimed the King’s gracious command:
"All you people, take heed!
The Great Cakravartin King saw all people and all sentient beings submerged in the ocean of suffering, unable to emerge from evil.
He gave rise to great compassion for all beings, carving a thousand lamps into his own body to seek out half a verse.

All you people should now, out of gratitude for the Great King’s great heart of compassion, transcribe this verse, recite it, study it, contemplate its meaning, and practice according to its teaching.
When the people heard these words, their hearts were filled with joy, and with one voice they praised the Great King, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"The Great King is truly a father of great compassion, who practices these ascetic austerities for the sake of all sentient beings.
We ought to go quickly and transcribe [the scripture].
Whether on paper or silk, or upon stone, or on trees, tiles, rubble, or leaves—on pathways, at major thoroughfares, and wherever many people travel—we shall transcribe it everywhere."
All who saw or heard it conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the Great King lit a thousand lamps as an offering to the Great Master; their light shone afar throughout the worlds of the ten directions. From within the light of those lamps, there also issued forth sounds reciting this half-verse, and all who heard the Dharma conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
That light shone upward as far as the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the brilliance of that lamp was able to completely eclipse the radiance of all the devas.
When the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven saw this light shining from afar upon his palace, he immediately thought to himself:
"By what cause and condition has this light appeared?"

He then immediately observed the world with his divine eye and saw that this Great Wheel-Turning King had cultivated his mind with great compassion; for the sake of all sentient beings, he had carved out a thousand lamps from his own body to make offerings to the Great Teacher, in order to deliver all sentient beings.
"Therefore, we shall now go into the world to exhort, admonish, and assist him, so that his mind may be filled with joy.
They immediately descended into the world, transformed themselves into ordinary men, went to where the king was, and asked the Great King:
"You have carved lamps into your body and practiced this asceticism for the sake of half a verse; what is it that you intend to achieve?"
He replied, "Good son! For the sake of all sentient beings,
I cause them to resolve upon the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the transformed person immediately resumed his form as Śakra, his radiance and majesty blazing forth with brilliant clarity.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied to the Great King:
"By making such an offering, do you wish to seek the status of a Heavenly King?"
"Is it the Māra King or the Brahmā King?
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying:
"I do not seek the noble status of a human or a deva; I truly desire to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of all sentient beings."

"May those who are insecure find security; may those who are unliberated find liberation; may those who have not crossed over be delivered; and for those who have not attained the Way, may they be enabled to attain it.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Great King, are you not perhaps deluded now?"
"Those who seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi must undergo diligent suffering for a long time before they can achieve success; how is it that you now wish to seek the unsurpassed Way?"
He replied to Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"Even if a glowing iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of my head, I would never, because of such suffering, retreat from the Unsurpassed Way."
"Although you have now spoken these words, I do not believe you.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King immediately stood before Śakra, the Heavenly King, and made this solemn vow:
"If I do not truly seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and instead deceive Śakra, the Heavenly King, may my thousand wounds never heal."
"If it were not so, this blood would have turned to milk and the thousand sores would have been healed.
As these words were spoken, everything returned to its former state. King Śakra said:
“Excellent, Great King!
You are truly one of great compassion!
One who cultivates great compassion and practices such asceticism will, before long, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"When you attain *sambodhi*, you must deliver me first.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, emitted a great radiance that illuminated the king's body, and together with hundreds of thousands of devas, they simultaneously resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the five hundred princes saw that their father the king’s bodily wounds had healed, they were filled with immeasurable joy. They immediately came forward, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Joining their palms toward their father, they spoke in unison with a single voice:
“It is unprecedented!
"Now our father, the King, is truly great in compassion, pitying all beings.
The King replied to the princes:
"If you are truly filial sons, you should resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

When these princes heard these words, joy arose in their hearts; moved by the profound kindness of their father, the King, they immediately gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon hearing his voice.
"The twenty thousand ladies and the hundreds of thousands of court maids were likewise.
At that time, among the assembly, there were sentient beings equal in number to the sands of seventy Ganges Rivers who all resolved their minds upon the path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, immeasurable devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, having seen and heard this, all gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and departed with joy.

Chapter Four: Generating the Bodhicitta In the *Mahā-upāya-buddha-pratyupakāra-sūtra*, Chapter Four: Generating the Bodhicitta. At that time, there was a great bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named King of Joy (*Ratnarāja*). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms and looked up toward the Tathāgata, saying these words:
“How does a bodhisattva recognize kindness and repay kindness?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Joyful King: "Good son,
listen attentively!"
Listen attentively!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who recognizes their debt of gratitude should resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
one who repays that debt should likewise instruct all sentient beings to cause them to resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one arouses the bodhicitta, how does one arouse it?
For what reason, O son of good family, is a bodhisattva able to arouse it?
Son of good family!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva first gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they establish a great vow and speaks thus:

"When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall bring great benefit to all sentient beings; I must certainly establish all sentient beings within Great Nirvāṇa, and I shall further teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them all to be fully endowed with the Prajñāpāramitā. This is called self-benefit, and it is also called benefiting others."

Therefore, one who first resolves upon bodhicitta is said to possess the causal conditions for bodhi, the causal conditions for sentient beings, the causal conditions for the true meaning, and the causal conditions for the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; they grasp the root of all wholesome dharmas.

Therefore, a bodhisattva is called "Great Goodness" and is also called the "Root of Virtue for All Sentient Beings," for they are able to destroy all evils of the three karmas—body, speech, and mind—of all sentient beings.
Of all vows existing in the mundane world, as well as all vows existing in the supramundane world, none can surpass Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; such a vow is unsurpassed and supreme.
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first gives rise to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are five things:
first, their nature;
second, their practice.
Third, the objective sphere;
fourth, the merit; fifth, the increase.
If a bodhisattva is able to give rise to the bodhicitta, they are then named a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; they will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the initial arousal of the bodhicitta is itself able to encompass all wholesome dharmas.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva arouses the bodhicitta and practices, they gradually attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
if they do not arouse the mind, they will ultimately never attain it.
Therefore, the arousal of the mind is itself the root of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see suffering sentient beings, they give rise to a heart of compassion; thus, by virtue of this heart of loving-kindness and compassion, they are able to arouse the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and by virtue of that mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they are able to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Because one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the arousal of the mind is called the root.

Because one practices the bodhisattva precepts (*śīla*) due to having aroused the mind of enlightenment, this arousal of the mind is called the root and the cause; it is called the branch and the leaf, and it is also called the flower and the fruit, and is further called the seed.
The bodhisattva’s resolve may be ultimate or non-ultimate. That which is ultimate never regresses or falls away until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
that which is non-ultimate involves regression and falling away.
There are two kinds of regression:
ultimate regression and non-ultimate regression.
Ultimate regression refers to those who ultimately cannot resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor can they seek out or cultivate its teachings.
Regarding those who do not ultimately regress: they seek the bodhicitta and cultivate its methods.
There are four kinds of this bodhicitta.

First, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family sees or hears of the inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, at that time they immediately give rise to a mind of faith and reverence, and think to themselves:
"The deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are inconceivable.
If these inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were attainable, then I too would have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Therefore, one should mindfully contemplate bodhi with a sincere heart and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
Furthermore, there are those who do not witness the inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, yet hear the secret treasury of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
having heard it, they immediately give rise to a heart of faith and reverence."
Because they have gained faith, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and the *mahā-prajñā*, they resolve their minds upon enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

Furthermore, there are those who do not see the inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, nor hear the Dharma; yet, seeing the time when the Dharma is perishing, they again form this thought:
"The unsurpassed Buddha-Dharma can extinguish the immeasurable suffering and affliction of sentient beings and bring about great benefit."
Only the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to cause the Buddha-dharma to abide long and not perish.
I, too, shall now resolve to attain bodhicitta, so that all sentient beings may be freed from their afflictions.
"May I undergo great suffering in this body for the sake of protecting and upholding the Buddha-dharma so that it may long abide in the world; thus I resolve upon the Bodhicitta.

Furthermore, there are those who do not see the time when the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Dharma perish, but see only the sentient beings of the degenerate age, who are possessed of heavy afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion;
who lack shame and remorse; and who are stingy and miserly.
Envy, hatred, delusion, suffering, affliction, and so forth;
lack of faith, wrong views, doubt, indolence, and so forth.
Having observed these things, one immediately forms this thought:
"In this age of great evil, sentient beings are unable to cultivate wholesome deeds.
In such a degenerate time, they cannot even give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles, let alone the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
I shall now resolve to attain bodhicitta; having resolved to attain bodhicitta, I shall then instruct all sentient beings to cause them to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King of Joy again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva knows gratitude and spontaneously gives rise to the bodhicitta;”
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s repayment of kindness, which consists in teaching all sentient beings to resolve upon bodhicitta:
when the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, first resolved upon bodhicitta during his time in saṃsāra, for what reason did he do so?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! In the past, during immeasurable kalpas of saṃsāra, because you gave rise to physical, verbal, and mental karma through heavy afflictions, you fell into the eight great hells, namely:”
The A-ha-ha hell, the A-pa-pa hell, the A-da-da hell, the Copper Cauldron and Great Copper Cauldron, the Black Rock and Great Black Rock, and so on, up to the Hell of the Fire Chariot.
At that time, I fell into the Hell of the Fire-Drawn Cart, where I was yoked alongside two others to pull the cart.

Ox-head Ābāng sat upon the cart with his lips sealed and teeth gnashing; he stared with wide eyes and blew forth fire from his mouth, eyes, ears, and nose, from which smoke and flames rose together. His body was exceptionally large, his arms and legs were coiled and knotted, and his complexion was a dark crimson-black. Holding an iron staff in his hand, he followed us and lashed us with it.
At that time, despite my suffering and pain, I exerted myself to pull the cart, striving with all my might to move forward.
My companions were weak and lacked strength, lagging behind.
Then, Ox-Head Ābāng pierced my belly with an iron fork and whipped my back with an iron staff; blood flowed forth, bathing me as it streamed down my body.
That person, in intense agony, cries out with a loud voice; the pain being unbearable, they may call upon their parents or call upon their wife and children.
Although they utter such cries, it brings no benefit to themselves.
When I saw this, I experienced great suffering and distress; out of compassion and because of the arising of a mind of loving-kindness, I gave rise to the bodhicitta.
For the sake of these sinful beings, I entreated Ox-Head Ābanga: "These sinners are truly pitiable."
"Please show me a little more compassion; grant me your mercy and pity.

Upon hearing this, Ox-Head Ābāng conceived a mind of wrath and immediately thrust a iron fork forward to pierce my neck. At that very moment, my life ended, and I was immediately freed from the offenses of a hundred kalpas within the Hell of the Burning Chariots.
"Because I have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I am immediately released from the retribution of the Ox-Cart Hell.
The Buddha told King Nandivardhana:
"The one who pulled the ox-cart was none other than my own self in this present life."
Because they have resolved their minds on Bodhi, they shall swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, one should know that when all sentient beings resolve their minds on Bodhi, the causes are not uniform:
some do so through a mind of loving-kindness, while others do so through a mind of anger;
Whether due to a mind of generosity or a mind of stinginess;
whether due to joy or affliction;
or due to separation from those one loves, or union with those one hates.
It may be due to associating with virtuous friends, or due to evil companions;
it may be due to seeing the Buddha, or due to hearing the Dharma.
Therefore, one should know that the arousal of the bodhicitta by all sentient beings varies from one to another.
"King of Joy!
You should know that such is the manner in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas recognize kindness and repay their debt of gratitude.
When this Dharma was spoken, eighteen thousand people gave rise to the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Among the entire great assembly, there were those who attained the stage of *srotāpanna* up to *arhat*.

At that time, devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans were likewise able to resolve upon the mind of a *śrāvaka* or a *pratyekabuddha*; hearing the Dharma, they rejoiced, prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
The Sutra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means, Scroll Two.
The Sutra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means, Scroll Three.
Translator unknown; included in the Later Han Records.
Chapter Five: On Discussion.

At that time, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for his mother, Lady Māyā, and the assembly of devas for ninety days; meanwhile, within Jambudvīpa, no one knew the whereabouts of the Tathāgata for those same ninety days.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers, exerted all his might and searched throughout the ten directions, yet he still did not know [the Tathāgata’s whereabouts].
Aniruddha, foremost in the divine eye, surveyed the trichiliocosm throughout the ten directions, yet he likewise could not see him.
Even the five hundred great disciples, unable to find the Tathāgata, were filled with grief and distress.

King Udayana, longing for the Tathāgata and harboring grief and anguish in his heart, immediately used ox-head sandalwood to fashion an image of the Tathāgata’s physical body; he paid homage to it and made offerings to it, no differently than when the Buddha was still present.
At that time, the Great King summoned the six teachers and consulted them regarding the whereabouts of the Tathāgata.
Then the six teachers spoke thus:
"Great King!..."
"You should know, Great King, that this śramaṇa Gautama is merely a creation produced by magical illusion.
The nature of illusory transformations lacks any true reality."
"You should know that our scriptures and the four Vedas state:
'Every thousand or two thousand years, a phantom person shall appear in the world.
This śramaṇa Gautama is precisely that person."
At that time, Anuruddha went to the Great King and said to him:
"Great King, you should know that the Tathāgata is currently staying near the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; seven days from now, he shall return to Jambudvīpa."

Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with joy; he issued a proclamation throughout the land to sweep and sprinkle the grounds, burn incense, and hang silken banners and canopies, as the people gathered together in competition to prepare various offerings of diverse delicacies, flowers, incense, and music.
At that time, the six heretical teachers saw the great crowd gathered together, providing various offerings and all kinds of delicacies.
The six teachers asked, "O people,
in making these offerings, do you wish to invite the king?"
"Is he the prince? He replied, "No."
"If it is not so, have you invited a great minister?
Or a brahmin or a householder?
If it is not so, is it a gathering of kinsmen?"
He replied, “No. I wish to invite the Buddha.”
The six teachers asked, "Who is this Buddha? He replied:
"O Omniscient One," he said again, "Who is this Omniscient One?"
He replied, "O Great Compassionate Father! Do you not know?"
The lineage of King Śuddhodana is the most noble and preeminent; from the beginning of the kalpa until now, they have been inherited through direct succession as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).
In recent times, for two generations, they have not been universal monarchs; yet, though they are no longer universal monarchs, they remain kings of Jambudvīpa.
There were three brothers; the eldest was named King Śuddhodana,
the next younger brother was named King Droṇodana,
and the youngest was named King Amṛtodana.
King Śuddhodana fathered two sons: the elder was named Siddhārtha, and the younger was named Nanda.
King Droṇodana likewise fathered two sons: the elder was named Devadatta, and the younger was named Ānanda.
King Amṛtodana had a daughter named Amṛtā.

At that time, the eldest brother, Prince Siddhārtha, went out of the city to observe the world; having witnessed the afflictions of old age, sickness, and death, he became filled with sorrowful reflection and ceased to eat.

Reflecting with compassion that all human life must encounter such afflictions—whether noble or base, among all sentient beings possessing form—none can escape them, he immediately departed the palace city at night.
He practiced asceticism for six years beneath the Bodhi tree, after which he attained all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*); therefore, he is titled the All-Knowing One (*Sarvajña*).
He attained Buddhahood through solitary awakening, becoming endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique dharmas, and even the knowledge of all modes.
Seven days after his birth, his mother’s life came to an end, and he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
"The Buddha has been preaching the Dharma for his mother for ninety days; after one more week, he shall return to Jambudvīpa.
When the six heretical teachers heard these words, jealousy arose in their hearts, and they were filled with grief, resentment, and distress.
Immediately, the assembly of the six teachers gathered together and discussed among themselves, saying:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama returns to Jambudvīpa, all the people will surely abandon us and provide offerings to Gautama."
"We are destitute and alone; we fear we shall not survive.
At that time, the six teachers again thought to themselves:
"We should now go quickly among the great multitude and proclaim these words:"
"O people, you should know!
This śramaṇa Gautama truly knows nothing.
A mere yellow-mouthed child who has recently departed from the palace of the Śākyas, he claims under the Bodhi tree to have attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā)."
You should know that these are but false words. Why is this so?

King Ajātaśatru came to invite Gautama, yet the only offering he provided was horse-barley. Gautama did not recognize it as evil and nevertheless accepted the invitation; thus, you should know that he is not omniscient.
Furthermore, he asked Ānanda:
"How many days remain until the end of the summer retreat? Ānanda replied:
"Seven days remain. Furthermore, he asked Ānanda:
"Why is there such a great clamor of crows and birds within the Jeta Grove?"
Ānanda said: "Various birds pecked at and ate them.
Only seven days after they were born, their mother passed away."
For this reason, you should know that such a person is one of meager fortune and is also an extremely wicked person. Why is this?
Because he has brought about the death of his own mother upon his birth.
Furthermore, he was neither compassionate nor filial, nor did he offer any support; despite receiving daily provisions morning and night, he instead abandoned her and entered the deep mountains.

He is likewise a person devoid of gratitude, for although his father the King took Gopī as his wife, he ultimately failed to observe the rites of a husband toward her, causing Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī to endure great suffering and distress.
Therefore, you should know that this Śramaṇa Gautama is ungrateful and does not acknowledge kindness;
his assembly has no distinction of rank, for each of his five hundred disciples claims to be the foremost.
Since the Master has no fixed dharma, his disciples likewise have no specific practice.

Even one who merely knows the number of grains, such as the bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta, is called foremost; the brilliant and wise Śāriputra is included among them, as is the dull-witted Bhadrapāla (Panthaka) bhikṣu.
Even the person of few desires, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, is included among them, as is the unchaste and wicked woman Utpalavarṇā from the city of Śrāvastī.
Even the young and ignorant child Cūḍapanthaka entered therein; even the extremely aged Subhadra, one hundred and twenty years of age, entered therein;
even the noble and honored Śākyas entered therein; and even the most lowly man among those who carried away filth in Rājagṛha entered therein.

Therefore, you should know that within the Dharma of Gautama, people of all sorts and conditions jostle one another to enter; there is no distinction between the noble and the lowly, and it is not worthy of reverence.
It is just like a great wind blowing various tree leaves until they are gathered together in one place—such is the Buddhist Dharma of Gautama.
"Just as various birds follow those discarded clothes and food left behind by people in the world, so do the followers of Gautama take whatever they find and eat it.
How is it that you people today wish to invite Gautama?"
When the multitude heard this, they were like the great earth, incapable of being shaken or moved.

The assembly gazed up at the Tathāgata with longing; although they heard the six teachers speak in such a manner, their minds remained like adamant, without increase or decrease, as they thirsted for the Tathāgata like one parched with thirst requires a drink.
After seven days had passed, the Tathāgata descended from heaven to Jambudvīpa.
Countless hundreds of thousands of devas followed the Tathāgata, emitting great radiance;
moved by his supernormal power, they performed hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial music.
Even all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the entire great assembly gathered like clouds, prostrating and making offerings.
At that time, King Udayana, surrounded by his great assembly, went out from afar to welcome the Tathāgata; he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that moment, the followers of the six heretical teachers gathered together and thought to themselves:
"Now our misfortune is about to arrive."
Although I have proclaimed these words among the multitude, they do not believe or accept them.
Now I shall go again before the great assembly of devas and humans to announce this; then its purity may be known.

At that time, after the six teachers had formed this thought, they went together with their retinue of eight thousand people, surrounding him before and behind, to approach the great assembly; having arrived, they withdrew and sat to one side.

At that time, there was also a son of a gandharva named Gandhamāla, who played a lute made of the seven precious substances and approached the place where the Tathāgata was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and performed music with drums and strings, singing songs that produced a subtle and wondrous sound; this sound was harmonious and elegant, gladdening the hearts of the multitude.
The śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others unconsciously moved their bodies and began to dance, while Sumeru, the king of mountains, surged, submerged, rose, and fell.

At that time, the Tathāgata entered the Samādhi of Having Characteristics; by the power of this samādhi, he caused the sound of the lute to be heard throughout the trichiliocosm—the sound fully expounding suffering, emptiness, impermanence, impurity, and non-self.

When heedless sentient beings hear this wondrous voice fully expounding how the Tathāgata knows gratitude and repays it, and how he practiced filial piety and support for his parents throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they are transformed.
All sentient beings followed the sound to Jambudvīpa and went to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the great assembly gazed up at the Tathāgata, their eyes never for a moment turning away.
At that time, the Tathāgata remained in silent meditative absorption, and the entire great assembly likewise remained silent.

From within the great assembly, a stupa made of the seven precious gems emerged from the earth and hovered in mid-air; countless banners and streamers hung above it, and hundreds of thousands of jeweled bells rang out spontaneously without being struck. As a gentle breeze blew upon them, they produced a subtle and wondrous sound.
At that time, the great assembly, seeing this jeweled stupa emerge from the earth, had doubts arise within their minds:
"By what causes and conditions has this jeweled stupa emerged from the earth?"
The assembly of śrāvakas, including Śāriputra and the others, exhausted their powers of thought and deliberation, yet they likewise did not know.
Even the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have long resided in this Sahā world, up to and including Maitreya Bodhisattva, likewise did not know.
At that time, the six teachers thought to themselves:
"For what reason and by what cause has this precious stupa appeared?
If someone comes to question me about it, I shall not know the answer."
"If one does not know this, how can one further be called 'all-knowing and all-seeing'? He then thought again:
"Gautama, why do you not quickly expound this matter for the sake of the great assembly?"
At that time, the Tathāgata emerged from samādhi.
Śakra-devānām-indra, the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, immediately spread celestial robes upon the lion throne.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata ascended this seat and sat cross-legged, like King Sumeru standing amidst the great ocean.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva observed the minds of the assembly; they all harbored doubts, and he himself had not yet fully understood.
He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition has this jeweled stūpa emerged from the earth?
The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Having appeared in the world, he taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, causing them all to become firm in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī.
Its great king was wise, benevolent, and virtuous; he always governed the country with the True Dharma and did not oppress the people.
The king was the ruler of sixty small kingdoms and eight hundred villages.
The king had no sons at all.
He personally made offerings and served mountain deities, tree spirits, and all manner of gods for twelve years, without ceasing or resting, seeking to obtain a son.
The first queen then perceived that she was pregnant; when ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son.
The boy was handsome, endowed with all the marks of excellence.
Once he was born, the various ministers and minor kings were summoned to examine his physiognomy for signs of good or ill fortune, and he was immediately given a name.
Because the crown prince was by nature virtuous and free from anger, he was named Kṣāntivādin (Enduring Patience).
As Prince Kṣāntivādin grew older, he delighted in practicing generosity; he was intelligent, compassionate, and benevolent, giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.

At that time, the Great King had six chief ministers whose natures were violent and cruel, deceitful, treacherous, and sycophantic; they acted with tyranny and lacked the Way, causing the people to grow weary and distressed.
These six ministers, knowing their own conduct was contrary to principle, constantly harbored jealousy and malice toward the Crown Prince.
"At that time, the Great King was afflicted by a grave illness; he was emaciated with suffering and his life hung by a thread.
Prince Kṣāntivādin went to inform the ministers:
'Our father, the King, is critically ill; what should we do now?'"
Upon hearing this, the ministers were filled with resentment and replied to the prince,
"The King’s life will not last long.
For what reason?"
"Because one seeks a wondrous medicine but cannot find it, you should know that the departure of life is not far off.
Upon hearing this, the Prince was overcome with anguish; he fainted and fell to the ground.
Then the six great ministers entered the quiet chamber and deliberated together, saying:
"If we do not remove Prince Kṣāntivādin, we shall never attain peace and security."
Having had this thought, the chief minister said,
"Prince Kṣāntivādin has no fault that can be removed.
Another minister spoke again:
"I possess a skillful means to remove it.
He then went to the Prince's location and reported to him, saying:
"I was just outside, seeking medicinal herbs among sixty small kingdoms and eight hundred villages, but I could not find any at all."
The Prince asked, "What is this medicinal herb you seek?
The minister replied:
"Prince, you should know that the one who seeks the medicinal herbs is precisely this man whose eyes and marrow must be taken from birth until his death, provided he harbors no anger.
If these medicines are obtained, the King’s life will be preserved;
if they are not obtained, his life will not last much longer."
"In all the kingdoms, there is no such person as this.
Having heard this, the Prince felt sorrow and distress in his heart, and immediately replied to the great minister:
"It seems that my own person is such a person."
"Why is this? Since my birth, I have never once felt anger.
The minister said:
"If the Prince is indeed such a person, this matter is likewise difficult.
Why is this? For there is nothing in the world more highly esteemed than one's own body."
The Prince said: "It is not as the ministers say.

If it would cause my father, the King, to recover from his illness, even if I had to sacrifice hundreds of thousands of bodies, it would not be difficult; how much less so this foul body of mine today?"
The minister replied,
"Such a matter shall follow the Prince's own will.
At that time, Prince Kṣānti felt great joy in his heart and thought to himself:
"If this medicine can cure the illness of our father, the King, you should prepare it with all haste.
Prince Kṣāntivādin then entered the palace, went to his mother’s quarters, prostrated himself at her feet, joined his palms toward her, and spoke these words:
"I now wish to offer this body of mine as a medicinal remedy to treat my father, the King."
"Fearing that my life may not be preserved, I have therefore parted from my mother.
I pray that you, Mother, do not grieve or suffer, nor harbor longing for your son.

Upon hearing these words, his mother’s heart was overcome with fainting; she lost her bearings in all four directions, like a person choking who can neither swallow nor spit out, unable to urge him forward nor restrain him.
She immediately went forward and embraced her crown prince, fainting from grief; she sprinkled cold water on his face, and after a long while, he revived.
At that time, the crown prince said to his mother:
"The life of our father, the King, cannot endure for long; it may end at any moment."
"You should prepare it immediately and have the King take it.
At that time, the Prince summoned the great ministers and the various minor kings, and in the midst of the great assembly, he spoke these words:
"I now bid farewell to this great assembly."
At that time, the minister immediately summoned a caṇḍāla to break the bone and extract the marrow, and to gouge out both eyes.
Then, the minister ground this medicine and presented it to the Great King.
The king immediately took it and his illness was cured.
Once he had recovered, he asked his ministers:
"From where did you obtain this wondrous medicine that has removed my suffering and preserved my life?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"This medicine has been prepared by Prince Kṣānti alone;
it is not something that can be accomplished by the power of the ministers."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end;
in a low voice, he asked his ministers, "Where is the Crown Prince Kṣāntivādin now? The ministers replied:
"The Prince is now outside; his body is wounded and his life is not far from its end.
Upon hearing these words, the King raised his voice and wept aloud:
"How strange! How tragic!"
"How strange! Alas!
he cried, throwing himself to the ground until dust covered his body:
"One such as I am now is truly devoid of feeling."
"How can one possibly take this son's medicine?
Having gone to where the son was, he found that his life had already ended.
The King, the Queen, and the various ministers and subjects formed a vast assembly, surrounding him from all sides.
His mother was filled with anguish and threw herself upon the corpse, crying:
"Because of the various transgressions and evils I committed in past lives, my son’s body must now endure such suffering.
Why does my own body not crumble into dust, rather than causing my son to lose his life?"

At that time, the father king and the various minor kings immediately used ox-head sandalwood to pile up a funeral pyre, cremated all the bodily relics of the Prince, and further erected stupas made of the seven precious gems to offer them worship.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, the sons of good family, and the great assembly:
"You should know that the Great King of Vārāṇasī at that time was none other than my father, Śuddhodana;
the mother at that time was none other than my mother, Māyā."
The Prince Kṣāntivādin was my very self in this life.

For immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the Bodhisattva served and supported his parents with clothing, food and drink, housing, bedding, and even his own flesh, marrow, and bones; such were his deeds, and by these causes and conditions, he attained Buddhahood for himself.

This jeweled stupa that has now emerged from the earth is precisely where I, for the sake of my parents, gave up these marrow bones and my very life, and immediately erected a stupa at this spot to make offerings.
"Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I shall immediately appear before you.

At that time, within the great assembly, immeasurable humans, devas, nāgas, and spirits, having heard these words, were filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy; their eyes brimmed with tears as they praised the Tathāgata’s hundreds of thousands of merits with one voice. They then immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings resolved to become *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
Furthermore, immeasurable people attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the path of arhatship;
moreover, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who would before long attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata now truly practices filial support for his parents.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva originally knew the virtues of a mother; because his original vow was such, he brought forth the body of a Tathāgata.
Because he had brought forth the Tathāgata and fulfilled his original vows, and because [the world] was unable to bear his prostrations, he passed away.
At that time, the great assembly, with one voice and in unison, praised Māyā: "Excellent, Māyā!"
"He shall attain birth as a Tathāgata, peerless among gods, humans, and the world.
At that time, Gadhāmāla rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"What meritorious deeds did Lady Māyā cultivate,
and by what causes and conditions was she able to give birth to the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:
"Listen well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

"In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān; he appeared in the world, and [so on] until the true Dharma and the semblance Dharma had both perished."
At that time, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī.

Not far from the city was a mountain called Āryāyatana (The Abode of the Noble Ones), so named because hundreds of thousands of pratyekabuddhas dwelt within its mountains, and immeasurable rishis possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) also resided there.
Because many sages and holy ones dwell within it, it is called the Mountain of the Holy Abode.
On that mountain, there was one sage who resided in the southern cave, and another sage who resided in the northern cave.
Between the two mountains there was a spring, and by the side of that spring was a flat stone.
At that time, the seer from the southern cave, having washed his clothes and rinsed his feet upon this stone, returned to his dwelling.
Not long after he had departed, a female deer came to drink from the spring water.
She arrived in succession at the place where the clothes were being washed and drank the wash-water used for removing stains from the garment upon that stone.
Having drunk the liquid from the filth on his clothes, he turned his head back and licked the place where he had urinated.
At that time, the female deer soon became pregnant and gave birth when the months were full.
Regarding the method by which the deer gave birth: she returned to the very place where she had originally conceived.
She went back to the waterside and stayed upon her original rock; there, crying out piteously and rolling about, she gave birth to a daughter.
At that time, the seer heard the deer’s piteous wailing and loud cries.

Hearing the sound of the deer’s great lamentation, the seer from the southern cave felt compassion in his heart; he immediately went out to look and saw that the female deer had given birth to a daughter.
At that time, the mother deer rolled about and licked her; seeing the seer approaching, she abandoned her and departed.
Then the seer beheld this girl, whose physical form was upright and handsome, and who was endowed with all the marks of a human being.

Having witnessed this, he felt compassion in his heart; he immediately wrapped the child in a garment of grass, brought him back, and gathered various exquisite fruits to nourish him according to the season. Gradually the child grew until he reached the age of fourteen.
His father, out of affection and concern for him, constantly maintained a perpetual fire so that it would never be extinguished.
One day, however, he was not careful and caused the fire to go out.
After his father had finished rebuking and scolding him, he said to his daughter:
"Since I was born, I have never allowed this fire to go out.
Why have you extinguished it today?"
"There is fire in the northern cave; you may go there to fetch it.
At that time, the Deer Woman followed her father’s instruction and went to the northern cave.
With every step she raised her foot, lotus flowers sprang forth; following her tracks, they were arranged in orderly rows like the lanes of a city street.
She went to the northern cave and requested a small amount of fire from that rishi.
At that time, the rishi, seeing the woman’s merit—such as the lotus flowers growing beneath her feet—replied:
"If you wish to obtain fire, you must circumambulate my cave seven times, keeping it to your right."
The ranks were arranged in clear and distinct order; as he took each step, lotus flowers sprang up beneath his feet.
After circumambulating seven times, he said to his daughter:
"If you wish to obtain fire, you must return by this right-hand path."
"I shall give you fire.
At that time, in order to obtain the fire, the Deer Woman departed according to his instructions.

Not long after the woman had left, the King of Vārāṇasī, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of ministers and a multitude of millions, with a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen, entered the mountains for a hunt, pursuing herds of deer.
King Bārāṇasī alone mounted his famous elephant and went to the hermitage of the seer at the northern cave; there he saw lotus flowers arranged in rows surrounding the cave.
At that time, the great king felt joy in his heart and exclaimed: "Excellent!"
Excellent! O Great Virtuous One, Divine Seer!
O Great Seer, Guide!
"The merit is so sublime; such is its nature!
At that time, the seer addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
"You should know that these lotus flowers are not something I am capable of producing.
The king asked,
"If it was not the Great Master, then by whom were they made?"
He replied, "Great King!
This seer of the southern cave has fathered and raised a daughter whose beauty and form are upright and perfect, endowed with all auspicious marks, such as are rarely found in the world."
"As that woman walked, lotus flowers sprang up beneath every step of her feet.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately went to the southern cave, saw the seer there, and prostrated himself at his feet.
At that time, the rishi came forth and inquired:
"Great King! Having traveled such a long distance, I hope you have not become utterly exhausted."
At that time, the great king replied to the seer, saying,
"I have heard that you have a daughter, and I wish to seek her hand in marriage.
Then the seer replied to the great king:
"I, a poor woman, have this one daughter who is young and ignorant, possessing no worldly knowledge.
Since her childhood, she has lived in these deep mountains; unacquainted with human affairs, she subsists on herbs and fruit."
"How can Your Majesty now wish to take her back?
Furthermore, this woman was born from an animal.
He then related the aforementioned matters to the king in full detail.
The king said,
"Even so, there is no suffering.
He then asked his father:
"Where is the Deer Woman now?
He replied to the Great King,
"She is here in this grass cave."
At that time, the Great King entered the cave and beheld the Deer Woman; his heart was filled with joy.

He immediately bathed her in fragrant water and adorned her body with famous garments, superior robes, and necklaces of a hundred jewels. Mounting a great and famous elephant, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of attendants and the performance of music and song, he returned to his own kingdom.
At that time, the Deer Woman, having never before seen such a great multitude since her birth, was struck with alarm and fear.
Then her father climbed to the summit of a high mountain and gazed at his daughter from afar, his eyes never turning away for a moment, and he thought to himself:
"As I look from afar at my daughter, she has gone so far that she is no longer visible; she will surely return to our home, wailing in grief and distress, with tears filling her eyes."
"I have raised this daughter until she reached the age of reason, yet now she has departed far from me.
He then thought further:
"I shall remain here; I ought not to go elsewhere."
"Why is this? If my daughter were to look back and fail to see me, it would cause her grief and suffering.
He stood there for a long while, but as his daughter departed, she did not appear again and ultimately did not turn her head to look back.
At that time, his father felt resentment in his heart and spoke these words:
"It was not false that you were born from an animal;
though I raised you from small, you have now grown into an adult."
"Though I was cherished by the King, I have instead been abandoned and cast aside.
She then entered the cave and, reciting and upholding incantations, cursed the girl:
"If the King treats you with such meanness, let it be as clear as day that I shall not spare him!"
"If the king receives you with courtesy, he shall be forced to retreat and fail in his purpose.
At that time, after the King of Vārāṇasī had arrived at the palace, she was honored as the foremost and named Queen Mṛgī.
The various minor kings, the hundred officials, and the multitude of ministers all came to offer their congratulations.
Upon seeing this, the king’s heart was filled with joy.
Not long thereafter, after several days had passed, he realized he was pregnant.
The king personally attended to his consort, providing her with fine and soft bedding, food, and drink.
When the ten months were complete, he looked forward to the birth of a son who would succeed him to the throne.
When the moon was full, she gave birth, and a lotus flower emerged.
Through the power of the rishi’s incantations, he provoked the king’s anger, and the king spoke these words:
"She has given birth to what is born of a beast; therefore, it is not false."
The king immediately dismissed his queen from her office and ordered someone to cast away the lotus flower.

A few days later, the King of Vārāṇasī, accompanied by his various ministers, entered the rear garden to amuse himself with sightseeing, where they performed songs and music, and engaged in contests of elephants, horses, and wrestlers.
Among them was a preeminent great strongman who, staggering and stumbling, kicked the ground with his foot; the earth shook everywhere, and the lotus pond trembled.

The king personally offered prayers and sacrifices to the deities of the mountains, rivers, ponds, and trees for twelve full years; thereafter, his first and most cherished lady became pregnant.
The second queen was likewise pregnant.
The king was greatly delighted; he personally attended to her needs, providing her with bedding, food, and drink that were all refined and soft.
When the ten months were complete, the prince was born, his physical form upright and handsome, adorned with exquisite beauty and endowed with all the marks of a great man.
The second queen also gave birth to sons.

The king was greatly delighted and immediately summoned his ministers, officials, and various physiognomists and Brahmins to divine their fortunes. He held the children up for them to see and commanded that names be bestowed upon them.
The physiognomist asked,
"When this child was born, what auspicious signs were there? He replied:
"The mother of the eldest prince has, from of old, been of a wicked nature and conduct, harboring resentment and jealousy, and being arrogant and conceited.
Yet, ever since she conceived him, her disposition has become disciplined and virtuous; her countenance is harmonious and joyful, and her speech is accompanied by smiles.
She anticipates others' needs to offer greetings, speaking gentle words for their benefit."
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, she regards them as her own infant.
The physiognomist replied,
"This is due to the child's merit that causes his mother to be thus."
He then established a name for him, calling him Prince Sudhana.
As for the prince born of the second queen, the physiognomist asked:
"At the time of this son's birth, what auspicious signs appeared?"

He replied, "Her mother has always been by nature gentle and virtuous; she would inquire after others' welfare with kindness and speak with such softness that her words were suited to the hearts of all.
Yet since becoming pregnant, her disposition has become sudden and violent, her speech coarse and foul, and she is full of jealousy, anger, and delusion."
The physiognomist replied, "This is the result of the child's own karma that has caused his mother to act in such a manner.
You should establish a name for him; let him be called Prince Pāpamitra."

Nurtured and raised until he reached the age of fourteen, Prince Śubhavyūha was intelligent, compassionate, and kind, and he delighted in practicing generosity. His parents loved him with partiality, cherishing him as they would their own eyes.
Prince Pāpamitra was by nature violent and evil; his parents detested him and would not look upon him with affection.
He was envious and jealous of his elder brother, constantly seeking to harm and obstruct him in every matter;
he was disobedient toward his brother, acting in opposition and with perverse defiance.
"Prince Shan-you, preceded and followed by his retinue, accompanied by musicians performing various entertainments, and surrounded by a great multitude, went out of the city to observe the sights.
There he saw farmers plowing the soil; as they turned up the earth, worms emerged, which crows followed and pecked at to devour."
Prince Śubhavyūha saw this from afar; moved by pity and grief, he thought, "I was raised in the deep seclusion of the palace and have never seen such a thing.
He asked those around him, "What is this that they are doing, harming one another so?"
The attendants replied, "Prince!
A kingdom exists because it relies upon its people; [without them, there would be no kingdom]."
That there are people is due to their reliance on food and drink;
that there is food and drink is due to their reliance on plowing fields and planting the five grains, by which they preserve their lives.
The Prince thought to himself:
"Alas! Alas! How bitter!"
Proceeding a short distance further, he saw men and women weaving together; they moved back and forth, looking around and shifting their positions, appearing exhausted and laboring in hardship.
The Prince asked, "What are you making?"
The attendants replied, "Prince!
These people spin and weave to produce various garments, in order to conceal their shame and cover their five limbs."
The Prince said, "This too is a laborious toil, not of one kind alone.
Continuing further on his way, he saw various people slaughtering oxen, camels, and horses, and flaying pigs and sheep.
The Prince asked, "Who is this person?
His attendants replied:
"These people slaughter and sell meat to sustain themselves and provide for their clothing and food.
At this, the prince’s hair stood on end and he spoke these words:
"How strange! How lamentable!"

"Alas! How cruel is the heart of the killer, who harms and injures both the strong and the weak! By killing living beings to sustain one's own life, one accumulates calamities that persist through many kalpas.
Continuing further on his way, he saw a multitude of people netting birds and baiting fish; they were unjustly slaughtering the innocent, with the strong bullying the weak.
The Prince asked,
"Who is this person? What is his name?"
The attendants replied,
"Prince! [It is for] netting birds and catching fish."
"Such things as these shall provide for our food and clothing.
Upon hearing these words, the Prince’s eyes filled with tears of sorrow:
"The sentient beings of this world create the roots of all manner of evils."
"Multitudes of sufferings do not cease; there is grief and no joy.
He then turned his chariot back to the palace.
The King asked the Prince:
"Why have you returned in such a state of grief and anxiety?
The Prince related the preceding events in detail to his father, the King.
Upon hearing these words, the King spoke to the Prince, saying:
"Regarding all these matters mentioned above, they have never been absent; why should you grieve?
The Prince said, "I now wish to request one boon from Your Majesty; will Your Majesty grant me leave to do so?"
The King said, "I have you, my only son, whom I love and cherish deeply; I shall not go against your wishes.
The Prince said:
"I wish to obtain all the treasuries of my father the king, including all wealth, jewels, food, and drink, to bestow them as gifts upon all beings.
The king said, "I shall grant you according to your wish; I will not oppose your intent."

Prince Shan-you then ordered his attendants to open the royal treasury and load precious jewels upon five hundred great elephants. He went outside the four city gates and issued a proclamation throughout the land:
"Whoever desires clothing, bedding, food, or drink, may take as much as they wish and depart."
The fame of Prince Kalyāṇamitra spread far and wide throughout the eight directions, and all people gathered like clouds.
Before long, one-third of the population had assembled.
At that time, the Minister of the Treasury entered and addressed the King:
"Of all the treasuries, the Crown Prince has already used one-third.
Your Majesty should consider this. The King said:
"This is the Crown Prince; we dare not disobey him.
After a short while, the ministers deliberated:
"The reason there is a kingdom is that it relies upon its treasuries."
"The treasuries are exhausted and the kingdom exists in vain.
He went again to inform the king:
"Of all the wealth and treasures, two-thirds have been spent."
"Your Majesty should consider this. The King said:
"This is my crown prince; I dare not disobey him."
"You may delay for a short while; do not satisfy his heart.
Prince Kalyāṇamitra wished to open the treasury.
At that time, the minister in charge of the storehouse was away on business; though he pursued him earnestly, they missed one another and did not meet.
Prince Shan-you said,
"How would this petty man dare to oppose my will?
It must surely be the instruction of our father, the King."
Now, a filial son should not exhaust the storehouses of his parents.
I should now seek wealth and treasures for myself to provide sufficiently for all sentient beings.
If I cannot provide clothing, bedding, food, and drink for all sentient beings and give them according to their wishes, how can I be called the crown prince of a great king?
He immediately assembled his ministers and officials to deliberate together, saying:
"In seeking wealth and profit, what occupation is most excellent?
Among them, a chief minister spoke:
"In the world, for seeking profit, none precedes the tiller of the soil; by sowing one, one obtains ten thousandfold.
Furthermore, another great minister said:
"In the world, for seeking profit, none precedes the raising of living beings; through grazing and breeding, their increase brings the greatest profit."
Again, another great minister said:
"In seeking profit within this world, nothing surpasses entering the sea to gather exquisite jewels.
If one obtains the maṇi jewel, one can satisfy all sentient beings according to their wishes."
Prince Śubhavyūha said, "Only this would bring me joy.
He then entered the palace and addressed his father, the King:
"You now wish to enter the great ocean to gather exquisite treasures.
Upon hearing these words, the king was like a man choking; he could neither swallow nor spit out the words. He said to the prince:
"The kingdom is yours, and you may take and use the treasures in the treasury as you please. Why must you now further enter the great ocean yourself?"
"You are my son, raised within the deep palace; when you slept, you lay upon curtains and canopies, and when you ate, you indulged your palate.
Now that you have traveled far along the roads, enduring hunger, thirst, cold, and heat—who knows of this?"
Furthermore, within the great ocean, there are many perils not limited to one: there may be malevolent spirits and venomous dragons;
there are turbulent waves, fierce winds, and swirling eddies;
there are mountains of water-bubbles and the great makara fish.
"In the past, out of ten million who set out, only one or two reached their destination.
Why do you now wish to enter the great ocean?
I will not permit you."
