Prince Shan-you immediately prostrated himself, stretching out his hands and feet in the four directions, and spoke these words:
"If my parents do not permit me to enter the great ocean, I shall give up my life right here and never rise again."
At that time, when the Great King and his consorts saw this, their eyes could not bear to look away for even a moment; they immediately stepped forward and exhorted the Prince:
"You should arise and take food and drink."
The Prince said,
"If you do not permit me to enter the great ocean, I shall never again eat or drink.
The King and his consort were filled with grief and distress.
Those on his left and right wept and wailed, distressed and tormented by grief; they fell to the ground in despair.
In this manner, they went without drink or food for one day, two days, three days, and up to six days.
His parents were filled with grief and anxiety, fearing he would not survive.
On the seventh day, they went before him, weeping as they embraced his hands and feet, and exhorted him with kind words: "Rise and eat."
"This provisional body of food must rely upon and depend on food and drink to remain sustained.
Without food and drink, your life cannot be preserved.
The Prince said:
"If my parents do not grant me permission, I shall surely perish here and never rise again.
At that time, the first wife addressed the king, saying:
"As this son's resolve is difficult to sway and must not be contravened, how can you bear to see him give up his life here?"
"I pray that Your Majesty will show compassion and grant me permission to enter the great ocean; thus, there may yet be a hope for survival among ten thousand possibilities.
If you do not grant this now, I shall surely perish here.
The King, unable to bear the refusal, granted his permission.
At that time, Prince Kalyāṇamitra immediately arose with joy and prostrated himself, placing his head at the feet of his father,
the King. His consorts on both sides and hundreds of thousands of court ladies asked one another,
"Is Prince Kalyāṇamitra now dead or alive?"
He replied, "The Prince has now arisen; he is joyful and eating.
The King asked the Prince:
"You wish so earnestly to enter the great ocean; what do you intend to do there? He replied, "Great King!"
"I wish to obtain the great mani-jewel to provide for all that sentient beings require.
At that time, the Great King immediately issued a proclamation everywhere:
"Who wishes to enter the sea?"
If you go and return, for seven lifetimes you shall lack nothing in terms of clothing, food, or precious treasures.
I shall provide whatever is required for your journey, including boats and vehicles.
Prince Good Friend also wishes to enter the sea to gather exquisite and wondrous *maṇi* jewels.
Upon hearing this, the multitude gathered together in joy; numbering five hundred, they all said, "Great King!
We shall now follow the Crown Prince."

"At that time, there was a master mariner in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī who had entered the great ocean many times before and after; he was well-acquainted with the routes and the signs of whether the way was open or obstructed."
He was eighty years old and both his eyes were blind.
At that time, the Great King of Vārāṇasī went to the guide’s place and said to him: “Guide!
"I have but this one son, who has never yet stepped outside the door.
I beseech you, Great Master, to exert yourself and enter the great ocean; I wish for him to follow along.
At that time, the guide raised his voice and wept aloud:
"Great King! The perils of the great ocean are manifold and its hardships are not one; of those who go forth, ten million may depart, but only one or two reach their destination.
How is it that Your Majesty now intends to cause the Prince to travel so far across such treacherous paths?"
The King said to the guide,
“Out of compassion, please grant me permission to follow you.
The guide replied:
"I dare not disobey.
At that time, Prince Good Friend prepared the travel provisions for five hundred people and transported them to the shore of the great ocean.
Then, his younger brother, Prince Evil Friend, thought to himself:
"Prince Shōmyō is constantly favored by his parents with partial affection.
Now that he has entered the great ocean to gather wondrous jewels, if he returns safely, my parents will surely abandon me."
Having formed this thought, he went to inform his parents:
"Now I also wish to follow my virtuous friend and enter the sea to gather wondrous jewels.
When his parents heard this, they replied:
"As you wish. When the road is urgent and perilous, brothers who travel together must surely protect one another.
Having reached the great ocean, he fastened his ship with seven iron chains and remained stationary for seven days.
When the sun first rose, Prince Zen'yū struck the drum and proclaimed:
"All of you, who among you wishes to enter the sea?
Those who wish to go shall remain silent."
If you should feel attachment for your parents, brothers, wife, children, or the pleasures of Jambudvīpa, do not return from here on my account. Why is this?
"Within the great ocean, obstacles are manifold; of those who go forth by the millions, only one or two reach their destination.
Thus he proclaimed, and the great assembly remained silent.
He immediately cut one cable and hoisted it onto the ship.
Day after day he made this proclamation; on the seventh day, he cut all seven cables, hoisted them onto the ship, and raised the sails toward the wind.
By the power of the Prince’s compassionate mind and merit, he encountered no obstacles and reached the Sea Isle, arriving at the Mountain of Precious Jewels.
Having reached the place of treasures, Prince Śubhavyūha immediately beat the drum and issued a proclamation:
"All you people, you must know that the road is vast and far."
"You all must quickly load the precious treasures and remain here for a full seven days.
He further spoke these words:
"These treasures are exceedingly heavy; even within Jambudvīpa, they have no equivalent value."
It is not good to carry too heavy a load, for the boat will sink and fail to reach its destination;
it is not good to take too little, for the road is so far that the gain will not compensate for the toil.
Having finished his preparations, he took leave of the others and spoke these words:
"May you all return from here in safety and well-being.
I intend to proceed further to gather mani-jewels."
"At that time, Prince Kalyāṇamitra and his blind guide proceeded forward on the road. After traveling for seven days, the water reached up to their knees.
Traveling further for another seven days, the water reached up to their necks."
Advancing seventeen [leagues], they floated across and reached the seashore;
the ground there consisted entirely of white silver sand.
The guide asked:
"What is this ground? the Prince replied,
"This ground is composed entirely of white silver sand."
The guide said: "In the four directions there ought to be a mountain of white silver.
Have you seen it yet?"
The Prince said, "In the southeast, a white silver mountain has appeared. The guide said:
"This path lies beneath this mountain.
Having reached that mountain, the guide said:
"Next, you should arrive at the golden sands."
At that time, the guide grew weary and fell to the ground in a swoon, saying to the prince:
"My life-force cannot endure much longer; I shall surely perish here."
The Prince then traveled east for seven days; there would be a mountain of gold.
From that mountain, he proceeded further for another seven days, and the ground there was entirely covered with blue lotuses.
Proceeding further for another seven [yojanas], the ground consists entirely of red lotus flowers.
Having passed these flowers, there should be a city made of the seven treasures, with defensive walls made purely of gold, watchtowers of silver, and barricade-boards of red coral;
it is interspersed with *śaṅkha* and *musāragalva*, and covered above by nets of pearls.
There are sevenfold moats and ramparts made of pure, deep-blue lapis lazuli—the dwelling place of the Great Ocean Dragon King, within whose ears there is a wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel.
Go and beg it from him!
If you obtain this jewel, it will be able to fill Jambudvīpa and rain down all kinds of the seven treasures, clothing, food and drink, medicine for the sick and emaciated, and music and performers.
In brief: it can rain down whatever all sentient beings require according to their wishes; for this reason, it is called the "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel" (cintāmaṇi).
If the Prince obtains this jewel, he will surely fulfill your original vow.
When the Guide had finished speaking these words, his breath ceased and he passed away.
Thereupon, Prince Sudhana immediately went forward and embraced the Guide, raising his voice in mournful wailing:
"How tragic is my fate! Having been born, I have lost my celestial protector!"
He then took the guide, covered him with golden sand, and buried him in the ground; he circumambulated him seven times to the right, prostrated himself, and departed.
He proceeded until he reached a mountain of gold, and having passed beyond that mountain, he saw blue lotuses covering the ground, beneath which were blue venomous snakes.
This snake possesses three kinds of venom: namely, the venom of its bite, the venom of its touch, and the venom of its breath.
These poisonous snakes coiled their bodies around the stalks of the lotuses, staring at the Prince with wide-open eyes and panting breaths.

At that time, Prince Shubhavyūha immediately entered the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind. By the power of this samādhi, he rose and proceeded on his way, treading upon lotus petals as he went; because of the power of his compassionate mind, the various venomous snakes did not harm him, and he proceeded directly to the dwelling place of the Dragon King.
On its four sides, the city has sevenfold moats; within these moats dwell venomous nāgas, who coil their bodies together, raising their heads and interlocking their necks to guard the city gates.
"At that time, when the Prince reached the exterior of the city gate, he saw various venomous dragons. He immediately conceived a mind of compassion for all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, thinking:
'If this body of mine were to be harmed by these venomous dragons, you, all sentient beings, would surely lose a great benefit.'"
At that time, the Prince immediately raised his right hand and addressed the poisonous nāgas: "You should know!
I now wish to see the Nāga King for the sake of all sentient beings."
At that time, the various venomous nāgas immediately cleared the way so that the Prince could pass, even through the sevenfold moats where the nāgas guarding the city resided.
Having reached the foot of the city gate, he saw two jade maidens spinning threads of crystal.
The Prince asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I am the handmaid who guards the outer gate for the Dragon King.
Having said this, she went forward and entered beneath the middle gate, where she saw four jade maidens spinning white silver thread.
The Prince asked again,
"Are you the wife of the Dragon King? She replied:
"No, it is merely a maidservant of the Dragon King who guards the middle gate.
After the Prince had finished questioning her, he proceeded forward to the inner gate, where he saw eight jade-like maidens spinning golden thread.
The Prince asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I am but a maidservant who guards the inner gate for the Dragon King.
The Prince said to her,
"Convey my message to the Great Ocean Dragon King:"
“Prince Kalyāṇamitra, the son of the King of Vārāṇasī in Jambudvīpa, has come specifically to see you; he is now at the gate.
At that time, the gatekeeper reported this accordingly.
Upon hearing these words, the king wondered at the reason for this and thought to himself:
"Were it not for one of pure virtue and goodness, there would be no way to traverse such a perilous road as this."
He immediately invited him into the palace, and the king went out to welcome him.

"The palace of that Dragon King had ground made of dark-blue lapis lazuli; its couches and seats were composed of the seven treasures, emitting various kinds of radiance that dazzled the eyes of men."
He immediately invited him to sit and exchanged greetings with him.

Prince Kalyāṇamitra then preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; through various means of teaching, he praised and expounded upon the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on humans and devas.
At that time, the Dragon King of the Great Ocean was greatly delighted in his heart and said, "You have traveled such a great distance to visit me;
what do you require? The Prince replied:
"Great King! All sentient beings in Jambudvīpa undergo inexhaustible suffering for the sake of clothing, wealth, food, and drink.
Now I wish to beg from the King the wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel within your left ear."
The Dragon King said, "Please accept my humble offering for seven days, and I shall provide for you.
At that time, Prince Kalyāṇamitra accepted the Dragon King's invitation; after the seven days had passed, he obtained a maṇi jewel and returned to Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the Great Ocean Dragon King sent various dragon deities to fly through the air and escort him, reaching this shore.
There he saw his younger brother, Pāpamitra, and asked him,
"Where are your followers and companions now?"
He replied: "Good friend!
The ship has sunk and everyone has perished; you are the only one left alive."
"Dragging this corpse along, I have managed to save my own life,
but all my wealth and possessions are now exhausted.
His good friend replied:
"The greatest treasure in the world is none other than one's own person.
His younger brother said, "Not so;
people would rather die wealthy than live in poverty."
"How do we know this to be so?
Previously, my brother went to a cemetery and heard various spirits of the dead discussing this very matter.
Prince Sudhana, being of a truly upright nature, spoke to his younger brother with truthful words:
"Although you have lost your treasure, it is of little consequence;
I have now obtained the Dragon King’s wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewel.
The younger brother said:
"Where is it now? The Good Friend replied,
"It is now within the topknot."
Upon hearing these words, the younger brother felt jealousy in his heart; filled with resentment and distress, he thought to himself:
"My parents have always shown me partiality and affection, and now they have further obtained this mani-jewel."
"My own body is now held in such loathing and contempt by my parents that it is worse than a discarded tile or stone.
Having thought this, he said to his good friend: "How wonderful!"
"Excellent! You have obtained this precious jewel.
Now, on this perilous road, you must provide it with special protection."
At that time, Kalyāṇamitra untied the precious jewel and instructed his younger brother, Pāpamitra, saying:
"If you become weary and fall asleep, I shall protect you;
if I fall asleep, you should protect me."

At that time, it was the turn of the evil friend to guard the precious jewel. While his elder brother lay sleeping, he rose and sought out two dry bamboo splinters; he then pierced both of his brother’s eyes and fled with the jewel.
At that time, Kalyāṇamitra immediately called his younger brother Pāpamitra, saying,
"A thief has pierced both my eyes with a stake and taken the precious jewel away.
However, Pāpamitra did not respond.
The elder brother was then distressed and cried out loudly,
"My younger brother’s evil friend seems to have been killed by bandits!
His voice shook the gods and spirits, yet for a long time there was no response.
At that time, the tree deity immediately raised its voice and said:
"Your younger brother, Pāpamitra, is your evil enemy; he has gouged out both your eyes and taken the precious jewel away.
Why do you now call for Pāpamitra?"
Having heard these words, Prince Good Friend was despondent and choked with sobs, suffering in grief and resentment.
At that time, Prince Evil Friend, carrying the precious jewel, returned to his native land and met with his parents, saying to them:
"Father and Mother!"
"By the merit of my own body, I have been fully saved;
yet because Prince Shonjō (Good Friend) and his companions possessed little merit, they perished, drowning in the water.

Upon hearing these words, the parents raised their voices and wailed loudly; they fainted and fell to the ground. Cold water was sprinkled upon their faces, and after a long while, they regained consciousness.
The parents said to the evil friend,
"How could you possibly bring such a face as this?
Upon hearing these words, the evil friend felt deep distress in his heart and immediately buried the precious jewel in the ground.
"At that time, Prince Good Friend had both eyes pierced; dry bamboo splinters were lodged within them, and no one came to extract them.
He wandered about and rolled on the ground, not knowing where to go."

At that time, he suffered greatly from hunger and thirst; seeking life, he could not find it, and seeking death, he could not find it. Gradually proceeding forward, he arrived at the kingdom of King Lichchhavi.
King Liśīva had a daughter who had previously been betrothed to Prince Śubhavyūha, the son of the King of Vārāṇasī.
King Liśīva had a cowherd named Yuyutsu, who, for the sake of King Liśīva, tended five hundred oxen, following them wherever there was water and grass.
"At that time, Prince Kalyāṇamitra was sitting in the middle of the road.

As the herd of oxen drew near and were about to trample him, there was a bull-king among them who immediately mounted the prince with all four legs, allowing the entire herd to pass by. Only after they had all gone did he shift his feet, turn around in a clockwise circle, and looking back with his head turned, he licked the prince's two eyes with his tongue and pulled out the bamboo splinters."
At that time, the cowherd soon caught sight of him from behind and asked, "Who are you?
Good Friend then thought to himself:
"I ought not now to recount my origins or describe these past events in detail, lest it cause my younger brother great distress.
He replied, "I am merely a blind beggar."
At that time, the cowherd looked him over from head to foot and, seeing that his physical appearance was extraordinary, said:
"My home is nearby; I shall provide for you.
Then the cowherd took the Good Friend back to his house, gave him various foods and drinks, and instructed all the men and women, both old and young, in the household:
"You all should attend to this man no differently than you do me.
After he had spoken thus for over a month, the family grew weary and distressed, saying:
"Our household resources are not abundant; how can we constantly provide for this blind man?"
Having heard these words, the Good Friend felt despondent in heart and mind.
When that night had passed and morning dawned, he said to the host:
"I wish to depart now."
The host replied, "What is it that makes you so ill at ease that you wish to abandon me and leave?
Kalyāṇamitra answered:
"The principle of guest and host does not permit this state to last long," said his good friend.
"If you truly love and cherish me, make for me a lute that produces sound."
"Please send me to a place where there are many people, to a great city or a large village.
At that time, the host immediately provided for him according to his wishes, escorting him to a populous area in the city of Rṣivadana, and he returned home in safety.
The good friend was skilled at playing the zither; its sound was harmonious and elegant, delighting the hearts of all.
The entire assembly together provided food and drink, even to the full satisfaction of the five hundred beggars on the path to Liśāvadavarta, so that they all obtained their fill.
At that time, the king had a fruit orchard that was lush and flourishing, yet it was constantly plagued by birds and sparrows.
The park keeper said to Sudāma,
"Protect this place from the birds for me, and I shall provide you with excellent sustenance."
The Good Friend replied, "I am blind in both eyes; how could I drive away the birds and sparrows for you?
The garden keeper said:
"I have a skillful means.
I shall tie ropes to the tops of the trees and attach copper bells to them.
You should sit beneath a tree; when you hear the sound of birds and small creatures, pull on the end of the rope."
The Good Friend replied,
"In this way, I am able.
Having led him to the foot of a tree and settled him there in safety, he then departed.
The good friend protected the birds and fledglings while simultaneously entertaining himself by playing the zither.
At that time, the daughter of King Liśavardhana, accompanied by her attendants, entered the garden to sightsee; seeing this blind man, she went to him and asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am merely a blind beggar.
When the princess saw him, love arose in her heart, and she could not bear to part from him.
The king sent a messenger again to summon his daughter.
The daughter said,
"I will not go."
"Please bring me food.
After he had finished eating and drinking with this blind man, he said to the Great King:
"Your Majesty, now that you have given me to this blind man, it perfectly fulfills my wish."
The king said:
"You are possessed by a malevolent spirit; your mind is deranged and disordered. Why do you dwell together with this blind man?
Do you not know better?"
"Your parents previously promised you in marriage to Prince Kalyāṇamitra, the King of Vārāṇasī.
Since Prince Kalyāṇamitra has now entered the sea and has not yet returned,
why do you wish to become the wife of a beggar?"
The woman said, "Even so,
even at the cost of my life, I shall never abandon you.
When the king heard these words, he could not refuse her.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to bring the blind man and confine him in a quiet chamber.
At that time, the princess went to the blind man’s location and said to him: “Do you know?”
"I now wish to become husband and wife with you.
Good Friend replied,
"Whose daughter are you, that you would wish to be my wife?"
She replied, "I am the daughter of King Liśāvadha. Sakhī responded:
"You are a princess, and I am a beggar; how can I show you respect?
The wife said, "I shall serve you with all my heart and never oppose your wishes."
After ninety days had passed in this manner, his wife went out on a minor errand without informing her husband; she returned only after a long time.
The Good Friend rebuked her, saying:
"You went out privately to the outside without informing me."
"Where have you been? The wife replied, "I did not go out on my own."
The husband said, "Whether I am being private with you or not, who would know?
His wife was distressed; her eyes filled with tears, and she immediately made this oath:
"If I have acted in secret, may both your eyes never recover;
if not, may one of your eyes be restored as it was before.

Having made this vow, the husband’s eye began to throb and twitch, and it was restored to its former state. The pupil shone with a brilliant light like a falling star, and his vision became so clear that he was able to see his wife.
The wife said,
"What do you think? Do you believe me?"
The good friend smiled with a faint smile.
His wife said,
"You do not recognize the kindness of those who have nurtured you."
"I am the daughter of a great king, while you are but a lowly man; yet I have served you with all my heart, and you do not acknowledge or believe me.
Her husband said, "Do you recognize me?"
He replied, "I know you; you are a beggar.
The husband said:
"No, I am Prince Kalyāṇamitra, the son of the King of Vārāṇasī.
His wife said, "You are a most foolish man; why do you speak such words?"
"Prince Kalyāṇamitra, the son of the King of Vārāṇasī, has entered the sea and has not yet returned; how can you now say that he is this man?
These are but false words.
I do not believe them."
The good friend said,
"Since my birth, I have never spoken falsely.
His wife said:
"Between the empty and the real, who would believe it?
The husband said,
"If I speak falsely and deceive you, may one of my eyes never be healed."
"If what I say is true, let my eye be restored to its former state so that you may see it.
Having formed this thought, his eye immediately became as he had vowed; its brilliance shone and pulsed, no different from how it was originally.

"Prince Shōmyō’s two eyes have been restored; his countenance is upright and handsome, his physical marks are complete, and his wondrous beauty is so transcendent that there is none to compare with him in the world."
When his wife saw him, joy arose in her heart as if she had encountered a sage or a holy one; she gazed upon his entire body, her eyes never turning away for a moment.
She immediately entered the palace and addressed her father, the King, saying:
"The husband I have now is none other than Prince Kalyāṇamitra."
The king said, "You are a foolish man, mad and possessed by demons, that you speak such words.
Prince Sudhana has entered the sea and has not yet returned; how can you now call this beggar the prince?"
The woman said, "No.
If you do not believe me, you may take a look for yourself."
The king immediately went to look; having seen him, he recognized him as Prince Kalyāṇamitra. Filled with terror, he spoke these words:
"If the King of Vārāṇasī hears of this matter, he will not fail to hold me in contempt."
He immediately went forward to apologize to Prince Shanyou,
saying, "I truly did not know. The prince said:
"There is no need for you to worry.
Bring these as a gift for me and give them to this cowherd.
King Līśavardhana then bestowed upon him gold, silver, precious jewels, garments, bedding, food, and drink, along with the five hundred cows he had released.
The man was filled with joy and praised him immeasurably:
"Prince Good Friend, though I have not bestowed even a small measure of kindness upon you, you are able to repay me with such wealth as this."
Then the cowherd cried out in a loud voice amidst the great assembly:
"Indeed, when one gives in secret, the reward comes forth openly; the matter of giving yields a fruit and retribution that is vast and far-reaching."

At that time, the hearts of the immeasurable great assembly were filled with joy; they all resolved to practice giving, seeking to provide relief for all beings, taking the pursuit of Buddhahood as their foundation.
The devas and spirits of the void praised those people, exclaiming: "So it is! So it is! and thus fulfilled their words.

"At that time, when Prince Kalyāṇamitra had not yet entered the great ocean and was still in the palace, he kept a white goose; whether in dressing, eating, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they were always together."
At that time, the lady went to where the geese were and said to them:
"When the Prince was alive, he was always with you.
Now that he has entered the great ocean and has not yet returned, his life or death remains undetermined, and I am unable to know the truth for certain."
"Why do you not now feel any sense of gratitude toward the Prince?
Upon hearing these words, the goose cried out in sorrow and writhed about, its eyes filled with tears, and replied:
"Great King and Queen!..."
"I wish that those who seek the Prince would not dare to disobey my command.
At that time, the lady herself wrote a letter and tied it to the neck of the goose.
The goose, calling out the name of the Prince, asked for the whereabouts of the Great Ocean; then, rising into the void, it flew away, wheeling and turning as it departed.
Upon seeing this, the lady felt a sense of reliance, thinking:
"Now this goose must surely bring certain news regarding whether my son is alive or dead.
It flew to the great ocean, searching everywhere throughout its course, yet could not find him.
Proceeding by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Rishabha and saw Prince Kalyāṇamitra from afar before the palace.
The goose drew in its body, tucked its wings, and went toward him; having reached him, it cried out piteously with joy.

The Crown Prince immediately took his mother’s letter, prostrated himself with his head to the ground in reverent salutation, broke the seal, and read it; he then learned that his parents had wept in sorrow day and night, missing him so deeply that they had lost the sight of both their eyes.
At that time, the Prince immediately wrote a letter, detailing the aforementioned matters and presenting them to his parents.
He then tied the letter to the neck of the goose; the goose, filled with joy, returned to Vārāṇasī.

When the parents received the prince’s letter, they leaped for joy and praised him beyond measure; they learned in full detail that the prince had been harmed by his younger brother, the evil friend, who had seized the precious jewel, causing the prince immeasurable suffering.
The parents immediately placed shackles on the hands and feet of their evil friend and bound his neck with a collar-lock, then cast him into prison.
They dispatched a messenger to inform King Liśākhya:
"Why have you now obstructed the crown prince, causing us such grief and suffering?"
Upon hearing these words, King Līśābha was struck with fear; he immediately dressed the prince in fine garments and escorted him to the border.
The prince sent a messenger to inform King Līśābha:
"My good friend has returned from the great ocean."

At that time, King Liśākhya prepared musical performances with attendants leading and following him; they swept and sprinkled the ground, burned incense, hung silk banners and canopies, and struck bells and drums to welcome the Prince from afar. Upon returning to the palace, he betrothed his daughter to him and dispatched him to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

When the parents heard that the Crown Prince had returned, they were filled with immeasurable joy. Mounting a great and famous elephant, they provided musical performances and entertainment; they swept and sprinkled the ground, burned incense, and hung silk banners and canopies as they went out from afar to welcome the Crown Prince.
The people of the kingdom, both men and women, hearing that the Prince had entered the great ocean and returned safely, were filled with immeasurable joy and all went out to welcome him.
Prince Shanyou came forward and prostrated himself at the feet of his parents.
The King and Queen were blind; unable to see the Prince’s appearance, they felt for him with their hands and asked, "Are you my son, Shanyou, or not?"
"Your parents think of you, and their grief and suffering are thus great.

After the Prince had finished inquiring after his parents' well-being, he raised his hand and spoke in a loud voice to thank all the minor kings, the various ministers, the people of the land, and the entire assembly, saying:
"I have troubled the great assembly; please return from here."
Prince Good Friend said to his father, the King:
"Where is my younger brother, Evil Friend, now?
The King replied:
"You need not inquire after him.
Such an evil person is currently in prison and must not be released. Prince Shan-you said:
“I pray that you will release my evil friend so that we may meet.
He spoke these words three times. The king, unable to refuse him, opened the prison gates.
At that time, the Evil Friend—his hands and feet bound by shackles and his neck fettered with a collar—went to see the Good Friend.
Seeing this, the elder brother went before their parents and said,
"Please release my younger brother from his shackles.
Once the shackles were removed, he immediately went forward to embrace him, consoling him with kind words and greeting him with gentle speech:
"Are you exhausted? Where is the precious jewel you were carrying?
He asked this up to three times, and only then did [the man] reply:
"Within that land," Prince Shan-you (Good Friend) recovered the precious jewel and went before his parents. Kneeling and burning exquisite incense, he immediately made this vow:
"If this precious jewel is indeed a wish-fulfilling gem, may my parents' two eyes become clear and bright as they were before."
Having made this vow, he was immediately restored to health.
When his parents saw their son, they leaped for joy and were filled with immeasurable celebration and good fortune.
At that time, on the morning of the fifteenth day of the month, Prince Kalyāṇamitra bathed himself thoroughly, donned fresh and clean garments, and burned exquisite precious incense.
Standing atop a high tower, he held a censer in his hand and prostrated himself before the maṇi jewel, making this vow:
"For the sake of all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, I have endured extreme hardship to seek this precious jewel."

At that time, a great wind arose from the east, blowing away the clouds and mists so that the void became brilliantly clear and pure. Furthermore, all the filth, excrement, urine, ash, dust, weeds, and thickets throughout Jambudvīpa were swept by the cool breeze and rendered completely clean.

By the majestic power of the jewel, throughout Jambudvīpa there fell a rain of naturally ripened non-glutinous rice—fragrant, sweet, soft, and fine, perfect in color and flavor—which filled the ditches and channels until they reached the knees in height;
next, there fell a rain of famous garments, superior robes, pearl rings, hairpins, and bracelets;
and finally, there fell a rain of gold, silver, the seven treasures, and various exquisite musical instruments.
To state the essentials: all the requisites for happiness required by all sentient beings are fully provided.

When a Bodhisattva cultivates great compassion and practices the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), they provide all sentient beings with every requisite for happiness; such is the nature of that deed.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Great King of Vārāṇasī at that time was none other than my father, Śuddhodana, who is present now;
the mother at that time was none other than my mother, Lady Māyā, who is present now."
At that time, Prince Pāpamitra was none other than Devadatta;
at that time, Prince Kalyāṇamitra was none other than myself. Ānanda!
In past lives, Devadatta constantly harbored an evil mind and sought to harm me.
Yet, through the power of my forbearance and by always thinking of bestowing grace upon him, he was thereby saved; how much more so now that I have attained Buddhahood?
When the Buddha preached this Dharma, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat;
furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people all resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
and even immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all resolved their minds toward the path of śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha said,
"This sutra is titled 'The Buddha’s Requital of Gratitude through Skillful Means to Fully Satisfy All Sentient Beings.
Having heard this sutra, the assembled multitude rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
Furthermore, although Devadatta followed the Buddha into the monastic life, his jealousy was profound and he schemed for gain and offerings.
Although he was able to recite many of the sixty thousand *Gandhahastin* sūtras, he could not escape the retribution of the Avīci Hell.
This man was on intimate terms with King Ajātaśatru; they were affectionate toward one another in heart and he placed full trust in his words.
At that time, Devadatta said to King Ajātaśatru:
"You may become the new king, and I, too, wish to become the new Buddha."
Ajātaśatru replied, "That is not so;
my father, the King, is still alive."
Devadatta said: "You should remove it;
I, too, wish to destroy the Buddha."
"Then, would it not be a joy for the new king and the new Buddha to transform sentient beings?
At that time, Ajātaśatru followed these words, took the life of his father the king, and reigned over the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Devadatta replied to King Ajātaśatru, saying,
"I wish to harm the Tathāgata. Ajātaśatru said:
“The Tathāgata possesses great supernormal powers and foreknows the thoughts of others; how could you possibly inflict harm upon him?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has many great disciples, such as Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Kiṃpila, and Anuruddha.”
Devadatta replied to Ajātaśatru, "Your Majesty, you must now assist me. Ajātaśatru said:
"What have you done? He replied, "Great King!"
"A restriction must be established so that no one is permitted to give robes, food, or drink to the bhikṣus.
King Ajātaśatru issued a proclamation throughout the land, saying:
"If anyone gives robes, food, or drink to the bhikṣus, their hands and feet shall be cut off."

These great disciples and the entire assembly, together with the Buddha, resided on Vulture Peak Mountain; they went for alms in succession, yet were unable to obtain anything at all for one day, and even up to seven days.
Śāriputra and all the other great disciples, by means of their supernormal powers, had gone to various directions to seek robes and beg for alms.
At that time, Devadatta said to King Ajātaśatru:
"The Buddha’s great disciples are all absent at present."
"The Tathāgata is alone. Your Majesty should dispatch a messenger to invite him.
Once he has entered the palace city, you must immediately give wine to five hundred great, wicked black elephants until they are utterly intoxicated and frantic."
"If the Buddha accepts our invitation and enters the city, we shall release a large, intoxicated elephant to trample him to death.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru dispatched a messenger to invite the Tathāgata.
The Buddha and five hundred arhats accepted the king’s invitation and proceeded into the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru released five hundred intoxicated elephants; they rushed forward in a wild charge, trampling everything in their path, snapping trees, and collapsing walls, while letting out deafening roars as they headed toward the Tathāgata.
At that time, the five hundred arhats were all seized with great terror; they leaped into the air and hovered above the Buddha.
Meanwhile, Ānanda surrounded the Tathāgata, so overcome by fear that he was unable to move away.

At that time, by the power of his compassion, the Tathāgata raised his right hand, and from the tips of his five fingers there emerged five lions. As they opened their mouths and roared, five hundred intoxicated elephants were struck with terror and fell prostrate upon the ground.
At that time, the Tathāgata, surrounded by the great assembly, entered the royal palace.
King Ajātaśatru immediately came out to welcome him and invited the Buddha to be seated;
once the Buddha was seated, the king sought mercy and repented, addressing the Buddha as follows:
“World-Honored One!
This is not my fault; it is Devadatta’s alone.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"I also know this. Devadatta has constantly sought to harm me; it is not merely now.
Even in past lives, he has always sought to harm me."
“By the power of my compassion, I am able to bring about their deliverance.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru joined his palms, stepped forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How did Devadatta harm and injure the Tathāgata in a past life?
Listen attentively! the Buddha said.
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, there was a great king who delighted in eating the flesh of wild geese; he appointed a hunter to constantly set nets to capture them.
At that time, a flock of five hundred wild geese was flying through the air from the north toward the south. Among them, the goose king fell into a net.
Thereupon, the hunter was filled with great joy; he immediately emerged from his grass hut, intending to seize and kill it.
At that time, there was a wild goose that cried out in grief with such intensity it vomited blood; it circled about and would not leave.
Then the hunter drew his bow, intending to shoot, yet the goose did not avoid the arrow, its gaze never wavering for a moment, as it beat its two wings and flew to join the Goose King.
A flock of five hundred geese hovered in the void, likewise refusing to depart.
At that time, the hunter saw one of these geese, which was crying out in grief with blood spitting from its mouth, gazing back with such longing.
At that time, the hunter thought to himself:
"Even birds and beasts can thus cherish one another so much that they do not spare their own lives; such is the nature of their conduct.
With what kind of heart, then, should I now kill this king of geese?"
Immediately, he opened the net and released them to let them go.
At that time, one goose cried out with joy and beat its wings to follow after them; the flock of five hundred geese surrounded them from front and back as they flew away through the air.
At that time, the hunter addressed the Great King, saying:
"I have captured a king of geese in my net; he should be sent to Your Majesty's kitchen to provide for the preparation of food and drink.
However, I saw another goose there who was crying out in grief until it vomited blood; it did not avoid the bow or the arrows, but paced about and would not leave."
At that time, thinking of this goose, he immediately released the goose king; the five hundred followers surrounded him from front and back as they flew away through the air.
When the Great King heard these words, his heart grew sorrowful, and he immediately gave rise to a mind of compassion:
"The mutual affection and care between birds and beasts for one another’s lives is such as this."
At that time, the great king immediately ceased the slaughter of geese and vowed never to hunt them again.
"Great King! You should know that the king of that time was none other than your present self."
The hunter of that time was none other than Devadatta;
the single goose that cried out in grief and spat blood was Ānanda;
and the flock of five hundred geese were the five hundred Arhats of today.
"The king of geese at that time was none other than my current self.
At that time, Ānanda’s mind felt the same lingering attachment as it does now, no different from before;
likewise, the five hundred arhats soaring through the void were also no different from how they are now."
"At that time, Devadatta constantly sought to harm me; yet, by the power of my compassion, he was thereby saved.

When this Dharma was spoken, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit of the path, or gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, or even the minds of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
"Furthermore, Devadatta’s evil intent did not cease, and he thought:
'I should now grow my ten fingernails until they are extremely long and sharp, and smear poison beneath them. "

When he goes to the place where the Tathāgata is and prostrates himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, I shall scratch the tops of his feet with my ten fingernails; the poison will enter his body, and he will surely lose his life.
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Tathāgata was as he had intended. He prostrated with his head at the feet and grasped them with his hands.
At that moment, the poisonous medicine was transformed into nectar, and it did nothing whatsoever to the body of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Devadatta, having failed to achieve his wish, thought again:
'The Tathāgata is now sitting at the foot of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.'"
"I should now climb the mountain and push down a rock from above to sever his life-vein.
Having formed this thought, he climbed the mountain and pushed down the rock, wounding the Buddha’s toe.
"My heart of compassion regards enemies and kin as equal.

Furthermore, Devadatta, in the distant past, incalculable eons ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a bhikṣu who practiced dhyāna and lived alone in a forest.
At that time, the bhikṣu suffered from lice and made an agreement with them, saying:
"When I practice dhyāna, you should remain silent, conceal yourselves, and dwell in stillness."
The louse was thus in accordance with the Dharma.
Later, at one time, a flea came to the louse's side and asked,
"How is it that your body and flesh are so plump and flourishing?"
The louse said,
"The master upon whom I depend constantly practices meditative concentration and instructs me regarding the proper timing for food and drink.
Because I consume my food according to the Dharma, my body is thus fresh and plump."
The flea said, "I,
too, wish to practice that Dharma.
The louse said:
"Very well, do as you wish.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately sat down to practice meditation.
Then, a louse from the soil, smelling the scent of blood and flesh, began to feed upon him.
"At that time, the bhikṣu felt great distress in his heart; he immediately took off his robes and burned them with fire.
The Buddha said, "The bhikṣu who was practicing dhyāna at that time was none other than Kāśyapa Buddha himself."
At that time, the louse was Devadatta; at that time, the flea was my own self.
For the sake of gain and offerings, Devadatta brought harm upon me.
Even up to the present day when he attained Buddhahood, Devadatta continued to act for the sake of gain and offerings; he shed the blood of the Buddha and was born directly into hell.

Devadatta constantly harbored an evil mind and sought to harm the Tathāgata; were one to recount these deeds, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon, yet the Tathāgata has always regarded him with compassion and pity through the power of his loving-kindness.
"Because I encountered Devadatta, I quickly attained Buddhahood; out of mindfulness of his kindness, I constantly bestow my compassionate pity upon him.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately dispatched Ānanda to go to hell to inquire after Devadatta:
"Can you endure your suffering?"
At that time, Ānanda, having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, went to the gate of the hell and asked the ox-headed attendant, Aṅgada: "Call Devadatta for me."
Gavāmpati replied, "To which Buddha's Devadatta are you referring?
Every Buddha of the past had a Devadatta."
Ānanda said, “I am calling Devadatta, Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that moment, Ox-Head Ābanga spoke to Devadatta:
“Ānanda is outside and wishes to see you.
Devadatta then said, “Welcome, Ānanda!”
"Does the Tathāgata still hold me in his compassionate regard?
Ānanda replied, "The Tathāgata has sent me to inquire after you: can your suffering be endured?"
Devadatta said, "My dwelling in the Avīci Hell is like a bhikṣu entering the bliss of the third dhyāna.
The Buddha said:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate great skillful means to guide and receive sentient beings;
though they undergo immeasurable great suffering within birth and death, they do not regard it as a calamity.”
"If anyone were to say that Devadatta was truly an evil person who has entered the Avīci Hell, such a thing is impossible.
At that time, the Tathāgata revealed to the great assembly the subtle, secret, and wondrous conduct of Devadatta’s great skillful means.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) up to the path of arhatship.
The celestial deities of the void rained down various heavenly flowers, covering the entire assembly; they played celestial music, emitted great radiance, and praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is truly unprecedented.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the entire great assembly bowed their heads to the ground in prostration and departed with joy.
The Sūtra on the Great Expedient Means of the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness, Volume Four;
The Sūtra on the Great Expedient Means of the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness, Volume Five.
Translator unknown; included in the Later Han Records.
Chapter Seven: On Loving-kindness (*Maitrī*) At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly who made offerings to him with reverence, respect, and praise.
At that moment, the Tathāgata dwelt in the sphere of immeasurable and profound practice, desiring to uproot the intense suffering of the three realms of existence for all sentient beings.

Desiring to eliminate the five hindrances and untie the ten fetters, and wishing to cause all sentient beings to attain liberation together and abide in the unconditioned, he then reveals two kinds of fields of merit: first, the field of merit involving conditioned activity;
[and second, the field of merit involving the unconditioned].
Second is the field of merit that requires no effort.

This refers to one's parents and teachers, the Buddhas, the Dharma, the Sangha, and all Bodhisattvas; by making offerings to these and all sentient beings, one gains merit and may advance toward the realization of the Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra and the other great disciples of vast wisdom, saying:
"You should know that the Tathāgata will before long enter parinirvāṇa."

When Śāriputra heard these words, every joint and limb of his body felt as if pierced by needles; overcome with grief and distress, he fainted and fell to the ground. Cold water was sprinkled upon his face, and after a long while, he regained consciousness.
He immediately rose, joined his palms, and praised the Buddha with these verses:
“The Buddha is like nectar; one can never hear enough of him.
If the Buddha were to become indolent, it would be of no benefit to anyone.”
In the ocean of birth and death across the five realms, one is like one fallen into foul mud;
because they are entangled by craving and desire, the ignorant are deluded by the world.
Having practiced correctly in previous lives, they bestow their gifts with equanimity.
Therefore, the mark between his eyebrows shines forth without limit.
His eyes are like the new moon, seeing through to the lands of the ten directions;
they cause the hearts and eyes of all people to rejoice greatly upon beholding him.

At that time, Śāriputra, having praised the Tathāgata with these and hundreds of thousands of other verses, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and addressed the great assembly—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans:
“O sons of good family!
The world is empty! How strange! How strange! The world is empty! How bitter!
Alas! The Eye of the World has been extinguished. How painful!
How painful!
The wondrous jewel-bridge of the Dharma shall now be shattered;
the unsurpassed tree of enlightenment shall now be broken;
the wondrous jewel-banner of victory shall now be toppled.
"The unsurpassed Buddha-sun has set behind the mountain of Great Parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing these words, the entire great assembly was struck with alarm; their hair stood on end, and they were seized with great terror.
The sun lost its brilliant radiance, the various mountains collapsed, and the earth shook violently.
At that time, Śāriputra, amidst the great assembly, spoke these verses:
“I behold the marks of the Buddha’s body, Compared to a mountain of purple gold;”
When the marks and signs and all virtues have ceased, only the name remains alone.
One should exert diligent effort to escape from the triple world;
by selecting various wholesome karmas, nirvana is the supreme peace and happiness.

When Śāriputra had spoken these verses to comfort and encourage the great assembly, he manifested great supernormal power, ascending into the air and transforming himself into a jeweled elephant with a thousand heads.
Each elephant’s body is coiled and entwined with the others,
with their thousand heads facing outward; each elephant has seven tusks,
and upon each tusk there are seven bathing pools.
Each bathing pool has seven lotus flowers;
upon each flower pedestal are seven transformation Buddhas,
and each transformation Buddha has Śāriputra as his attendant.

Each of these Śāriputras emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, summoning from afar those with whom they had a karmic connection.
Once those with such connections had assembled, Śāriputra again manifested a massive body that filled the void of space;
he could appear large and then small, enter the earth as if it were water, and emerge without leaving any gap or opening where he had passed.
Sometimes fire issued from the lower part of his body while water flowed from the upper part, as he leaped and vanished within the void;
sometimes he manifested himself as a thousand or a hundred, even up to an infinite number.

Having displayed these various supernatural transformations, he descended from the sky and went among the great assembly, extensively preaching the Dharma for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them, causing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to arhatship;
additionally, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people gave rise to the aspiration for the vehicles of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha.
At that time, after Śāriputra had performed such immeasurable benefits, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"With what heart could I now behold the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa?"
Having uttered these words, he immediately ascended into the air; fire issued from his body, and he spontaneously cremated himself, entering parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the great assembly, longing for Śāriputra, could not turn their eyes away for a moment. Filled with yearning, they raised their voices and wailed aloud, until dust covered their bodies;
the sun lost its brilliance, and heaven and earth shook violently.
At that time, the great assembly gathered the relics and erected a stupa to make offerings to them.

Then, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people surrounded the stupa; because they were mindful of Śāriputra, their hearts were filled with anguish, and they wandered about distractedly, losing their right mindfulness.
At that time, by the power of his compassion, the Tathāgata manifested a transformation-body of Śāriputra within the great assembly.
When the multitude saw Śāriputra, their hearts were filled with joy, and their grief and suffering were immediately dispelled.
Because of their hearts of joy, they all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, Ānanda perceived that the minds of the assembly were all filled with doubt. He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“For what reason, Śāriputra, has he entered parinirvāṇa before the Tathāgata, causing this great assembly to suffer such grief and distress?
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly:
“It is not only today that Śāriputra has entered parinirvāṇa before the Tathāgata.”
"In past lives as well, they were unable to bear seeing me, and so they first entered parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“Śāriputra passed into parinirvāṇa in a previous life; what were the circumstances of that event?
The Buddha said, “Listen well!”
In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī.
The king of that Vārāṇasī was named Mahāprabha.
King Mahāprabha ruled over sixty small kingdoms and eight hundred settlements.
That king constantly harbored a compassionate heart; he bestowed gifts upon all and never acted contrary to people's wishes.
At that time, there was a minor king on the frontier who constantly harbored evil and rebellious intentions.

Meanwhile, King Mahāprabha, on every fast day of each month, loaded five hundred great elephants with precious jewels, money, clothing, and food and drink, and placed them in the great marketplace as well as outside the four city gates to bestow as alms upon all.

At that time, the enemy nations and hostile kinsmen heard that King Mahāprabha was practicing universal giving and never refusing anyone's wishes; those who required clothing, food and drink, gold, silver, or rare treasures were allowed to take as much as they desired and depart.
At that time, a minor king of a bordering state, hearing of King Mahāprabha’s virtue in practicing generosity, conceived feelings of jealousy and immediately assembled his ministers, saying:
"Who among you can go to that kingdom of Vārāṇasī and beg for the head of King Mahāprabha?"
None of the ministers were able to go.
The king issued another proclamation:
"Who among you can go to that kingdom of Vārāṇasī and beg for the head of King Mahāprabha?"
"To whoever can go and retrieve it, I shall give a reward of a thousand pieces of gold.
Among them, a certain Brahmin said, "I am able to go and beg for it; simply provide me with provisions for the journey."
"This country is more than six thousand *li* from Vārāṇasī.
The king immediately provided him with provisions and sent him to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa traveled until he reached the border of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
The earth shook in six ways, startling the birds and beasts, who scattered and fled in all directions;
the sunlight was obscured, the moon lost its brilliance,
and the five planets and various lunar mansions deviated from their regular courses.
Red, black, and white rainbows appeared constantly by day and night;
shooting stars fell from the sky;
and within that kingdom, the springs, bathing pools, flowers, and fruits that were once lush and delightful all withered and dried up.
At that time, the brahmin went to the city of Vārāṇasī and stood outside the gate.
Then the guardian deity spoke to the gatekeeper, saying:
"This most wicked brahmin has come from afar, desiring to beg for the head of King Mahāprabha."
"Do not let him enter.
At that time, the brahmin remained outside the gate for seven days, unable to proceed further, and said to the gatekeeper:
"I have come from afar, wishing to see the Great King."
At that time, the gatekeeper entered and informed the king:
"A certain brāhmaṇa has come from afar and is now standing outside the gate.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately went out to welcome him, as a son meets his father, and prostrated himself before him.
"Whence have you come?
Having traveled these roads, I hope you have not grown weary?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"I have heard of your majesty’s virtues in another land: your generosity never opposes the wishes of others;
your fame is heard afar, reaching upward to the azure heavens and downward to the Yellow Springs.
From near and far, people sing your praises; these words are indeed true and not empty. Therefore, I have come from afar, traversing mountains and rivers."
"Now I wish to obtain something.
The king said, "I am now known as 'The Giver of All. Whatever you seek, do not hesitate or feel any doubt."
The brahmin said, "Is this truly so?
I do not require any other thing;
I now wish to perform a great sacrifice and beg for the head from the King."
Having heard this, the king reflected deeply within himself:
"Since beginningless birth and death, I have pointlessly lost these bodies, never having acted for the sake of the Dharma;
I have pointlessly undergone birth and death, exhausting my spirit."
Now, regarding this body, I deeply desire to seek Bodhi and vow to reach all sentient beings.
If I do not give it now, I would contradict my original resolve.
If I do not offer this body as a gift, by what cause shall I attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi?
The King said: "Excellent!
I must briefly attend to my own affairs; I shall entrust the sovereignty of the kingdom to my consort and the crown prince."
"After seven days have passed, I shall bestow it upon you.
At that time, the Great King entered the palace and informed his consorts:
"All affectionate attachments in the world must inevitably end in separation; [therefore, I entrust my daughter to you]."
"In human life there is death; in the completion of affairs there is failure.
Things are born in spring and wither naturally in autumn and winter.
When the Prince heard these words, he was like a person choking: he could neither swallow them down nor spit them out.
“Great King! For what reason and by what cause do you now speak these words?
The king replied:
"A brāhmaṇa has come from afar wishing to beg for my head;
I have already granted him his request.
Upon hearing these words, the queen and the crown prince threw their bodies to the ground and wailed aloud with a loud cry. They tore out their hair, rent their garments, and spoke thus:

"Great King! Among all that is valued in the world, nothing is more precious than one's own body. How is it that today you can so easily renounce what is difficult to give, holding it forth to bestow upon others?
At that time, the five hundred ministers said to the brāhmaṇa:
"What use have you for this head, foul, putrid, and filled with pus and blood?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "I am begging for it myself; why do you ask me?"
The minister said, "Since you have entered my kingdom, I must question you, and you must answer me. At that moment,
the brahmin was about to answer truthfully, but his heart was filled with terror, fearing that the minister would take his life.
At that time, the five hundred ministers said to the brahmin: "Do not be afraid.
For the sake of the Great King, we now grant you fearlessness."
"O poor Brahmin, why do you have such an urgent need for this head of pus and blood?

We five hundred people shall each provide one head made of the seven treasures; let us trade with you and give you whatever else you require, so that for seven generations your family shall lack for nothing."
The Brahmin said, "I do not need it.
At that time, the ministers, their wishes unfulfilled, felt deep distress in their hearts; raising their voices in lamentation, they wept and addressed the Great King, saying:
"Great King! How can you now bear to abandon this kingdom, its people, your queen, and your crown prince, and forever cast us aside for the sake of a single Brahmin?"
The king said, "Now,
for the sake of you all and all sentient beings, I shall sacrifice my body as an act of giving.
When the chief minister heard the king's words and realized that he was determined to give his body to the brāhmaṇa, he immediately reflected to himself:
"How can I now witness the Great King abandoning this life and body?
Having reflected thus, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and took his own life with a blade.
"At that time, the Great King entered the rear garden and summoned the brahmin, saying:
'You have come from afar to beg my head from me.
Out of a heart of compassion and pity for you, I shall not refuse your wish.'"
"May I, in a future life, obtain the head of wisdom to bestow upon you all.
Having spoken these words, he immediately rose, joined his palms, and paid homage toward the ten directions, saying:
"May the compassionate pity of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the majestic spiritual power and assistance of the venerable Bodhisattvas cause this matter of mine to be surely accomplished."
He said to the brahmin,
"Take it with you as you wish. Then the brahmin spoke:
"The King possesses the strength of a great athlete;
should he experience intense pain at this critical moment, he might suddenly change his mind and repent, and being unable to endure the suffering, he might even turn back and harm me."
"If Your Majesty truly can do this, why not bind your own hair to the branch of a tree?
When the king heard these words, compassion arose in his heart:
"This brāhmaṇa is both timid and frail."
"If you cannot sever my head, I shall lose a great benefit.
He then followed these words, bound his hair to a tree himself, and said to the Brahmin:
"Sever my head and place it back into my hand."
"I shall give it to you with my own hand.
Then the brahmin took the sword in his own hand and immediately stepped forward toward the tree.
At that moment, the tree deity struck the brahmin on the head with her hand, and he fell to the ground, unconscious.
At that time, King Mahāprabha said to the tree deity, "You do not assist me;
on the contrary, you create obstacles to the wholesome Dharma.
When the tree deity heard these words, his heart was filled with distress, and he immediately uttered these words:
"How strange! How bitter!"—
thus they cried as blood rained down from a cloudless sky.
Heaven and earth shook violently, and the sun lost its brilliant luster.
At that time, the brahmin severed the king’s head and carried it back to his own country.
Then, the five hundred princes and the various ministers collected the remaining bodily relics of King Mahāprabha and erected a stūpa to make offerings to them.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The chief minister of that time, who heard that King Mahāprabha had given his head as an offering and could not bear it in his heart, and thus immediately took his own life, was none other than Śāriputra here now.
The King Mahāprabha of that time was I myself, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.”

When a bodhisattva practices such asceticism, vowing for the sake of sentient beings and mindful of the kindness of all Buddhas, they thereby transcend [all obstacles] and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Therefore, Śāriputra, hearing that the Tathāgata intends to enter nirvana, your eyes cannot bear to witness it; you have already attained extinction beforehand, no different from what was originally intended.
In ages past, you likewise could not bear to see me relinquish my body and life.
In this rear garden, beneath this very tree, I have given away my heads as a Universal Monarch a full one thousand times; how much more so other parts of my body, such as my limbs and hands?
While these causes and conditions for ascetic practice were being explained, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people attained the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*;
and yet more immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people resolved their minds upon the paths of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*.
The entire assembly—including devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans—having heard the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, departed with joy.

Furthermore, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a band of five hundred thieves who constantly waylaid travelers on the road to plunder them, unjustly ensnaring the innocent and cutting off the royal highway.

At that time, the King of Magadha immediately raised a fourfold army and went to capture them; he sent them to a place in the deep mountains with precipitous cliffs, where he took each thief one by one, gouged out both their eyes, and cut off their ears and noses.
At that time, the bodies of the five hundred bandits were racked with agony, and their lives hung by a thread.
Among these five hundred men was one who was a disciple of the Buddha; he addressed the great multitude, saying:
"Our lives now are not far from ending. Why do we not, with all our hearts, take refuge in the Buddha?"
At that time, the five hundred people simultaneously raised their voices and cried out these words: "Namo Śākyamuni Buddha!

At that moment, while the Tathāgata was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, by the power of his compassion, a great wind arose on Mount Yugandhara, shaking the forests and raising clouds of sandalwood dust that filled the void of space.
The wind immediately blew toward that deep mountain where the bandits were, scattering [the medicine] into their eyes and upon the wounds of their bodies, which were restored as they were before.
At that time, the bandits regained both their eyes and their bodily wounds were healed; the blood was transformed into milk, and they all spoke these words:
"We have now received the profound grace of the Buddha, and our bodies are at peace and well."
"One who would repay the Buddha's kindness should swiftly resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having uttered these words, the entire great assembly spoke with one voice, saying:
"For all sentient beings who have not yet found peace, we shall bring them peace;..."
I shall liberate all sentient beings who are not yet liberated;
I shall deliver those who have not yet been delivered;
and I shall cause those who have not attained the Way to attain nirvana.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s compassion, skillful means, and supernormal powers are inconceivable.
When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, there were five hundred men dwelling in Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa who blocked the roads, plundered people, and committed various unlawful acts.

At that time, the Tathāgata, through the power of skillful means, manifested a person riding a great elephant named Mahānāman, his body clad in armor and weapons, carrying a bow and arrows, and holding a spear and a javelin in his hands.

The great elephants he rode were all adorned with the seven treasures, and the man himself was likewise adorned with the seven treasures; his pearl rings and ornaments all emitted radiance as he entered the perilous path alone and proceeded toward Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
At that time, five hundred bands of thieves in the mountains saw this man from afar and said to one another:
"We have been robbers for many years, yet we have never seen such a person as this."
At that time, the leader of the bandits asked the men, "What did you see? They replied:
"I saw a man riding a great and famous elephant, adorned with necklaces and ornaments, as well as the elephant's trappings—all made entirely of the seven treasures.
It emitted a great radiance that illuminated and shook heaven and earth."
"He has come along the road and is moreover alone.
If we were to capture this man, our livelihood—food and clothing—would not lack for seven generations."
At that time, having heard these words, the leader of the bandits felt great joy in his heart; he secretly issued a command to his men, saying:
"Be careful not to strike or shoot them; seize them gently."
They immediately surrounded him from front and back, all shouting out at once.
At that time, five hundred people raised their voices in unison.
Then the emanated man, moved by the power of compassion and feeling pity for them, drew his bow and loosed his arrows, shooting at them.

At that time, each of the five hundred men was struck by an arrow; the pain from their wounds was so unbearable that they all immediately collapsed to the ground, rolling about and wailing loudly as they rose together to pull out the arrows.
The arrow was so firm that it could not be withstood by force.
At that moment, the five hundred men were seized with terror, thinking, "We shall surely die now; there is no doubt."
"Why is this? For this single individual is difficult to oppose; such a person has never existed since time immemorial.
Then, speaking with one voice, they addressed him with a verse:
“Who are you, O noble one? Is this the power of incantations, or are you a nāga, a spirit, or a deity? With a single arrow you have shot five hundred;
the pain is beyond description, and we take refuge in your person.”
"Extract the poisonous arrow for me; I shall follow your instructions and not dare to disobey.
At that time, the transformed person replied with a verse:
"In inflicting wounds, none is worse than evil; in shooting arrows, none is worse than anger."
"This strength none can uproot; it can only be removed through extensive learning.
When the transformed person had spoken this verse, he immediately resumed his Buddha-body and emitted a great radiance that shone throughout the ten directions.
All sentient beings who encounter this light shall have the blind see, the lame regain their stride, and those with crippled limbs or paralysis regain the use of their hands and feet;
likewise, those who are deluded by false views shall behold the true words.
In brief: all that was not to their liking shall be fulfilled according to their wishes.
At that time, the Tathāgata instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened the five hundred people, preaching various teachings to them.

At that time, the five hundred people rejoiced upon hearing the Dharma; their bodily sores were healed, and their blood turned back into milk. Immediately, they gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and together, in one voice, spoke this verse:
"We have now resolved our minds To bring vast benefit to all sentient beings;
We should always maintain reverence And study in accordance with the Buddhas."
Through the power of the Buddha’s compassion, one is uprooted from suffering and the body and mind find peace;
one should thus contemplate the Buddha’s kindness, as well as that of the Bodhisattvas,
spiritual friends, teachers, parents, and all classes of sentient beings.
"His mind is impartial toward enemies and kin; In his kindness and virtue, there is no duality.

At that time, in the void of space, the gods of the desire realm, including Kauśika and others, rained down various celestial flowers and performed divine music to make offerings to the Tathāgata. With one voice and in unison, they spoke this verse:
"By the merit of our past lives, Our radiance is most magnificent and adorned."
With all manner of wondrous offerings, may all beings be benefited.
A World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter, and the sublime Dharma is likewise difficult to hear.
Having planted the roots of myriad virtues in past lives, one now meets the Divine One among the Śākyas.
Recalling the Buddha’s kindness, we too shall resolve to attain the Way.
Having now beheld the Buddha, all the merit of our three karmas,
for the sake of all sentient beings, we dedicate toward the unsurpassed path.
At that time, after the devas had spoken these verses, they circumambulated the Buddha a hundred thousand times, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and departed through the air.
Furthermore, the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means, kindness, and roots of goodness is inconceivable.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the kingdom of Vaiśālī who clung to false views and was greedily attached to pride.
Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to his house, where they preached the Dharma to comfort him; however, he did not believe or accept it, remaining obstinately attached to his erroneous doctrines.
His family was immensely wealthy with immeasurable treasures, yet he had no son; once he passed away, his fortune would have been confiscated by the state.
Having reflected on this, he made offerings to various mountains and tree spirits for ninety days, after which his wife perceived she was pregnant and, when the months were full, gave birth to a son.
The boy was handsome, endowed with all the marks of excellence; his parents cherished him, and the multitude revered him.
When he reached the age of twelve, he went out with his peers to sightsee.
On the road he encountered a drunken elephant that charged and trampled him, and he immediately passed away.

When his parents heard of this, they raised their voices and wailed aloud; they threw themselves upon the ground, fell into a state of frantic madness, covered their bodies in dust, tore out their hair, and spoke these words:
"How meager was our fate! To lose our treasure while still alive!"

He went to where the child was, embraced the corpse, and wailed aloud with a piercing cry; he fainted and then revived, his mind falling into madness and delusion. He wandered about naked until he beheld the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata, by the power of the roots of goodness of his benevolence and compassion, manifested a son for them.
At that moment, the parents immediately came forward to embrace him with immeasurable joy; their madness and delusion were instantly extinguished, and they regained their original minds.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately preached the Dharma for them.
Because they heard the Dharma, they immediately resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, the power of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness and compassion is inconceivable.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka raised a fourfold army and marched against the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Having captured the Śākya princes, he dug pits and buried them, making the pits level with their armpits so that they could not move.
After one week had passed, the Tathāgata, by the power of his roots of goodness consisting of loving-kindness and compassion, immediately transformed that ground into a bathing pool.

The water of that pool possessed the eight meritorious qualities, and it was filled with exquisite fragrant flowers—namely, padma flowers and puṇḍarīka flowers—in blue, yellow, red, and white, each as large as a chariot wheel.
Various species of birds sang together in mournful harmony.
When the sons of the Śākyas witnessed this event, joy arose in their hearts, and they immediately conceived the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Once they had generated the bodhicitta, King Virūḍhaka immediately gave wine to five hundred black elephants until they were completely intoxicated with frenzy; he then equipped their feet with iron armor and fastened sharp swords to their trunks.
He immediately sounded the evil drum and released a multitude of elephants to trample the Śākyas.
Their limbs and joints were crushed, and their skin and bones were mangled and strewn across the ground.
Yet, by the power of the Tathāgata’s compassion, their bodies and minds remained peaceful and joyful.
Because body and mind are at peace and happy, one gives rise to the bodhicitta;
because one has given rise to the bodhicitta, one attains a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;
because the mind is equanimous, one does not give rise to anger.
Because their minds were free from anger, they were reborn in the heavens at the end of their lives.
Having been born in the heavens, they immediately used their divine eyes to look back upon their former conditions and said to one another:
"It is by the compassionate grace of the Buddha that we have attained birth in the heavens."

The palaces of the seven treasures, the named garments and superior robes, the various radiances of the body, the subtle and exquisite music, and all instruments of pleasure—all these are the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, we shall give rise to great compassion to benefit all sentient beings.

Wherever the Buddha-dharma is propagated—whether in cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, beneath trees, in palaces, or in private dwellings—wherever it is recited, copied, or its meaning explained, we shall provide whatever is needed according to their wishes at those places of propagation, ensuring they lack for nothing.
Should there be warfare, epidemics, or famine, we shall protect them day and night, never abandoning them in our hearts.
