At that time, having made these vows, the bodies, lives, physical strength, and radiance of the devas became twice as brilliant as usual; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they departed, flying through the air.
Furthermore, the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means, kindness, and roots of goodness is inconceivable.

At that time, King Virūḍhaka, having invaded the Śākya kingdom and slaughtered the Śākyas, selected Śākya women—choosing those who were beautiful, possessed extraordinary talent, and each had countless attendants. He took five hundred such women, surrounded by them before and behind, and returned to his own country while performing songs and music.
The queen and her court ladies ascended the main hall, sat cross-legged, and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"I am now joyful; my well-being is immeasurable."
Then the Śākya women asked King Virūḍhaka,
"How are you happy now? He replied:
"I have defeated the enemy.
The Śākya women said,
"You have not defeated him."

Even if all the fourfold army of your kingdom were unable to match a single member of my Śākya clan, nevertheless, as these Śākyas are disciples of the Buddha, they do not contend over material things; thus, I shall allow you to be victorious.
If you were to give rise to evil, you have previously raised armies three or four times against the kingdom of Śrāvastī, yet you always retreated.
When you first went there, my Śākya clansmen said:
"This King Virūḍhaka does not recognize the bounds of gratitude; on the contrary, he has given rise to wicked rebellion."
If we were to engage them in battle, there would be no distinction between the wise and the foolish, nor any clarity regarding right and wrong.
We should now strike fear into them so as to cause them to retreat and disperse.
He immediately established a vow, saying:
"Now, let all of you shoot at him together, ensuring that the arrows do not wound him.

He then raised his fourfold army and went upstream to the place called Li-li, forty *li* away. There he drew his bow and shot at him; the arrows followed one after another in succession, each shaft meeting the next so that their feathered ends touched.
When King Virūḍhaka saw this, he was struck with terror and retreated back home.
After ninety days had passed, he again raised a fourfold army to wage war against the Śākyas.
At that time, the Śākyas deliberated together, saying:
"The wicked Devadatta knows no shame; he has come once more, wishing to harm us.
Thereupon, the Śākyas again established a solemn vow:
"Today, all of you shall shoot at armor together, taking care not to injure anyone.
Then the Śākyas all shot at it simultaneously, causing the armor and weapons worn by everyone to be shattered and torn apart, so that they stood there naked.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka, harboring fear and trepidation in his heart, immediately assembled his ministers and deliberated with them, saying:
"We now fear we shall not all survive.
Among them, a chief minister addressed the Great King, saying:
"These Śākyas are all disciples of the Buddha; they uphold the precept against killing and practice loving-kindness and compassion.
Had it not been for this, our lives would have perished long ago."
The King said, "If this is indeed so, you may advance further.
At that time, the Śākyas halted with their hands joined, and the army of Devadatta drew close.
Among the Śākyas, there was a certain brāhmaṇa who said to the Śākya sons:
"Now that this calamity has arrived, why do you remain so composed? The Śākyas replied:
"We do not contend with material things now;
if we were to contend with him, we would no longer be disciples of the Buddha.
At that time, the brahmin took offense at these words, sprang forward before Śākya, and fought with Virūḍhaka, shooting seven arrows for every one of his.
Before long, the number of those wounded and killed increased further.
The four armies were scattered and retreated.
At that time, the Śākyas again thought to themselves:
"We should not now associate with this evil man as his comrades.
They immediately assembled the Śākya community and collectively expelled this man of the Brāhmaṇa caste.
Once they had been expelled, the four armies of Virūḍhaka ravaged the houses and destroyed the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
By these causes and conditions, you have achieved victory.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka felt shame and remorse; he summoned the caṇḍālas and immediately had their ears and noses cut off, and severed their hands and feet.
Having severed her hands and feet, they immediately placed her upon a carriage and abandoned her among the burial mounds.

At that time, the Śākya women rolled about on the ground; deprived of both hands and feet, they wailed with bitter lamentation, their bodies wracked by agonizing suffering, with but little life remaining.
At that time, the Śākya women each called out the names of their parents, brothers, and sisters; some even called upon the heavens and cried out to the earth in immeasurable agony.
Among them, the foremost Śākya woman addressed the other women, saying: "Sisters!..."
You should know that I have heard from the Buddha:

"If there is a person who, even in the midst of an urgent crisis, can give rise to a single thought of mindfulness of the Buddha and take refuge with a sincere heart, they shall immediately attain peace and security, and each shall have their wishes fulfilled."
Then the five hundred Śākya women, with one voice and single-mindedly, called to mind the Buddha: “Namo Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Again he cried out: "Alas! Alas! What suffering!"
How painful! How painful! Alas!

"Bhagavān, Sugata! As they uttered these words, by the power of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness born of loving-kindness, a great cloud of great compassion arose in the sky and rained down a rain of great compassion upon the bodies of all the women.
Once they had received the rain, their bodies, hands, and feet were restored to their former state.
The women rejoiced and together cried out these words:

"The Tathāgata, our compassionate father, the unsurpassed World-Honored One, the wondrous medicine of the world, the eye of the world, is able to uproot suffering within the triple realm and bestow happiness."
Why is this? Because we have now been delivered from suffering and hardship.
We should now be mindful of the Buddha’s kindness, and we should be mindful of repaying that kindness.
The women thought to themselves:
"By what means shall we repay the Buddha's kindness?

The Tathāgata’s body is a vajra-body, an eternally abiding body, a body free from hunger and thirst, a body of subtle and wondrous form; it is fully endowed with hundreds of thousands of dhyānas, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the inconceivable thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics."
Possessing the two adornments, we abide in Great Nirvana;
we regard all sentient beings equally as we do Rāhula, viewing enemies and kin with impartiality, and we likewise expect no recompense.
We who are here now wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness; we shall together leave the household life, practice and uphold the prohibitive precepts, and protect and maintain the True Dharma.
Having reflected thus, she immediately sought out her robes and bowl and went to the Bhikṣuṇī-vihāra in Rājagṛha to seek ordination.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs saw the Śākya women, who were young in years and possessed of beautiful and upright features, and said:
"How is it that you can now renounce what is so difficult to renounce and go forth together?"
"We should explain to him the pleasures of the five worldly desires, saying: 'Wait until your term has expired, and then leave the household life; would that not be most delightful?
If he returns to lay life, he will surely offer his robes and alms bowl to us.'"
Having reflected thus, he immediately related the aforementioned matter to the daughters of the Śākya clan.
Upon hearing it, the daughters were filled with distress, thinking:
"In this place of security, how can there be such great terror?"
Just as a meal of delicacies mixed with poison,
so too is what this bhikṣuṇī has said.
I already fully understand that the five worldly desires possess many faults and afflictions.
"Why do you instead praise its excellence and urge us to return to our own homes to dwell amidst the five desires?
Having spoken these words, he raised his voice and wept bitterly, then departed from the monks' quarters.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Huāsè (Utpalavarṇā), who asked the women:
"Why are you weeping? The women replied:
"You have not achieved your wish.
The bhikṣuṇī asked, "What was your wish?"
She replied, "I wish to go forth into homelessness, but I have not received permission.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā asked:
"If you wish to leave the household life, I can ordain you.
Upon hearing this, the women were filled with joy; they immediately followed him and were ordained as his disciples.
At that time, the Śākya women, having received permission, were filled with a mixture of grief and joy, and spoke these words:

"Upādhyāya, you should know that while we lived at home, our sufferings were manifold: the death of our kinsmen, the cutting off of our ears and noses, and the amputation of our hands and feet; our calamities were most grievous."
At that time, the Upādhyāya replied to his disciples:
"What need is there to speak of your hardships?
When I was living at home, I bore many kinds of suffering; those matters were numerous."
Then the Śākya women knelt on their right knees and addressed their teacher, saying, "We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions of the sufferings of household life.

At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī Puṣpā immediately entered into samādhi; by her supernormal powers, she emitted a great radiance that illuminated Jambudvīpa, summoning all those with karmic connections—devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans—to the great assembly, whereupon she spoke of her own accord:
"When I was at home, I was a citizen of Śrāvastī.
My parents married me off to a man from the north.
According to the customs of that country, when a wife becomes pregnant and is about to give birth, she returns to her parents' home."
In this manner, after several years had passed since her successive births, she became pregnant once more.
On the day she was about to give birth, both husband and wife mounted their carriage and horse and returned together to her parents' home.
Along the way there was a river with a long, cascading torrent.
The road was vast and desolate, fraught with many dangers from bandits.
Having reached the river, he was unable to cross it and stayed overnight on its bank.
During the first watch of the night, my belly suddenly pained me, and I immediately sat up.
Not long thereafter, I gave birth, and a son was born.
Among the grass on the riverbank was a large, venomous snake that, smelling the scent of fresh blood, immediately came toward me.
Before it had reached my location, my husband and the slave were sleeping in the path.
The snake went to where the slave was and immediately bit him to death;
it then went to where her husband was, and since he was asleep and did not wake, it also bit him to death.
At that time, I cried out:
"Snake! Snake! she cried, but her husband did not respond; her husband and servant were already dead.
At that time, the venomous snake also bit the oxen and horses.
When the sun had risen, the husband’s body was swollen and putrefied; his bones and joints were disarticulated, and he lay in a state of utter disorder upon the ground.
Overcome by grief, sorrow, and terror, they fainted and fell to the ground;
they wailed aloud with loud cries, beating their breasts with their hands;
they tore out their own hair and covered their bodies in dust.
Soon thereafter, he fell into a swoon and cast his entire body into the water.
Suffering such grief and distress for several days, he remained alone on the bank as the water gradually receded.

Carrying the small child, she held him with her hand; the woman who had recently given birth placed the infant in her skirt and held it in her mouth, then immediately stepped forward and entered the water.

When they reached the middle of the river, she looked back at her eldest son and saw a fierce tiger running and chasing him; as she cried out with her mouth open, her skirt slipped from her body, and the infant was submerged in the water.
He reached out with his hand to feel for them, but in the end he could not find them;
the one on his back slipped from his grasp and fell into the water, where it soon sank and was lost;
and the one on the shore was devoured by a tiger.
Having seen this, my heart and liver were rent asunder and I spat out warm blood, crying out with a loud voice:
"How strange! How strange!"
"I have now suddenly witnessed such a cruel calamity!
Having said this, he reached the shore and collapsed to the ground in a faint.
Not long after, a large caravan arrived.
At that time, among my companions was an elder who had been a long-standing acquaintance of my parents.
I went forward and inquired after their welfare.
The elder then replied to me, saying:
"Last night a fire broke out at your parents' home; everything was consumed by the flames, and both your parents have perished.
Upon hearing this, I fainted and fell to the ground, regaining consciousness only after a long time.
Before long, a band of five hundred thieves arrived and scattered the rest of the group.
At that time, the leader of the thieves took me away.
According to the custom of the thieves' wives, I was constantly made to guard the gate; whenever there was an emergency or someone pursued by others, I had to open the gate quickly.
Later, at one time, her husband went out with a band of thieves to commit robbery and plunder.
At that time, the wealthy owner of the property, the king, and the local villagers joined forces to pursue them, and he was immediately returned to his home.
At that time, his wife was inside the house giving birth to a son.
Although her husband called out from outside the gate two or three times, no one opened the door from within.
Then the leader of the bandits thought to himself:
"This woman now wishes to harm me.
Having thought this, he immediately climbed over the wall and entered, saying to his wife:
"For what reason do you not open the door?"
The wife said,
"It is because of giving birth that I have not been able to do so.
When the bandit leader saw this, his anger subsided slightly, and he spoke to his wife, saying:
"When a woman is pregnant, she is bound to have a child.
Because you are about to give birth, you have brought harm upon me; what use is this child?
Go quickly and kill it!"
At that time, his wife felt compassion in her heart and could not bear to kill him.
Then the leader of the bandits drew his sword and struck, severing his hands and feet, and said to his wife,
"Can you eat him now?"
"If you do not eat it, I shall cut off your head.
At that time, out of fear, the wife immediately returned to eating it.
Once she had resumed eating, her anger subsided.
"Later, her husband again committed robbery and was captured by the king, who immediately punished him for his crime.
According to the law for dealing with such thieves, his life must be taken and he is to be buried alive together with his wife."
At that time, my body was adorned with exquisite necklaces.
Then, a person who coveted those necklaces opened the grave during the late hours of the night, took my necklaces, and carried me away as well.
After a short time had passed, the royal officers who were on watch captured him; they adjudicated him according to the law, sentencing him as one would for the crime of a thief.
The law for punishing thieves was to execute him and then bury him alive together with his wife.
Because the burial was not secure, during the following night, many tigers and wolves dug up the grave, opened it, and devoured the corpse.
For this reason, I was able to escape immediately.
Having emerged, he was disoriented and bewildered, not knowing east from west, and so he immediately ran off.
Seeing many people on the road, he asked them:
"O people, you should know that I am now in great distress."
"Where might one find the ability to forget sorrow and eliminate affliction?
At that time, there was an elderly brahmin who, out of a heart of compassion, spoke to me, saying:
"I have heard that within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, there is much peace and security, and no decline or distress."
Having heard this, my heart was filled with joy; I went to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and left the household life.
By practicing the stages of cultivation in succession, I immediately attained the fruits of the Path, achieving the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
"For these reasons, you should know that when I was at home, my diligent exertions were such as this.
It was by these causes and conditions that I personally attained the Way.
When the Śākya women heard these words, their hearts were filled with great joy, and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The members of the assembly each made their own vows and departed with joy.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the Bhikṣuṇī Gautamī, addressed all the Bhikṣuṇīs, Śikṣamāṇās, Śrāmaṇerikās, Upāsikās, and all women, saying:

"The great benefit of the Buddha-Dharma, all its merits, and its threefold fruits of retribution exist only within the ocean of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-Dharma; all sentient beings have a share in them, yet we women are not permitted [to receive them] by the Tathāgata."
Because all women have many doubts and delusions, they cling to things and find them difficult to relinquish.
Due to this clinging, their various karmic fetters and afflictions bind them limitlessly; ignorance and craving shroud their minds.
Because this shrouding of the mind is so heavy, they are submerged in the waters of craving and cannot emerge on their own.
Because of the two kinds of inferior wisdom, and due to indolence, pride, and laziness, they are unable to adorn their present bodies with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;

they lose the supreme fruit of being a Wheel-Turning Sage King within the cycle of birth and death; and because they fail to gather sentient beings through the ten wholesome dharmas, they also lose the unsurpassed position of a Brahma King.
[Yet,] they are able to establish the True Dharma, exhorting and requesting it so that all sentient beings may obtain benefit and happiness.
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not permit women to delight in becoming his disciples.

Because Māra, the Pāpīyas, as well as all heterodox teachers with false views, have for a long night been malicious and perverse, clinging to erroneous doctrines, destroying the True Dharma, and slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; therefore, the Tathāgata does not permit women to delight in entering the Buddha-dharma.
"For the sake of all women, I requested the Tathāgata three times, desiring to seek the Buddha-dharma; though I did so up to three times, he still did not grant my request.

At that time, having failed to achieve my wish, my heart was filled with regret and resentment, and overcome by sorrow, grief, and suffering, I immediately left the Jetavana Monastery, my eyes brimming with tears of lamentation."
"At that time, Ānanda immediately asked me:
'Mother, for what reason are you so sorrowful?
I then replied to my attendant Ānanda:"
"I wish to seek renunciation and practice the Buddha-dharma; I have requested the Tathāgata three times, yet the Tathāgata has not granted my request.
For this reason, I am filled with sorrow."
At that time, Ānanda immediately replied to me, saying:
"O woman, do not grieve.
I shall petition the Tathāgata to enable you to enter the Buddha-dharma."
Having heard these words, Gautamī was filled with great joy.
At that time, Ānanda entered and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I now wish to petition the Buddha for one vow.
The Buddha said,
"I grant you leave to speak it."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The woman Gautamī nursed and raised the physical body of the Tathāgata.
Even until his attainment of Buddhahood today, he was established through reliance upon that mother."
A mother has rendered great kindness to the Tathāgata;
since the Tathāgata permits all sentient beings to enter the Buddha-dharma, how much more so should he permit a mother?
The Buddha told Ānanda: “It is as you have said.
It is not that the Tathāgata is unaware of the profound debt of gratitude women owe him; it is simply that he does not delight in allowing women to enter the Buddha-dharma.”

If the Tathāgata were to permit women to enter the Buddha-dharma, the True Dharma would gradually diminish and eventually perish within five hundred years; for this reason, the Tathāgata does not take pleasure in permitting women to enter the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, Ānanda prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Ānanda reflects upon the past Buddhas, all of whom possessed the fourfold assembly; why is it that our Śākyamuni Tathāgata alone does not possess them?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If Gautamī loves and delights in the Buddha-dharma, exerts great diligence, and purely cultivates the eight rules of respect, she shall be permitted to enter the Buddha-dharma."
Ānanda immediately prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then went outside, saying to the woman:
“Ānanda has already entreated the Tathāgata, so that you may receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.”
Having heard these words, Gautamī was filled with great joy and said to Ānanda: "Excellent, Ānanda!
You have been able to earnestly entreat the Tathāgata so that this woman may fulfill her original vow."
Ānanda fully proclaimed the Tathāgata’s earnest instruction.
Upon hearing it, the woman was filled with a mixture of grief and joy:
"This body of mine is an impermanent body; today I have finally been able to exchange it for a precious body."
Now, this life of mine perishes and changes from moment to moment, a succession of fluxes without constancy; today, for the first time, I trade it for a precious life.
All that I possess—body, life, and wealth—is shared through various conditions and has no true master; today, I have finally obtained precious wealth in exchange.
Reflecting thus upon these merits and benefits, I conceived a sense of profound reverence and a desire to make offerings to Ānanda,
and said to him: "Venerable Ānanda!
"May you have no further concern!
We shall fully practice and uphold the secret teachings of the Tathāgata; even at the cost of our lives, we shall never backslide or abandon them.
The Tathāgata shall now proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Eightfold Respect, which is difficult to violate."
At that time, the mother Gopā, having cultivated her mind with great compassion for the sake of all women of the future, addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If, in the midst of the evil world of the future, there should be virtuous women who believe in, delight in, love, and revere the Buddha-dharma, we only pray that you will grant permission for them to receive this same example.
The Buddha said: "Excellent!

If there are women who protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, gradually training in and practicing the precepts, generosity, extensive learning, and all wholesome dharmas—whether as laypeople or renunciants—in the three refuges, the five precepts, up to the full precepts, as well as the various liberations and the factors conducive to enlightenment, they are permitted to practice these all at will. They shall likewise attain these three kinds of fruits and rewards: rebirth among humans, devas, or nirvāṇa."
When Gautamī heard these words, her heart was filled with joy, and she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If this is indeed the fruit of retribution, it is truly the grace of the Buddha."
The Buddha said: "Do not speak thus.
The Tathāgata never bestows a favor upon sentient beings, nor does the Tathāgata ever calculate that he has conferred a favor upon them."
To calculate those to whom one owes a debt of gratitude is to destroy the Tathāgata’s mind of equanimity. Kauṭamī!
You should know that regarding all sentient beings, whether they owe a debt of gratitude or not, the Tathāgata possesses no partiality.
Why is this? If there are sentient beings who harm the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not feel anger;
if there are sentient beings who smear sandalwood juice upon the Tathāgata’s body, the Tathāgata does not feel joy.
The Tathāgata regards all sentient beings— whether enemies or kin—
with universal equanimity; it was solely for the sake of Ānanda,
and not out of partiality toward the Tathāgata, that he enabled these women to enter the Buddha-dharma.

Kauṇḍinya! In the future, at the end of the age, if there are bhikṣuṇīs or any other virtuous women who constantly and with a sincere heart mindfully recollect the kindness of Ānanda, invoking his name to make offerings, and honoring, respecting, and praising him without interruption.
"If you are unable to do so, you must constantly, throughout the six periods of day and night, ensure that your minds do not forget it.
Then, Kautamī addressed the bhikṣuṇīs and all virtuous women, saying:
"We should, with a sincere heart, take refuge in the Great Teacher Ānanda."

If there are women who desire peace and security, as well as auspicious karmic fruits, they should always, on the eighth day of the second month and the eighth day of the eighth month, don clean and pure garments, wholeheartedly observe the eightfold precepts of the fast, and practice great diligence throughout the six periods of the day and night.
Ānanda immediately employed his great majestic spiritual power to provide protection and assistance in response to the request; thus, it was obtained exactly as wished.
At that time, the great assembly in the gathering heard the Dharma with joy, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Gratitude through Great Expedient Means, Scroll Five.

Chapter Eight: Upāli. At that time, the Tathāgata was surrounded by a great assembly who made offerings to him with reverence, respect, honor, and praise.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat and observed the minds of the assembly, seeing that they were all filled with doubt:
"O Tathāgata, World-Honored One!
Why have you permitted a person of lowly birth such as Upāli to follow the Buddha and leave the household life?"

Because you permitted his renunciation of the world, you have brought disgrace upon all kings of the Kṣatriya caste, increased their lack of respect, and defiled their faith; thus, you have caused them to lose the field of merit forever and have led the prince Śuddhodana’s son, the bhikṣu Nanda, to give rise to a mind of contempt.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly: "Listen well!

You may indeed say that the Tathāgata lacks impartial great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, and the fivefold wisdom-samādhi; but you must not say that the bhikṣu Upāli was truly a person of low birth, who practiced inferior conduct, made inferior vows, and exerted inferior diligence."
"You may indeed speak of the Tathāgata as having afflictions, being impermanent and subject to change; however, you cannot say that Upāli was a low-born person who left the household life.
The Tathāgata, through his perfect and universal knowledge, proclaims words of truth; you should all faithfully accept the Buddha’s words."

The Tathāgata, knowing and seeing the faults and afflictions of birth and death, attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha and became a Buddha; Upāli also followed him into homelessness, attaining the three insights and six supernormal powers, and being fully endowed with the eight liberations. He was held in ever-increasing veneration by the great assembly of devas and humans; he protected and upheld the True Dharma, being foremost in the mastery of the Vinaya, worthy of offerings, and capable of enabling sentient beings to achieve the three kinds of wondrous fruits—namely, those of the present life, the next life, and subsequent lives.

Therefore, you should know that Upāli’s extraordinary and wondrous conduct was especially due to his being a Bodhisattva of Great Compassion; he had already planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas in the past, and he was foremost in upholding the Vinaya among the teachings of those Buddhas, as well as foremost in upholding the Vinaya within the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the bhikṣu Nanda rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the feet of Mahākātyāyana, and proceeded in order to stand before Upāli, bowing slightly while keeping his palms joined.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses for Nanda:
"Nanda, you should know this:
do not grieve over poverty, nor shall you lose your wealth and nobility."
"The Dharma for those who have left the household life ought to be thus.

Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, exhortation, benefit, and joy, as well as his various discourses on the Dharma, Nanda felt great happiness in his heart. He immediately adjusted his robes and prostrated himself, placing his head at the feet of Upāli.
At that moment, the heavens and earth shook in six ways; their bodies and minds became supple, they attained their own benefit, and what was to be done had been accomplished.
The Buddha told Upāli:

“Quickly let out a lion’s roar regarding the Three Jewels and the Four Truths, and the distinctions among the seven assemblies of the laity and the ordained—namely, the three refuges, the five precepts, and even all the precepts: the precept of benefiting sentient beings, the precept of purifying afflictions, the precept of regulating majestic deportment, the dhyāna-precept, and the untainted (anāsrava) precept—and cause the Three Jewels to flourish.”
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is only because the Tathāgata has drawn me in and protected me with his majestic spiritual power that I am able to ask even this small question.”
“What is meant by the Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
If the Three Jewels have no intrinsic nature, how can one distinguish and speak of the different names for the Dharma and the Saṅgha?”
Regarding those who take refuge in the Triple Gem, how should they practice it?
If the three refuges were one, one should not speak of them as three.
If one speaks of the three refuges, how can there be the names of the seven classes of followers?
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Taking refuge in what is called ‘taking refuge in the Buddha’?”
At that time, the Tathāgata explained each term one by one, answering:
“Buddha means ‘awakened,’ because he has awakened to and understood the characteristics of all phenomena.

Furthermore, all sentient beings have long been slumbering within the three realms; since the Buddha’s Dharma-eye has opened, he awakens himself and awakens others, and is therefore called ‘Awakened.’”
"The Buddha is able to attain all dharmas and to expound all dharmas.
He asked: "How does the Buddha expound all dharmas?"
"Is it taught according to the occasion, the assembly, and what is appropriate?
Or is it taught according to specific schools and their respective traditions? He replied:
“The Buddha taught all dharmas according to the capacities of beings and the requirements of the time.
Later, his disciples compiled the Dharma-piṭaka, arranging them by category.

Sometimes the Buddha established rules for his disciples regarding the gravity of offenses—whether they were *sāvaśeṣa* (with remainder) or *anavaśeṣa* (without remainder)—and these were compiled as the Vinaya-piṭaka.”

At times, he taught the mutual arising of cause and effect, as well as the characteristics of the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and karma; these were compiled as the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
For the sake of gods and worldly people, he taught the Dharma according to their needs, which was compiled as the Ekottara Āgama; this is what those who encourage and transform others study.
For the sake of sentient beings with sharp faculties, he taught profound meanings, known as the Madhyama Āgama; this is what scholars study.
The teaching of various methods corresponding to dhyāna constitutes the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, which practitioners of seated meditation study;
that which refutes all non-Buddhists constitutes the *Dīrgha Āgama*. He asked:
"If the Buddha were to speak of everything, there is a sutra which says:
'The Buddha sat beneath a tree, took a branch with its leaves, and asked his disciples:
"Are these leaves on the branch more numerous, or are the leaves on the tree more numerous?'"
He replied, "There are more leaves on the tree.
The Buddha said:
"I know the dharmas as the leaves upon a tree; I have taught the dharmas as the leaves in my palm.
How then can it be said that the Buddha has taught everything?

He replied: "There is 'all' in terms of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and 'all' in terms of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); what is being said here is 'all' in terms of specific characteristics. Some say:"
"The Buddha is able to speak of everything, yet sentient beings cannot receive it all.
It is not that the Buddha is unable to speak. Others say:
"One should say 'All-Knowing' (sarvajña) and speak directly; one must not say 'All-Speaking' (sarvabhāṣin). Question:
"If the Buddha knows and is able to speak, and Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also rely on that knowledge to speak, why are they not called Buddhas?"
He replied: "No.
The Buddha knows that both [knowledge and teaching] are exhausted."
The followers of the Two Vehicles know that there is something inexhaustible regarding their explanations of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Buddha understands all dharmas and is able to give names to them all;
the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot do so.
Furthermore, the Buddha has attained boundless dharmas and is able to expound them boundlessly;
the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot do so.
Furthermore, there are those that are shared and those that are unshared: what the followers of the Two Vehicles have attained is shared, whereas what the Buddha has attained is unshared.
That which is attained by the śrāvakas is known by all three vehicles;
that which is attained by those of the middle vehicle is known by both vehicles;
and that which is attained solely by the Buddha is unknown to the two vehicles, being known only by the Buddha alone.

Furthermore, as the box is large, the lid must also be large; since the Dharma and the characteristics of the Dharma are boundless, the Buddha, with his boundless wisdom, knows and teaches the boundless Dharma.
The wisdom of the two vehicles is limited, and therefore it does not accord with the characteristics of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are the faculty and its object.
The faculty is the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya).
The object is the phenomena that serve as the focal point for wisdom.
In the Buddha, both the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*artha*) are fully perfected, such that there is no dharma among those perceived by wisdom that is not exhausted;
for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), both the faculties and their objects are incomplete.
Furthermore, the Buddha receives the name of "one who has attained knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*), because he understands the characteristics of all dharmas exactly as they are.

The followers of the Two Vehicles do not exhaustively know the fundamental source of phenomena, nor do they possess universal comprehension; therefore, their knowledge cannot be called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
For these various reasons, the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot be called Buddhas.
"Bhagavān" cannot be transmitted through sound, nor can it be explained by means of its literal meaning.
Why is he called the World-Honored One?
Because he is able to know all remedial dharmas.

Furthermore, the languages and sounds of worldly dharmas differ, and worldly people cannot understand one another; the Buddha knows them all, and is therefore called "World-Honored One" (Lokajyestha).
Furthermore, he instructed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Ordinary persons of the two vehicles claim for themselves that they have attained the Dharma."
"Perhaps he delights in silence, or has entered meditative concentration, or for some other reason, he keeps it secret and does not speak of it.
However, regarding the Dharma attained by the Buddha, out of the power of his compassion, he delights in teaching it to others.
Furthermore, why is it so?
It is because he has destroyed the three poisons that he is entitled to be called the World-Honored One (Bhagavat).
[The interlocutor] asks:
"If the followers of the Two Vehicles also destroy the three poisons, why are they not called World-Honored Ones? He replied: "It is not so."
The followers of the Two Vehicles may regress, whereas the Buddha does not regress.
There are three kinds of regression:
regression from the fruit, regression from that which is not the fruit, and regression from what is employed.
Regarding regression from the fruits: among the Śrāvakas, one may regress from the three higher fruits, but not from the lower fruit.
Among those of the Middle Vehicle, there are two types; if one becomes a Pratyekabuddha through practice cultivated over a hundred kalpas, one does not regress from that fruit.
If one was originally of the lower vehicle and attained the three fruits [of the śrāvaka] before becoming a pratyekabuddha, then there is regression from those fruits.
The fruit of Buddhahood does not regress.

Regarding "regression from non-fruits": this refers to those who were oriented toward the three vehicles and regressed before attaining them, or those who, while practicing the three types of karma as bhikṣus, became indolent and failed to progress.
In all that one cultivates, to regress and fail to apply diligence is called "regression due to lack of fruition.

As for "regression through non-application," it refers to not bringing to manifestation the dharmas one has attained; for example, regarding the Buddha’s ten powers or the ten knowledges of the Hīnayāna, one employs only one while the others remain unused.
It is like reciting a sutra of one hundred thousand words: if one does not recite it, all that was gained through its use is lost.
In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there is retrogression from non-attainment; in the Middle Vehicle (Mahāyāna), there is likewise retrogression from non-attainment.
However, for a Buddha, there is no retrogression from non-attainment, because he never fails to apply himself diligently in all practices.
The two vehicles have a "retrogression" (parihāṇi) in terms of their functional application, whereas for the Buddha, it is not fixed.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Among the ten powers, he employs one and does not employ the other nine; therefore, it is called retrogression."
Some say: "There is no case where one does not regress.
For example, when reciting a sutra of two hundred thousand words, because the power of an ordinary person is inferior, they may finish it in one day or two days; [yet they may still regress]."
The Buddha can complete his recitation in an instant.
The Ten Powers are likewise: they function exactly as they are employed.
Because there are no obstructions, there is no failure in their application.
It is further said:
"The Buddha never acts without purpose.
For example, when he puts on the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, he does not do so in the manner of ordinary worldlings; rather, it is entirely for the sake of benefiting sentient beings."

"Regarding all dharmas employed, one employs those that are beneficial and does not employ those that are not beneficial; it is not that they cannot be employed, but rather they are set aside because they are of no use.
Although each has their own understanding, they say that [the truth] cannot be fixed.
"The Buddha's intention is inconceivable. He asked:
"For what reason do the Śrāvakas fall back from the three fruits, yet do not fall back from the lower fruit?"
He replied: "One falls away from the three fruits because they have already been attained;
one does not fall away from the lower fruit because it has never been attained."
Just as when a person who is hungry obtains fine food, they do not forget it even after a long time, this principle is likewise.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Regarding the lower fruits, patience (*kṣānti*) acts as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), while knowledge (*jñāna*) acts as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)."
Regarding the three fruits, because wisdom acts as the path of non-obstruction and wisdom acts as the path of liberation, there is falling back.
It is also said:
"In the path of seeing the truths, there is no falling back."
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) involves regression,
because it abandons the notions of purity and impurity by severing the fetters.
The path of cultivation involves oppression, whereas the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga) is without oppression.

"Because one who has seen the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya) is free from oppression, and because one who has seen the Truth perceives the principle of the fetters (saṃyojana), subtle [afflictions] arise only through reflection; therefore, there is no retrogression due to oppression.
It further says:
"The power of the wisdom that has seen the Truth is strong, like a great beam weighing down objects."
"Because the wisdom of reflection is weak, one falls back.
It further states:
"The two minds of patience and knowledge regarding the realm of desire during the vision of the truths can sever the nine grades [of afflictions];"
"The two minds of patience and knowledge in the upper realms sever seventy-two grades of fetters, exhausting those of the formless realm; therefore, one does not fall back.
For this reason, he alone is named the World-Honored One (Bhagavān).
Furthermore, the Buddha has severed all residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), whereas those of the Two Vehicles have not yet exhausted theirs.
For example, the Bhikṣu Go-pālaka constantly chewed like an ox because he had come from among oxen in previous lives;

likewise, there was a bhikṣu who, though he had attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), would always look at himself in a mirror because he had come from among courtesans in previous lives.
"Just as a certain bhikṣu who leaps over threshing floors and throws himself from pavilions did so because he had come from among monkeys throughout successive lifetimes;
yet he cannot be called the World-Honored One.
Generally speaking, when one says 'Thus have I heard,' it refers to the time when the Buddha was still in the world."
The phrase "I have heard" (evam mayā śrutam) refers to the period after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa.
Those who compiled the Dharma-piṭaka say "I have heard"; yet, during the twenty years that the Buddha preached the Dharma, Ānanda did not hear it all—how, then, could he say "I have heard"?
He replied: "It was said:
'The devas spoke to Ānanda.'"
Again it says:
"The Buddha entered into a mundane state of mind so that Ānanda would know.
And again it says:
"I heard it from the bhikṣus.
He further said:
"Ānanda requested a boon from the Buddha, saying:"
"I pray that the Buddha will not give me old clothes, nor allow others to invite me for meals.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma and out of reverence for the Buddha, I shall attend to whatever the Buddha requires, not for the sake of food or clothing."
The bhikṣus see the World-Honored One twice each day, at dawn and dusk; may I not be like them, but have the opportunity to see him whenever I wish.
Furthermore, may all the Dharma taught by the Buddha during his twenty years [of ministry] be explained to me in full.
Question: "By what means can the Dharma-verses taught during twenty years be explained? Answer:

“The Buddha, through his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), can expound immeasurable teachings within a single phrase, and can likewise condense immeasurable teachings into the meaning of a single phrase.
Although the Buddha has merely shown the initial outline, Ānanda has fully understood it all, owing to his swift acumen and powerful faculty of retention.”
Regarding the eighty thousand dharmas, it is further said:

"Just as a tree—consisting of its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves—is called a single tree, so too the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma from beginning to end for the sake of sentient beings is called a single Piṭaka."
"In this manner, there are eighty thousand;
furthermore, it is said:
'A single sitting of the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is called one Piṭaka.'"
Thus there were eighty thousand;
it is also said:
"Sixteen characters constitute half a verse, and thirty-two characters constitute one verse."
"In this way there are eighty thousand;
furthermore, it is said that a long or short verse consists of forty-two characters as one verse."
"In this way there are eighty thousand;
furthermore, it is said:
'The recitation of the precepts once every half-month constitutes one Piṭaka.'"
"In this way, there are eighty thousand;
furthermore, it is said:
'The Buddha himself stated that sixty-six thousand verses constitute one Piṭaka.'"
Thus there were eighty thousand;
furthermore, it says:
"The Buddha said:..."
“There are eighty thousand afflictions, and there are likewise eighty thousand medicinal dharmas.
This is called the “Treasury of Eighty Thousand Dharmas. He asked:
"Why is it that in the Sūtras and Abhidharma the Buddha is not placed at the beginning, whereas in the Vinaya recitation alone the Buddha is placed at the beginning?
He replied: "Because he is supreme."
Because the Buddha alone exercises such restraint.
As in the sūtras, while the disciples may preach the Dharma,
there are times when Śakra Devānām Indra himself speaks of being foremost in generosity.
Why is this? Because by means of my giving, I have become a celestial king and my wishes are fulfilled as I desire; the Buddha has spoken thus.
At times, the Buddha manifests a transformation-buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha), and the transformation-buddha preaches the Dharma.
The Vinaya is not like this; it is taught by all Buddhas, and for this reason, the Buddha is placed at the beginning.
Furthermore, while the Sūtras provide explanations according to various circumstances, the Vinaya does not do so.
If there is business within the dwelling, one must not perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) immediately but must certainly go outside;
if there is business with laypeople, it must be performed in the midst of the assembly;
if there is business in the village, it must likewise be performed in the midst of the assembly.
If there is a matter concerning the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), it must be settled in relation to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; for this reason, the Buddha is placed at the beginning.
As for Vaiśālī, some countries are named after their kings, some are designated by their lands, and some are titled after their cities.
This country is named after its dragon;
the village of Kalandaka is named after its bird.
It is also said:
"Regarding the village head named Sujāta: he was obtained through his parents' prayers and petitions to the deities, hence he was named 'Obtained by Prayer.
As for 'wealthy,' there are two kinds of wealth: first, that which belongs to the category of sentient beings;
second, that which does not belong to the category of sentient beings."
Those who are not sentient beings possess much gold, silver, and the seven treasures, as well as granaries, treasuries, wealth, silks, fields, and houses;
those who are of the class of sentient beings possess slaves, servants, laborers, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, villages, and fiefdoms—therefore, they are called "wealthy."
As for "noble" (guì): some are lords of fiefs, while others possess virtuous qualities and are revered by all people; hence they are called noble.
They take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the Three Refuges precepts.
Question: "What is the nature of the Three Refuges?
Answer: "Some commentators say:"
"The Three Refuges are instruction; they do not possess the nature of instruction.
When receiving the Three Refuges, one kneels on the right knee with palms joined and recites the Three Refuges with the mouth; this is called the instruction of body and speech.
If there is a purely concentrated mind, there may be bodily and vocal non-informative action (*avijñapti*); this is called informative and non-informative action.
It is further said:
"The three refuges are of the nature of the three karmas; namely, the karmas of body, speech, and mind."
It is further stated:
"The Three Refuges are the wholesome five aggregates.

Taking the wholesome five aggregates of sentient beings as the Three Refuges and taking the Triple Gem as that which is taken refuge in—wherein "taking refuge" has the meaning of providing rescue and protection.
For example, suppose there is a person who has committed an offense against a king and flees to another country seeking protection.
The king of that other country says:
"If you seek fearlessness, do not leave my territory and do not disobey my instructions; I shall certainly protect you."
Sentient beings are likewise: bound to Māra and burdened with the offenses of birth and death, they turn toward the Triple Gem to seek protection.
If they are sincere toward the Triple Gem, having no other recourse and not transgressing the Buddha’s teachings, the wicked Māra King can do nothing against them.
Once there was a pigeon being pursued by a hawk.
It entered the shadow of Śāriputra, yet its trembling fear did not cease;
it then moved into the shadow of the Buddha, becoming calm and free from terror. Though the great ocean might be moved, this pigeon remained unmoved.
The reason for this is that the Buddha possesses great kindness and great compassion, whereas Śāriputra does not;
the Buddha’s residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted, whereas Śāriputra’s are not yet exhausted;
the Buddha cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, whereas Śāriputra practiced asceticism for sixty kalpas.
"For this reason, although the pigeon entered the shadow of Śāriputra, it still felt fear;
yet upon entering the shadow of the Buddha, it was without fear. He asked:

"If taking refuge in the Triple Gem can eliminate transgressions and quell fears, why did Devadatta also take refuge in the Triple Gem, leave the household life out of faith, receive full ordination, yet commit the three heinous crimes and fall into the Avīci Hell?"
He replied: "As for those who provide rescue and protection, they save only those who can be saved.
Devadatta’s transgressions are profound and vast, and moreover, this is a fixed karma; therefore, he is difficult to save."
He asked: "If one has committed great sins, the Buddha cannot save them;
if one is without sin, there is no need for the Buddha to save them."
"How can the Three Jewels provide protection?
He replied, "Devadatta took refuge in the Three Jewels with a lack of sincerity; his threefold refuge was incomplete."
Constantly seeking gain, offerings, fame, and reputation, he calls himself an omniscient person and vies with the Buddha.
Because of these causes and conditions, although the Triple Gem possesses great power, it cannot save him.

For example, although King Ajātaśatru committed the crime of parricide and was destined for the Avīci Hell, because he turned toward the Buddha with a sincere heart, his Avīci offense was extinguished and he entered the Kālasūtra Hell instead.
"Just as the gravest crimes among humans are completely extinguished in seven days, this is called the power of the protection of the Triple Gem. He asked:
"If Devadatta’s offenses cannot be saved, there is a sutra that says:"
"If a person takes refuge in the Buddha, they shall not fall into the three evil realms.
What is the meaning of this? He replied:
“Because Devadatta has taken refuge in the Triple Gem, although he has entered the Avīci Hell, his suffering is slight and he occasionally finds temporary relief.
It is like a person in a place of terror within a mountain forest or a vast wilderness; if they recollect the merits of the Buddha, their fear is immediately extinguished.”
"Therefore, taking refuge in the Triple Gem brings unfailing protection.
"Within the Four Noble Truths, under which truth are the Three Jewels subsumed?
Within the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), under which faculty are they subsumed?"
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), by which element is it subsumed?
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), by which base is it subsumed?
Among the five aggregates (*skandha*), by which aggregate is it subsumed?
"Regarding the Three Jewels within the Four Noble Truths, they are subsumed under the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and partially enter into the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).

Among the faculties (*indriya*), they are subsumed under three faculties: the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of 'knowing' (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of 'one who has known' (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), they are subsumed under the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*)."
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it is subsumed within the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*);
among the five aggregates (*skandha*), it is subsumed within the untainted five aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*).
Within the Four Noble Truths, the Jewel of the Buddha is partially included within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Among the Four Noble Truths, the Jewel of the Dharma is subsumed within the Truth of Cessation;
among the Four Noble Truths, the Jewel of the Sangha partially enters the Truth of the Path.
Among the twenty-two faculties, the Jewel of the Buddha is subsumed within the faculty of "I-have-known."
The Jewel of the Dharma, being the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) truth of cessation, is not subsumed under the faculties (indriya).
Within the twenty-two faculties, the Jewel of the Saṅgha is subsumed under the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).

As for the Jewel of the Buddha, within the eighteen elements (dhātu), it partially enters into the mind element (manodhātu), the mind-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu), and the dharma element (dharmadhātu).
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it is partially included within the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*);
among the five aggregates (*skandha*), it is partially included within the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).
Within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the Jewel of the Dharma is partially included within the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the Jewel of the Dharma is partially included within the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

This is because the Jewel of the Dharma is not subsumed under the five aggregates (*skandha*); the aggregates are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), whereas the Jewel of the Dharma is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the Jewel of the Sangha is partially included within the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the phenomenon element (*dharmadhātu*).
"Among the twelve bases (āyatana), they are partially included within the mind base (manāyatana) and the phenomena base (dharmāyatana);
among the five aggregates (skandha), they are partially included within the untainted five aggregates. Question:
“Does one who takes refuge in the Buddha take refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha, or does one take refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods of time?
He replied: “One takes refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because the Dharma-body of the Buddhas is identical.”
To take refuge in one Buddha is to take refuge in all Buddhas of the three periods of time, because there is no difference among the Buddhas.

Some say: "If one takes refuge in all Buddhas of the three periods of time, there are devas who speak of themselves, saying, 'I am a disciple of Kāśyapa Buddha,' or 'I am a disciple of Krakucchanda Buddha,' and so forth, each claiming within the context of the seven Buddhas, 'I am a disciple of such-and-such a Buddha.'"
"For this reason, one should properly take refuge in a single Buddha, not in those of the three periods of time.
Others said: "It should not be so."
Why is this? As stated in the *Vaiśravaṇa Sūtra*:
"King Vaiśravaṇa took refuge in the Triple Gem; he took refuge in the Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
"For this reason, one should take refuge in all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
He asked: "If that is so, how should we understand the meaning of the various devas each claiming to be disciples of a particular Buddha?"
He replied: "How can that which the various devas have said be taken as a definitive authority?
There are devas who each claim a single Buddha as their teacher, yet they also take refuge in all Buddhas of the three periods of time; they simply cite one Buddha as their witness."
Question: "What kind of taking refuge is called 'taking refuge in the Buddha'? Answer:
"The words of taking refuge revolve toward omniscience and the qualities of one beyond training. [Question:
"Does one take refuge in the form-body (rūpakāya) or in the dharma-body (dharmakāya)?
[Answer: It is said:
"One takes refuge in the Dharma-body, not in the form-body, because one does not regard the form as the Buddha.
He asked: "If the form-body is not the Buddha, why is it that shedding the blood of the Buddha's body constitutes a heinous offense?"

He replied: "Because the physical body (rūpakāya) is the vessel for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and is that upon which the Dharma-body relies, if one harms the physical body, one incurs the offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
It is not because the physical body is the Buddha that one incurs the offense of immediate retribution."
“Regarding ‘taking refuge in the Dharma,’ what is it that one takes refuge in that is called taking refuge in the Dharma?
He replied: “Taking refuge in the turning away from speech, the severing of desire and the absence of desire, and the state of exhaustion which is nirvāṇa—this is called taking refuge in the Dharma.”
Question: "Does one take refuge in the exhaustion of one's own body, or the exhaustion of another's body? Answer:
"To take refuge in the limit of one's own body and the limit of the bodies of others—this is called taking refuge in the Dharma.
"If one takes refuge in the Sangha, in what does one take refuge?"

He replied: "Taking refuge means turning toward the excellent and auspicious field of merit—the virtues of the śrāvakas who are in training and those who are beyond training; this is called taking refuge in the Saṅgha."
"Is this taking refuge in the Saṃgha of conventional truth, or the Saṃgha of ultimate truth?
If it were taking refuge in the Saṃgha of ultimate truth, then when the Buddha conferred the three refuges upon Tiwei and Boli, he should not have said:
'In the future there will be a Saṃgha; you should take refuge in it.'"
"The Sangha of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) always abides in the world.
He replied: "Because the Sangha of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is that upon which the Sangha of the ultimate truth relies, it is said:"
"There will be a Saṃgha in the future; you should take refuge in it.
Furthermore, this was said because he wished to show respect for the Saṃgha of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The Buddha himself said:
"Among all assemblies, the assembly of the Buddha is foremost.
It is like how from milk comes curd, from curd comes butter, and from butter comes ghee."
"Among these, the finest and most sublime is the clarified butter (sarpis); likewise, it is with the community of the Buddha's disciples.
If there is an assembly of monks gathered therein—the four who have entered the paths and the four who have attained the fruits—they are the unsurpassed field of merit."
Among all ninety-six kinds of assemblies, he is the most honored, the most supreme, and peerless; therefore it is said:
"In the future there will be a Saṃgha; you should take refuge in it."
"This does not violate the correct principle. He asked:
"The Buddha is also the Dharma, the Dharma is also the Dharma, and the Sangha is also the Dharma."
"It is indeed a single dharma; what difference could there be?
He replied, "Although it is a single dharma, from the perspective of its meaning, there are naturally distinctions."
Speaking in terms of the Three Jewels: the great wisdom that is without teacher and all the merits of the stage of no-more-learning constitute the Jewel of the Buddha;
the unconditioned state of the cessation of suffering constitutes the Jewel of the Dharma;
and the merit and wisdom of the Śrāvakas in both the stages of learning and no-more-learning are called the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
In terms of the Dharma: the dharmas of those beyond training and those who have nothing further to learn are called the Jewel of the Buddha;
the unconditioned state of the Truth of Cessation, which is neither a dharma of training nor one beyond training, is called the Jewel of the Dharma;
and the dharmas of Śrāvakas in training and those beyond training are called the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
In terms of the faculties (*indriya*), the Buddha is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*);
the Dharma Jewel is not a faculty;
and the Sangha consists of the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
In terms of the Truths (satya), the Buddha is a partial entry into the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya);
the Dharma Jewel is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya);
and the Sangha is a partial entry into the Truth of the Path.
In terms of the fruits of the śramaṇa, the Buddha is the śramaṇa and the Jewel of the Dharma is the fruit of the śramaṇa;
the Saṃgha is the śramaṇa and the Jewel of the Dharma is the fruit of the śramaṇa.
From the perspective of the *brāhmaṇa*, the Buddha is the *brāhmaṇa* and the Jewel of the Dharma is the fruit of the *brāhmaṇa*;
the Saṅgha is the *brāhmaṇa* and the Jewel of the Dharma is the fruit of the *brāhmaṇa*.
In terms of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), the Buddha is the holy life, and the Jewel of the Dharma is the fruit of the holy life;
the Sangha is the holy life, and the Jewel of the Dharma is the fruit of the holy life.
In terms of cause and effect, the Buddha is the cause and the Jewel of the Dharma is the effect;
the Sangha is the cause and the Jewel of the Dharma is the effect.
In terms of the Path and its fruit, the Buddha is the Path and the Jewel of the Dharma is the fruit.
The Sangha is the Way, and the Dharma Jewel is the fruit.
The Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher; the Buddha is born from the Dharma.
The Dharma is the mother of the Buddha; the Buddha abides in reliance upon the Dharma.
Question: "If the Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher, why is the Dharma not placed first among the Three Jewels? Answer:

"Although the Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha, the Dharma is not propagated without the Buddha; as it is said, 'the Way is propagated by means of persons. For this reason, the Buddha is placed first.
At that time, Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If, when receiving the Three Refuges precept, one first recites the Dharma Jewel and subsequently recites the Buddha, does this constitute the completion of the Three Refuges? He replied:
"If one lacks understanding and speaks out of sequence, one incurs no offense oneself, and the Three Refuges are nonetheless established."
"If one understands something but explains it erroneously, one incurs an offense and the Three Refuges are not established.
He asked: "If one recites the names of the Buddha and the Dharma but does not recite the name of the Sangha, is the Three Refuges established?"
If one recites the names of the Dharma and the Saṃgha but does not recite the name of the Buddha, does this constitute the Three Refuges?
If one recites the names of the Buddha and the Saṃgha but does not recite the name of the Jewel of the Dharma, does this constitute the Three Refuges?
He replied, “The three refuges are not established. He asked:
"If one does not receive the Three Refuges, can one obtain the Five Precepts?
If one does not receive the Three Refuges, can one obtain the Eight Precepts?
If one does not receive the Three Refuges, can one obtain the Ten Precepts?"
"If one does not perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, can one obtain full ordination? He replied,
"In all cases, one cannot."
If one receives the five precepts, one must first receive the three refuges; once the three refuges are completed, one then obtains the five precepts.
The reason for stating the names of the five precepts is to enable the person before one to recognize the names of these precepts.
Just as one obtains full ordination immediately after the conclusion of the formal ritual of the white fourfold motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*),
so too are the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), the four defeats (*pārājika*), and the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣas taught merely for the sake of knowledge.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Once the three refuges have been received and the precept against killing has been proclaimed, at that moment one obtains the precepts.
The reason for saying that by receiving one precept one obtains the five is that if one can uphold even one precept, one is capable of upholding all five.
Furthermore, because the power and scope of the five precepts are mutually interconnected, and because one has also made a vow in one's original intention to receive the five precepts;
it is further said:
"Only after the reception of the five precepts is completed does one obtain the precepts."
Among all such explanations, it is the correct principle that one who has received the three refuges obtains the five precepts.

This is according to the ritual of the white fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*); the same applies to the reception of the eight precepts or the ten precepts, as explained for the five precepts.

“If one has first received the Three Refuges and become a lay follower (upāsaka), and later receives the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the ten precepts, is it necessary to undergo the Three Refuges again?”
Answer: "One does not receive the Three Refuges.
One obtains the precepts in their entirety because one has previously received the Three Refuges."
"If one has not previously received the Three Refuges, but proceeds directly to the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), will they obtain the precepts? Answer:
"Whether receiving the Five Precepts, the Eight Precepts, or the Ten Precepts, if one simply receives the Three Refuges, one immediately obtains the precepts."

If one receives the full precepts (*upasampadā*), they must be obtained through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; the full precepts are not attained by means of the three refuges alone.

For those who possess the full precepts, the merit is profound and weighty; it cannot be achieved without many conditions and much effort. Therefore, it is only after the three refuges, the ten monks, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* that they are obtained.

The merit and power of the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the ten precepts are slight; therefore, if one receives the Three Refuges, one immediately obtains the precepts without requiring many conditions or much effort.
“Having received full ordination, why do you speak only of the four *pārājika* offenses and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, and not mention the other sections?
“These two categories of precepts are the most serious.”
If one precept is violated, a second will never arise again.
Even if it should arise, it is difficult to do so; yet, through the *parivāsa* and *mānatva* penances, one may subsequently be cleared of the offense within an assembly of twenty monks.

If one is able to uphold that which is difficult to uphold, then the other categories of precepts, being easy to uphold, need not be mentioned; therefore, only these two categories are taught, and the others are not.
He asked: "Is this prātimokṣa precept an outflow-free (anāsrava) precept?
Or is it a dhyāna precept?"
He replied: "It is neither the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla) nor the dhyāna precepts.
These prātimokṣa precepts exist only when the Buddha is in the world."
If the Buddha does not dwell in the world, then these precepts do not exist.
However, the dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts exist at all times, whether the Buddha dwells in the world or not.
The *prātimokṣa* precepts are obtained through instruction, whereas the dhyāna and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precepts are not obtained through instruction;
the *prātimokṣa* precepts are obtained from another, whereas the dhyāna and outflow-free precepts are not obtained from another.
The Prātimokṣa precepts exist at all times—whether one is asleep or awake, and whether the mind is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral;
however, the dhyāna and untainted (anāsrava) precepts exist only within a dhyāna or untainted state of mind, and not in any other states of mind.
The *prātimokṣa* precepts exist only among humans; the dhyāna precepts and the untainted (*anāsrava*) precepts exist among both humans and devas.
The *prātimokṣa* precepts exist only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the dhyāna and untainted precepts are accomplished in both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*).
The *prātimokṣa* precepts belong only to the disciples of the Buddha; the dhyāna precepts are possessed by both [Buddhist disciples] and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
He asked: "Among the five precepts for upāsakas, how many are actual transgressions (dosa), and how many are prohibitive transgressions (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya)?"
He replied: "Four are actual transgressions (*sāvadya*), while the precept against drinking alcohol is a prohibitory transgression (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*).

The reason drinking alcohol is grouped with the four transgressions to form the five precepts is that drinking alcohol is the root of heedlessness (*pramāda*) and can lead one to violate those four precepts."

For example, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a lay follower who, because he drank alcohol, committed adultery with another's wife and stole and killed another's chicken. When others asked him, "Why do you act in this way? he replied: "I did not drink the alcohol myself; it was drunk by my father. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by my mother. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by my younger brother. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by my nephew. Because he spoke such words, he fell into hell. Furthermore, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by my grandfather. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by my grandmother. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by my uncle. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by my cousin. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by my great-grandfather. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by my great-grandmother. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by my great-uncle. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by my great-cousin. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by my ancestors seven generations back. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by my ancestors seven generations back. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by my ancestors seven generations back. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by my ancestors seven generations back. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by all sentient beings. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by all sentient beings. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by all sentient beings. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by all sentient beings. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the earth. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the earth. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the earth. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the earth. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the water. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the water. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the water. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the water. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the fire. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the fire. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the fire. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the fire. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the wind. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the wind. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the wind. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the wind. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by space. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by space. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by space. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by space. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the four great elements. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the four great elements. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the four great elements. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the four great elements. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the five aggregates. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the five aggregates. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the five aggregates. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the five aggregates. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the six sense bases. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the six sense bases. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the six sense bases. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the six sense bases. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the twelve links of dependent origination. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the twelve links of dependent origination. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the twelve links of dependent origination. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the twelve links of dependent origination. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the eighteen realms. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the eighteen realms. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the eighteen realms. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the eighteen realms. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the three poisons. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the three poisons. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the three poisons. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the three poisons. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the four types of birth. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the four types of birth. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the four types of birth. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the four types of birth. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the four modes of existence. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the four modes of existence. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the four modes of existence. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the four modes of existence. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the five destinies. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the five destinies. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the five destinies. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the five destinies. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the six heavens of the desire realm. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the six heavens of the desire realm. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the six heavens of the desire realm. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the six heavens of the desire realm. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the seven stages of consciousness. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the seven stages of consciousness. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the seven stages of consciousness. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the seven stages of consciousness. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the eight liberations. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the eight liberations. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the eight liberations. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the eight liberations. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the nine successive abodes. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the nine successive abodes. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the nine successive abodes. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the nine successive abodes. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the ten stages of the bodhisattva. I did not commit the adultery; it was committed by the ten stages of the bodhisattva. I did not steal the chicken; it was stolen by the ten stages of the bodhisattva. I did not kill the chicken; it was killed by the ten stages of the bodhisattva. Because he spoke such words, he also fell into hell. Again, he said, "I did not drink the alcohol; it was drunk by the eleven branches of the path. I did not commit the adultery; it was
He replied, “I did not.
