Because he was deranged by alcohol, he was able to break four precepts all at once.
There are those who, because of drinking alcohol, are able to commit four of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), with the sole exception of causing a schism in the Sangha.
Although this is not a result of past karma, there is the retribution of insanity; because of drinking alcohol, one becomes deluded and disordered, just like a madman.
Furthermore, because one is distracted by alcohol, one neglects and loses one's right livelihood—namely, sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, and assisting in communal affairs.
Although this is not an actual transgression, for these reasons and conditions, it is equivalent to an actual transgression.
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Regarding the Upāsaka precepts, are they obtained only with respect to sentient beings, or are they also obtained with respect to non-sentient things?”
Is the precept obtained only with respect to sentient beings who can be killed, stolen from, sexually violated, or deceived?
Or is it also obtained with respect to sentient beings who cannot be killed, stolen from, sexually violated, or deceived?
He replied: "One obtains the four precepts with respect to sentient beings, and one obtains the precept against drinking alcohol with respect to non-sentient things.
Whether a sentient being may be killed or not, may be sexually approached or not, may be stolen from or not, and whether one may speak falsely or not—in all such cases, the precept is obtained."
From the Avīci Hell below to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana above, throughout the trichiliocosm, and even unto the Tathāgata—all sentient beings who possess life obtain these four precepts.

Because at the time of first receiving the precepts, one refrains from all killing, all stealing, all sexual misconduct, and all false speech without limitation or restriction, for this reason there is no being among all sentient beings who does not obtain the precepts.
In the method of receiving the precepts, one first expounds the Dharma for them, guiding and enlightening them so that they may give rise to a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings.
Once they have attained this superior state of mind (*adhimukti*), they then attain the superior precepts (*adhiśīla*).
Now, upon receiving the dharma of the precepts, one obtains four precepts with respect to each and every sentient being.
These four precepts, when differentiated, constitute twelve precepts.
Regarding sentient beings, there are three causes and conditions for the arising of these four evils: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, and not speaking falsely.
First, it arises due to greed;
second, it arises due to hatred;
third, it arises due to delusion.
Upon all sentient beings there are twelve evils; by reversing these evils, one obtains the form of the twelve virtuous precepts.
It is likewise so for all infinite sentient beings.

Even if there were hundreds of thousands, millions, or tens of millions of Arhats who entered Nirvana, the precepts previously obtained from these Arhats would remain fully accomplished from beginning to end; this precept would not be lost simply because the Arhats have entered Nirvana.

When one receives the precept against drinking alcohol, throughout the beginning and end of this single life, one obtains the "color of the precept" (śīla-rūpa) upon every drop of all the alcohol existing within the three thousandfold world system; this is because at the time of receiving the precept, one vows never to drink any alcohol whatsoever.
"Even if the alcohol is completely consumed, the precept remains constantly accomplished and is not lost.

"When one first receives the precepts, one obtains the precept of celibacy regarding the three orifices of all women; if one subsequently marries a wife, does this constitute a violation of that precept?"
He replied: "There is no offense.
The reason for this is that he originally received the precept against sexual misconduct with respect to women."
Now, this is one's own wife; because it is not an act of sexual misconduct, one does not violate this precept.
By inferring from this principle, all cases are likewise so.

Whether regarding the eight precepts or the ten precepts, whether concerning sentient beings or non-sentient things, the attainment of the precepts is also like this, as is the case with the two hundred and fifty precepts.
Each and every sentient being attains seven precepts; when analyzed according to their meaning, there are twenty-one precepts.
For example, regarding a single sentient being, seven evils of body and speech may arise. Generally, the arising of these evils has three causes and conditions: first, they arise because of greed;
[the second is because of hatred, and the third is because of delusion].
Second, they arise from anger;
third, they arise from delusion.

These seven evils arise through these three causes and conditions. Seven times three makes twenty-one evils. By turning away from evil, one attains the precepts; upon a single sentient being, one attains twenty-one forms of the substance of the precepts (*śīlavarṇa*).
It is the same for all sentient beings.
Inferring from this principle, one may at once attain immeasurable precepts;
yet one cannot at once violate them all, nor can one at once abandon the precepts.
Regarding the dharma of breaking precepts: if one breaks a grave precept, there is no further spiritual progress.
Even if one returns the precepts and receives them again later, one will not obtain the precepts once more.

If one breaks a grave precept among the eight precepts of the fast, one may subsequently receive the eight precepts again, or receive the five precepts, or receive the ten precepts, or receive the full ordination—including both the dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free precepts—but in all such cases, they are not obtained.

If one has already broken a grave precept among the five precepts, even if one receives the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the full ordination, along with the dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free precepts, none of them are obtained.
If, after breaking the five precepts, one wishes to relinquish the five precepts and receive the ten precepts instead, there is no such possibility.

If one has already abandoned the precepts and then receives the five precepts again, or receives the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the full precepts, as well as the dhyāna-precepts or the outflow-free precepts, none of these will be obtained.

If one has violated any of the ten precepts or the grave precepts within the full set of precepts, and wishes to advance further, or wishes to relinquish the precepts and receive them again, it is as explained in the section on the five precepts.
Question: "Among the three types of precepts—the dhyāna-precepts, the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts, and the prātimokṣa precepts—which precept is the most excellent? Answer:
"The dhyāna-precepts are superior. Some say:
"The prātimokṣa-precepts."
The reason for this is that while these precepts exist only when a Buddha appears in the world,
the dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts exist at all times.
One obtains the *prātimokṣa* precepts with respect to both sentient beings and non-sentient entities, whereas the dhyāna and outflow-free precepts are obtained only with respect to sentient beings.

The *prātimokṣa* precepts are obtained through a mind of universal loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; the dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precepts are not obtained through such a mind.

Indeed, that which can sustain the Buddha-dharma among the seven assemblies within the world, ensuring that the fruits of the paths of the three vehicles continue without interruption, is entirely rooted in the *prātimokṣa*. The dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free precepts are not so; therefore, the *prātimokṣa* is the most honored and supreme within the triple world.
At the time of first receiving the precepts, once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been performed, the precepts are fully accomplished.
From the very first moment of thought, the form of the precepts is called "action" (*karman*) and is also called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*).
From the second thought-moment onward, the form of restraint (*śīla-rūpa*) arises; however, this is merely karma and not a path of action (*karmapatha*).

Why is this so? Because the form of restraint in the first thought-moment fulfills the intention and aspiration, and since it is permeated by volition (*cetanā*), it is termed a "path of action consisting of volition" (*cetanā-karmapatha*).
Since the subsequent forms of restraint arise spontaneously with the preceding restraint as their cause, they are designated simply as "karma" and not as "paths of action."

The first moment of thought regarding the precepts consists of both informative action (*vijñapti*) and non-informative action (*avijñapti*); subsequent moments of the arising precepts consist only of non-informative action and lack informative action.
This first moment of thought regarding the precepts is also called "precept" (*śīla*), "wholesome conduct" (*kuśala-caryā*), and "restraint" (*saṃvara*).
"Furthermore, the precepts that arise in succession also possess this same principle.
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Among the three periods of time, in which period does one receive the precepts?"
He replied: "One receives the precepts in a single present thought-moment.
The past and future are phenomena (dharma) and not sentient beings; therefore, one does not receive the precepts therein."
"The present single thought is the sentient being; therefore, one obtains the precepts. He asked:
"Is the precept obtained within a wholesome mind?"
Is it obtained within an unwholesome mind?
Within an indeterminate mind?
Or is it obtained within a state of no-mind?
He replied: "All may attain it.

First, having paid homage at the feet of the Saṃgha with a virtuous mind, one receives the robe and bowl and requests a preceptor. One then earnestly seeks the precepts, kneeling on the right knee with palms joined, and after the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been performed, the color of the precepts (*śīla-rūpa*) is accomplished through the continuity of that virtuous mind; this is called attaining the precepts within a virtuous mind."

If, during the preceding sequential procedures, one has constantly generated a wholesome mind and performed various preparatory acts, yet at the time of the formal *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts such as greed or hatred, and thereby accomplishes the form of the precept within that [unwholesome] mind, this is called "attaining the precept within an unwholesome mind."
Because of the power of one's original wholesome mind and the wholesome force of the instruction, one attains this precept; it is not through the power of an unwholesome mind.

First, one initiates the ritual action with a wholesome mind; at the time of the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, even if one is drowsy or asleep, the form of the precept (*śīla-rūpa*) arises within that sleeping mind. This is called "attaining the precept within the neutral state."

First, one initiates the ritual action with a virtuous mind; at the time of the formal motion and the threefold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), if one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one accomplishes the form of the precepts at that very moment. This is called "attaining the precepts while in a state of no-mind."
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a layperson does not receive the five precepts but directly receives the ten precepts, would they obtain the precepts?
The Buddha replied:
"At one time, one obtains two kinds of precepts: one obtains the Upāsaka precepts and the Śrāmaṇera precepts.
If one does not receive the five precepts or the ten precepts, but directly receives the full precepts (Upasaṃpadā), one obtains all three kinds of precepts at once."
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If one receives full ordination and simultaneously obtains the three types of precepts, why is it necessary to follow a sequence by first receiving the five precepts, next the ten precepts, and finally the full ordination?”
He replied: "Although one may simultaneously obtain the three types of precepts, the cultivation of the Buddha-dharma must necessarily follow a sequence.
First, one receives the five precepts to discipline oneself; as faith and joy gradually increase, one next receives the ten precepts."
Having received the ten precepts, their roots of goodness deepen further, and they next receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
In this sequential manner, they attain the flavor of the Buddha-dharma; their profound joy becomes firm and solid, making it difficult for them to fall back or be defeated.
Just as when traveling upon the great ocean, one gradually enters deeper waters, so too it is with entering the ocean of the Buddha-dharma.
If one were to receive full ordination all at once, one would lose the proper sequence and violate the rules of dignified conduct (*vinaya*).

Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who attain the fruits of the path by receiving the five precepts, or there may be sentient beings who attain the fruits of the path because they receive the ten precepts; for these various reasons, the Tathāgata has taught this sequence.
If one first receives the five precepts and subsequently receives the ten precepts, at the time of receiving the ten precepts, one also accomplishes two types of precepts:
the five precepts and the ten precepts.
Having received the ten precepts, if one subsequently receives the full precepts (upasampadā), at the time of receiving the full precepts, one accomplishes three types of precepts.
The five precepts, the ten precepts, and the full precepts.

Among the seven ways of receiving the precepts, only those received through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) are obtained sequentially across three stages; the remaining six ways of receiving the precepts are obtained in a single moment and do not involve this sequential process of three stages.
If one simultaneously receives the three types of precepts, and when wishing to relinquish them, says:
"I am a śrāmaṇera, not a bhikṣu," then the full precepts (upasaṃpadā) are lost, while the other two types of precepts remain.
The five precepts and the ten precepts;
or if one says: "I am an upāsaka, not a śrāmaṇera."
"In that case, one loses the ten precepts, while the remaining five precepts remain;

if one says, 'I completely renounce everything—both lay and monastic—and am now a lay follower (upāsaka) who takes refuge,' then all three types [of precepts] are lost simultaneously, yet the Three Refuges themselves are not lost.
If one acquires the three types of precepts sequentially, the order of their relinquishment follows the same sequence as described in the section on the simultaneous acquisition of the precepts."
“If a former lay follower (upāsaka) leaves the household life and receives the ten precepts, does he abandon the five precepts?
He replied, “He does not abandon them.”
One merely loses the name and the sequence, but does not lose the precepts.
One loses the name of an upāsaka and gains the name of a śrāmaṇera;
one loses the sequence of a layperson and gains the sequence of a renunciant.
"If a śrāmaṇera receives full ordination, does he lose the ten precepts and the five precepts? He replied, "He does not."
One merely loses the name and the sequence, but does not lose the precepts.
One loses the name of *śrāmaṇera* and gains the name of *bhikṣu*;
one loses the sequence of the *śrāmaṇera* and gains the sequence of the *bhikṣu*.
From beginning to end it is always this same precept, yet its names change according to the time.

It is like the leaves of a tree: they are green in spring and summer, yellow in autumn, and white in winter. Because they differ according to the seasons, the leaves appear different, yet from start to finish they are but the same leaf.
The precepts are also like this: they are always one and the same precept, yet they differ according to the occasion.
It is also like milk, curd, butter, and clarified butter (ghṛta); although there are distinctions among these four stages and they differ accordingly, they are nonetheless one and the same substance.
"The precepts are also like this: although there are differences in the three periods [of time], the precepts themselves are no different.
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one who receives the upāsaka precepts is unable to receive all five precepts, but instead receives one, two, or even four precepts, does he obtain the precepts?"
He replied, “I cannot. [The other asked],
“If you cannot, there is a sutra that says:”
"Partial upāsakas, majority upāsakas, and complete upāsakas.
What is the meaning of this? He replied:

"The reason for making this statement was to clarify the relative magnitude of the merit derived from observing the precepts; it did not mean that there is such a thing as receiving the precepts in this manner.
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one receives the five precepts for one day, two days, or even up to ten days, is it permissible to receive them in such a way?"
He replied: "I may not.
The Buddha originally established the precepts, each with its own specific limits."
If one receives the five precepts, they must be observed for as long as life lasts;
if one receives the eight precepts, they must necessarily be received for one day and one night. For this reason, it is not permitted [to receive them otherwise].
Now, the precepts conferred through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations) have superior, intermediate, and inferior grades:
The five precepts are the lower grade of precepts; the ten precepts are the middle grade of precepts; and the full precepts are the upper grade of precepts.
Within the five precepts, there are likewise three grades:
if one receives the precepts with a low-grade mind, one obtains a low-grade precept.
If one receives the precepts with a mind of medium grade, one obtains precepts of medium grade;
if one receives the precepts with a mind of superior grade, one obtains precepts of superior grade.
The ten precepts and the full precepts likewise each have three grades, as explained in the case of the five precepts.

If, after having received the precepts with an inferior grade of mind, one subsequently receives the ten precepts with a superior, middling, or superior grade of mind, the previously obtained five precepts undergo no further increase or improvement.
Beyond the five precepts, one obtains the five superior precepts, such as the precept against eating at improper times and so forth.
The previously obtained five precepts constitute the original inferior grade; that is, the five precepts of the initial inferior grade.
If one receives the full ordination with a mind of medium or superior grade, the five precepts previously obtained neither increase nor improve.

They remain as the original five precepts; however, regarding all other precepts beyond those five, because the mind at the time of receiving full ordination is superior, one obtains the superior precepts.
Inferring from this, there is no such thing as receiving the *prātimokṣa* precepts repeatedly.
In terms of their sequence, the five precepts are of inferior grade, the ten precepts are of middling grade, and the full set of precepts (*upasampadā*) is of superior grade.
Inferring from this principle, it can also be understood that one may receive the five precepts with a superior-grade mind, which constitutes a superior-grade precept;
with a middle-grade mind, one receives the ten precepts, which constitute a middle-grade precept;
and with an inferior-grade mind, one receives the full precepts, which constitute an inferior-grade precept.
For this reason, according to the superior, middling, or inferior nature of one's mind, the attainment of the precepts differs; there is no fixed limit.
If one requests a preceptor to receive the ten precepts, one obtains the ten precepts even if the preceptor is not present before them.
If, at the time of receiving the ten precepts, the preceptor dies, then if one hears of or knows of his death, the reception of the precepts is not valid;
if one does not hear of his death, the reception of the precepts is valid.

If one undergoes the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations) for receiving the precepts, and the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is not present before the assembly, one cannot receive the precepts because the number of the Saṃgha is incomplete.
If the number of the Saṃgha is complete, one may receive the precepts even if there is no preceptor.
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“May a lay follower who observes the five precepts engage in buying and selling?
The Buddha replied:
"You may engage in buying and selling;
however, you must not perform five types of activities:
first, you must not engage in the trade of livestock as a profession."
If one possesses livestock and sells them directly, this is permitted, provided they are not sold to butchers;
secondly, one must not engage in the trade of bows, arrows, swords, or staves as a profession.
If one possesses [liquor] oneself and sells it directly, this is permitted;
thirdly, one must not take the sale of wine as a profession.
If one possesses it oneself, even selling it directly is permitted.
Fourth, one must not press oil, for it kills many insects.
This is the established custom in India and the regions from Kapiśī onwards: if there are no insects within the hemp, there is no fault in pressing the oil.
Fifth, one must not engage in the business of dyeing with the five primary colors, as it kills many insects.
The dyeing methods of foreign lands such as Laṅkā involve the killing of many insects; therefore, they are not permitted.
This means that even the method for dyeing blue in the land of Qin involves the killing of many insects and thus falls within the category of the five major types of dyeing.
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since the eightfold precept includes the practice of not eating past midday, there are actually nine items; why is it named after only eight matters?"

He replied: "The essence of the fasting rite (upavāsa) is the practice of not eating after midday. Eight matters assist in accomplishing the essence of this fast, supporting it together; thus it is called the 'Eight-Limbed Fasting Rite' (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa). For this reason, one speaks of the 'eight precepts,' not nine."
“If a person who has received the eight precepts, among which of the seven assemblies do they belong?
“Although they have not received lifelong precepts, because they possess the one-day and one-night precepts, they should be called an upāsaka.”
Some say: "If one is called an upāsaka, there are no lifelong precepts;
if one is not an upāsaka, there are precepts for one day and one night."
"He is merely called a person of intermediate status.
This is stated in a sutra.
Upāli then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Is there a *prātimokṣa* precept outside of the seven assemblies?
He replied, "There is;
it is the eightfold fast-day precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*)."
Inferring from this principle, if one receives the eight precepts, one does not belong to the seven categories of practitioners.
When receiving the ritual for the eight precepts, one should state, "For one day and one night, I shall refrain from killing," so as to bring the verbal commitment to a definitive conclusion.
"Do not allow it to be confused with the lifelong precepts. He asked:
"Regarding the method for receiving the eight precepts, may one receive them all at once for two days, three days, or even up to ten days?"
He replied: "The Buddha originally established the precepts for one day and one night; they must not exceed this limit.
If one has the strength to receive them for a full day, once that period has passed, one should receive them again in succession."
Thus, according to one's capacity, whether great or small, one does not calculate the number of days.
As for the method of receiving the precepts (upavāsa), it must necessarily be received from another person.
From what kind of person should one receive them?
One receives [the precepts] from the community of the five groups.
Once the eight precepts have been received, if one beats or strikes sentient beings, the fast is not pure.
Even if one does not beat them on that very day, if one intends to beat sentient beings on the following day, it is likewise not pure.
In brief: if one performs acts of improper conduct with body or speech, although the fast is not technically broken, there is no pure dharma;
even if body and speech are pure, if the mind gives rise to thoughts of greed, thoughts of malice, or thoughts of harm, the fast is likewise called impure.
If one's three karmas of body, speech, and mind are pure, yet one does not cultivate the six recollections, this is called impure fasting.
Having received the eight precepts, to cultivate the six recollections with diligence is called pure fasting.
A sutra states:
"If one becomes the king of Jambudvīpa, one possesses sovereign mastery over all the people, gold, silver, wealth, and treasures within Jambudvīpa."
Although he possesses such merit, if it were divided into sixteen parts, the merit of the King of Jambudvīpa would not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
This refers to the final, pure eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*).

If a person wishes to receive the eightfold precepts but first indulges in sensual pleasures, performs music, greedily eats meat, engages in various forms of merriment, or commits such acts of negligence, and only afterwards receives the precepts—whether before noon, at noon, or after noon—they shall not obtain the precepts at all.

If one originally had no intention to observe the fast but engaged in various forms of negligence, yet later encounters a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) and immediately undertakes the fast, one attains the merit of the fast regardless of whether it was before, during, or after the midday hour.

If one wishes to observe the fast but is hindered by circumstances such that one cannot do so freely, and subsequently observes the fast once those difficulties have been resolved, one attains the merit of the fast regardless of whether it was before or after midday.
Question: "If one wishes to observe the rules for the daytime fast (divā-vrata) but not the nighttime fast, will one obtain the eight precepts?
If one wishes to observe the nighttime fast but not the daytime fast, will one obtain the eight precepts?"
He replied: "It is not permitted.
The reason for this is that the Buddha originally authorized the observance of the one-day and one-night fast (upoṣadha) for a fixed duration; it must not be violated."
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If it were not so, as it is said in the *Carman* [Leather] Sūtra:
'Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was in a wilderness region and saw various hungry ghosts undergoing various punishments; some received blessings by day and underwent punishment at night;'"
Some may experience blessings by night and suffer retribution by day.
The reason for this is that in their previous human lives, they observed the precepts by day and committed evil deeds by night;
or they observed the precepts by night and committed evil deeds by day. It is because of these differences that the results vary.
"What is the meaning of this? He replied,
"Whatever constitutes a jātaka or a causal narrative (nidāna) is not to be relied upon."
Regarding what is said here, it is neither Sūtra nor Vinaya, and thus its meaning cannot be established as definitive reality.
Furthermore, it is said:
"This was perhaps a transformation created by Kātyāyana to deliver Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa; he thereby moved his mind to awakening, but it was not an actual event."
Once one has received the fast, if one wishes to relinquish it, it is not necessary to do so before the fivefold assembly.
If one wishes to eat, merely speaking to a single person constitutes the relinquishing of the fast.
"Regarding those who obtain the *prātimokṣa* precepts, speaking in terms of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), only those in the human realm obtain the precepts; the other four realms do not.
For example, because beings in the heavenly realm are deeply attached to pleasure, they are unable to obtain the precepts."
Once in the past, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, because one of his disciples was ill, ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to consult Jīvaka.
It happened that he encountered the devas entering the Nandana Grove.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana was standing by the side of the road, yet none of the gods looked back at him.
Jīvaka arrived later; seeing Maudgalyāyana, he merely raised one hand and drove his carriage straight past.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"This person was originally among humans as my disciple; now that he enjoys heavenly blessings, he has become so attached to celestial pleasures that he has completely lost his original resolve."

He immediately used his supernormal powers to restrain the chariot and bring it to a halt. Jīvaka descended from the chariot and prostrated at the feet of Maudgalyāyana. Maudgalyāyana rebuked him for his impropriety through various causes and conditions, to which Jīvaka replied to Maudgalyāyana:
"Because I am among men, I am a disciple of the Great Virtuous One; therefore, I raised my hand to inquire after your welfare."
"Have you ever seen among the devas anyone like this?
Because those born in the heavens are deeply attached to pleasure, their minds lack self-mastery;
that is why they are like this. Maudgalyāyana said to Jīvaka:
"A disciple is ill; how should he be treated?
Jīvaka replied, "The primary method is simply to abstain from food."
At one time, Maudgalyāyana exhorted Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
"The appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter; why do you not approach him frequently to inquire about and receive the True Dharma?
In order to clarify Maudgalyāyana’s intention, Śakra dispatched a messenger to command a certain son of heaven to come.
He called out three times in succession, yet [the deity] still did not come.

This celestial son had only one wife and one musical consort; because his attachment to sensual desire was so deep, although the King of Devas' command was weighty, he could not bring himself to sever [his ties].
Later, having no other choice, he came; Śakra asked him, "For what reason have you come?
and he answered with the truth.
Śakra addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"This devaputra has only one celestial maiden and one musical ensemble with which he entertains himself; he cannot bring himself to part with them."

How much more so when one becomes a Heavenly King, possessing various palaces and towers, countless celestial maidens, and divine *sūdhā* food of a hundred flavors appearing spontaneously; with hundreds of thousands of musical performances for one’s own entertainment, one looks toward the east and forgets the west.

"Although one knows that a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter and the True Dharma is difficult to hear, because one is bound by the fetters of defiled pleasures and lacks self-mastery, what can be done about it?
In the ritual for receiving the precepts, one must first make a firm vow with a courageous mind to resolve upon them; only then does one obtain the precepts."
The devas are deeply attached to pleasure and their power of wholesome roots is weak; by what means could they obtain the precepts?
Hungry ghosts suffer from the pains of hunger and thirst, their bodies and minds burning with anguish;
those in the hells endure immeasurable afflictions and various forms of torment, their minds so intensely pained that they lack the conditions to obtain the precepts.
Among animals, due to karmic obstructions, there is no understanding and no dharma for receiving precepts.

Although it is stated in various sūtras that nāgas receive the dharma of fasting, they do so out of a virtuous mind by undertaking the eight precepts; for one day and one night they obtain the merit of a virtuous mind, yet they do not obtain the precepts because of their karmic obstructions.
Speaking in terms of the four continents, only those on three continents—
Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, and Pūrvavideha— as well as the people on the islands in the intermediate oceans between these three continents, can all receive the precepts.
Just as in Aparagoyānī, the Buddha dispatched Piṇḍola to perform great Buddhist works there, where there are four assemblies;
likewise, there are bhikṣus in the eastern direction who also perform Buddhist works there.
Only in Uttarakuru is there no Buddha-dharma, nor can one receive the precepts; because of the obstruction of their karmic rewards and due to their ignorance, they do not accept the noble Dharma.
There are four kinds of persons:
first, men; second, women;
[third, boys; fourth, girls].
Third, eunuchs; fourth, those with dual sexual organs.
Among these four types of persons, only men and women may receive the precepts; two types of persons do not receive them: eunuchs and those with dual sexual organs.

Among men and women, those who have killed their father, mother, or an arhat; shed the blood of a Buddha; disrupted the *saṃgha* that turns the wheel of Dharma; defiled a bhikṣuṇī; lived as a "thief-monk" (*caura-vāsin*) or a "transgressor"; or severed their roots of goodness—such persons as these are entirely incapable of receiving the precepts.
Viewed from a broader perspective, those who receive the teachings of the Buddha through defilement are hardly worth mentioning.

Whether they be devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits; whether they be inhabitants of Uttarakuru, or those with no sexual organs or dual organs; and all manner of such sinful persons—all are fully capable of receiving the Three Refuges.
Question: "Do the Buddhas of the three periods of time attain the same precepts? Answer:
"It is not equal. Generally, one who attains the precepts receives them with respect to both sentient beings and non-sentient beings.

Yet, when one Buddha appears in the world and delivers countless *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, then when a subsequent Buddha appears in the world, one cannot receive the precepts with respect to those very beings."
In this way, the Buddhas attained the precepts at different times, each case being unequal.
For example, when Kāśyapa Buddha delivered countless *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, Kāśyapa Buddha attained the precepts for all of these sentient beings;
however, Śākyamuni Buddha did not attain the precepts for any of these same sentient beings.
All Buddhas have three equalities:
first, equality in the accumulation of practice;
second, equality in the Dharma-body.
Third, regarding the deliverance of sentient beings and so forth:

all Buddhas, throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, cultivate the bodhisattva practices and fully perfect the fivefold Dharma-body, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities;
they all deliver countless *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, causing them to enter *nirvāṇa*.
Question: "The sutras state:
'When one Buddha appears in the world, he delivers ninety nayutas of sentient beings, leading them into nirvana.'"
"Why is it said that there are 'incalculable asaṃkhyeya' sentient beings? He replied:
"This sutra states:"

Regarding the statement, "When one Buddha appears in the world, he delivers ninety nayutas of sentient beings," it merely says that there are so many sentient beings who attain deliverance from that Buddha.
As for sentient beings, some attain liberation directly from the Buddha, some from his disciples, and some attain liberation through the bequeathed Dharma.
When it is said that "ninety nayutas of sentient beings" [attain liberation], this refers specifically to those who attain liberation in the presence of the Buddha himself.
In short, countless asaṃkhyeya sentient beings enter nirvana without remainder.
Although the three types of equality of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are identical, the precepts they attain are not identical.
Question: "Regarding the precepts of non-restraint (akuśala-saṃvara), which are obtained with respect to both sentient beings and non-sentient things—can they be obtained in their entirety, or not?"

He replied: "One acquires the vow of non-restraint (akuśalasaṃvara) only with respect to sentient beings; one does not acquire this evil vow with respect to those who are not of the class of sentient beings. Some say:
"It is said: 'One acquires the unwholesome precepts (duḥśīla) only with respect to those sentient beings that can be killed, not with respect to those sentient beings that cannot be killed.
Yet it is also said:
'One acquires the unwholesome precepts with respect to all sentient beings, whether they can be killed or cannot be killed.'"
"Just as a butcher slaughters sheep, constantly harboring the intent to kill and making the resolve to slaughter them without limit;

even if one is currently not killing while among humans or devas, through the succession of future births, there is the possibility of falling among sheep. Therefore, one incurs the negative precepts (*duṣkṛta-śīla*) toward all sentient beings."
The twelve types of evil discipline are also like this.
The twelve types of evil discipline are:
first, the butcher; [and so forth].
Second, butchers; third, pig breeders;
fourth, poultry keepers;
Fifth, those who catch fish;
sixth, hunters; seventh, bird-trappers.
Eighth, catching pythons;
ninth, incanting dragons;
tenth, serving as a jailer.
Eleventh, those who commit robbery;
twelfth, those whom the royal household regularly dispatches to apprehend robbers—these are the twelve types of persons with evil vows (*akuśala-saṃvara*).
Occupations such as sericulture and the like are all considered not to be free from evil vows.
There are three occasions for relinquishing the vows of non-restraint (*akuśala-saṃvara*):
at the time of death; when desire is completely exhausted;
and when one receives the vows of restraint (*kuśala-saṃvara*).
Just as when one receives the three refuges,
at the first recitation one immediately abandons unwholesome precepts;
at the second and third recitations, one immediately obtains wholesome precepts.
"When a person performs unwholesome precepts, at what time do they abandon wholesome precepts and acquire unwholesome precepts?
He replied: "One explanation says:..."
"I am a butcher," he said,
and immediately abandoned his virtuous precepts;
this was stated a second and a third time:
"I am a butcher," and he immediately obtains the evil precepts.
It is also said:
"At whatever time one abandons the virtuous precepts, one immediately acquires the unvirtuous precepts.

If a person of virtuous precepts has not yet vowed to become a butcher, but merely engages in acts of killing with a butcher out of greed for profit, at that moment they are said to have violated their virtuous precepts."
"If one seeks to abandon the precepts of goodness and seeks to obtain the precepts of evil, one will certainly obtain the precepts of evil by personally vowing to become a butcher.
If one receives the precepts of evil, they are obtained through one's own vow; they are not received from another.

If one wishes to receive the precepts of evil discipline (akuśala-śīla) for one day, two days, or even up to ten days, one year, or two years, they shall be obtained according to one's wish, in accordance with the duration of the vow.

The reason for this is that these unwholesome dharmas follow the current of birth and death and lack the sense of superior progress; therefore, they are obtained immediately upon the occurrence of the respective action, unlike the wholesome vows of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means, Scroll Six;
The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means, Scroll Seven.
Translator unknown; included in the Later Han Records.
Chapter Nine: On Cultivating Intimacy Furthermore, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas recognize kindness and repay it;
they cultivate great skillful means to benefit sentient beings, manifesting these in an unimpeded manner according to what is appropriate and suitable for each occasion.

"Good son! There appeared in the world a Buddha named Fearless King Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who manifested in the world to guide and receive those with whom he has a karmic connection."
When his conditions were exhausted, he transferred his spirit and entered nirvana.
After his parinirvāṇa, among the True Dharma there was the son of a brahmin who was intelligent and wise; he received and upheld the five precepts and protected the True Dharma.

A son of a brahmin, having gone abroad on business to another country, reached the middle of his journey where there were many dangers from bandits; he traveled as part of a caravan of five hundred people.

Upon reaching a perilous road, at the place where they halted, five hundred bands of bandits were constantly stationed there, surrounding them from front and back, intending to plunder their traveling companions.
At that time, the leader of the bandits secretly dispatched one man to observe the companions, intending to set out at the opportune moment.
At that time, there was another person among the bandits who had previously been a close friend of this brahmin’s son; because of their friendship, he came first to inform him, saying: "Good man!..."
"You should know that bandits will rise up during the first watch of the night.
At that time, there will be great turmoil, and fearing you may be harmed, I have come to inform you.
You must secretly devise a means to depart far away by yourself, without letting your companions know."
At that time, having heard these words, the brahmin’s son was like a person choking, unable to swallow and unable to spit out.

He wished to tell his companions, yet he feared that his companions would harm this one man; if he were to harm this man, he feared that his companions would fall into the three evil realms and undergo immeasurable suffering.
If he remained silent, the bandits would harm his companions, and if they killed his companions, he feared that the bandits would fall into the three evil realms and undergo immeasurable suffering.
Having formed this thought:
"I shall employ great skillful means to benefit sentient beings, not for my own sake.
The suffering of the three evil realms is what is appropriate for me."
Having reflected thus, he immediately took up a blade and severed the life of this thief, ensuring that his companions were safe and free from harm.
At that time, the group of companions spoke with one voice, saying:
"O great son of a Brahmin!..."
"You are a superior person and one of pure goodness; why do you commit such a great evil today?
At that time, the Brahmin’s son knelt on his right knee with palms joined, feeling deep shame and remorse, and said:
"I ought not to commit evil today, yet I do so for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and my companions."
At that time, his companions spoke again, saying:
"You have killed a person yourself; what benefit is this to us?
He replied to the people:
"This man is an evil thief who intends to harm his fellow companions.
For the sake of these companions, I shall take this man's life so that they may return home in safety.
As for my own karmic retribution, I am willing to endure it in hell."
At that time, the five hundred companions raised their voices and wept bitterly; with grief and joy mingled together, they spoke these words:
"Among all things in the world, nothing is more precious than life, and nothing is more feared than death."

The reason for this is that all sentient beings will renounce gold, silver, precious jewels, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, clothing, and food and drink in order to save their own lives; thus, we, as a group of companions, shall be born anew.
Having spoken these words, [they said]: "This son of a Brahmin, for the sake of sentient beings, has not declined to endure manifold sufferings and the retribution of the three evil realms.
Today, we must remember his profound kindness."
"To repay this profound kindness, you should now swiftly resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having spoken these words, he immediately caused them to generate that resolve.
At that time, the five hundred bandits spoke again, saying:
"You are a superior person, a man of pure goodness; how could you possibly commit such a great evil?"
The Brahmin’s son said:
“I truly know that I ought not to commit such a great evil;
however, it is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings and protecting the lives of you all.”
Then the bandits said, "You have killed the man yourself; what benefit is that to us?
At that time, the Brahmin’s son replied to the bandits:
"I was aware of you all being here from the beginning, but I remained silent and did not inform the king or my companions.
For this reason, your lives and well-being have been kept secure."
At that time, having heard these words, the bandits thought to themselves:
"Our very lives have been restored. They immediately stepped forward, joined their palms, and addressed the youth:
“Excellent, Great Being!
O cultivator of great compassion!
We pray that you command us as to what we should do.”
He replied, "That which I must do is simply to swiftly resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.
At that time, out of gratitude for his kindness, the bandits immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon hearing his voice.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“A bodhisattva who diligently seeks vigor, wishing to adorn awakening and wishing to repay the Buddha’s kindness, should always keep all sentient beings in mind with the thought that they are like an only son.”
Good son! You should know that the Brahmin’s son at that time—could he have been anyone else?
It was none other than my own self.
By these causes and conditions, he transcends nine kalpas and swiftly attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva practices great skillful means by knowing kindness and repaying it.

When the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove Monastery, there was a bhikṣu who suffered from a malignant ulcer; pus and blood flowed constantly from his entire body, and he was so despised by the multitude that no one would approach him. He lived in a dilapidated room on the outskirts.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately manifested his supernormal powers, concealing the great assembly so that none would know.
The Tathāgata went alone to where the sick bhikṣu was; according to the latter's needs, he took water and washed him.
Having reflected thus, he caused all the devas of the desire realm to know it.
Śakra-devānām-indra, surrounded before and behind by his retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, rained down various celestial flowers and played diverse heavenly music as he stood in mid-air.

At that time, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven held in his hand a subtle and exquisite water-jar adorned with a hundred merits, filled to the brim with the pure water of great compassion; he immediately went forward to welcome [the Tathāgata], prostrated himself with his head at the Tathāgata’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the Tathāgata extended his arm, adorned with the merit of a hundred blessings, and emitted a great radiance from his five slender, long fingers, shining afar upon the various devas. When the great assembly had gathered, the Tathāgata went in person to where the sick bhikṣu was; he then emitted light from the crown of his head, illuminating the sick bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu encountered the light, and his agonizing pain was immediately dispelled. Within the pus and blood, he rose up to take refuge and prostrate himself, yet his body did not follow.

The Tathāgata then took the precious vase from Śakra, Lord of the Devas, with his right hand and poured it over the head of the sick bhikṣu; with his left hand, he stroked and wiped the bhikṣu’s body, and all the sores on his body were restored to health as soon as they came into contact with the Tathāgata’s hand.
Having been restored to health, he felt immeasurable joy and exclaimed: "Namo Śākyamuni!
Namo to the Great Compassionate Father!"
Homage to the Unsurpassed and Most Victorious King of Physicians!
Today my physical illness has been cured, yet I still have a mental illness.
May the Tathāgata, out of compassion, bestow upon me the medicine of the Dharma to eliminate all the grave afflictions of my body and mind.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the sick bhikṣu:
"The Tathāgata now recalls your profound kindness;
the Tathāgata now wishes to repay your kindness."
At that time, the sick bhikṣu was filled with immeasurable joy and wonder.

The Buddha then instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him; the bhikṣu, being thus delighted, immediately attained the fruit of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and being endowed with the eight liberations.
Śakra Devānām-Indra and his retinue, along with immeasurable devas, all fell into a web of doubt:
"How is it that the Tathāgata has deigned to humble his divine majesty to wash the wounds, pus, and blood of a sick bhikṣu, and speak of repaying his kindness?"
"What is this matter? We pray that you will analyze and explain it for us.
The Buddha addressed Śakra-devānām-indra and the great assembly of devas and humans: "Listen well!
I shall now relate for you the events of a former life.
Śakra Devānām-Indra!
In the distant past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a king who was cruel, rebellious, and unrighteous; he oppressed others unjustly and seized their wealth by force.
At that time, the wicked king and a commander of five hundred men were close allies in heart; they secretly made a pact, saying:
"If there should be anyone who commits an offense against the state, you must punish them severely; both authority and favor shall be yours."
‘If you obtain wealth or goods, share them with me.
At that time, those who constantly administered lashes and whips would ensure that those who acquired much wealth did not keep it;
as for those who had no wealth, they were sometimes even deprived of their lives—this was their constant practice.
At that time, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who had committed a minor offense and was being led away to be handed over to five hundred [officials] to receive the punishment of the whip.
Hearing that this lay follower was a virtuous and good person, they immediately ordered that he not be subjected to the agony of the lashes, and thus he was delivered from the peril.
For this reason, his joy was immeasurable.
Kauśika, you should know that those five hundred at that time were these very sick bhikṣus.
The upāsaka was none other than my own self in this present life.

For this reason, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the Bodhisattva has regarded even slight kindness as a heavy debt to be repaid, never forgetting it until the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra and the immeasurable host of devas rejoiced immeasurably; forty-eight thousand devas resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having generated the bodhicitta, they played celestial music and each returned to their respective abodes.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are good sons or good daughters who recognize kindness and repay it, they should practice four matters:
First, to draw near to virtuous friends;
second, to listen to the Dharma with a sincere mind;
third, to contemplate its meaning.
Fourth, practicing according to what has been taught.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
first, following the Dharma and not following the person.
Second, following the meaning rather than the letter;
third, following wisdom rather than consciousness;
fourth, following sūtras of definitive meaning rather than sūtras of non-definitive meaning.
To practice these eight dharmas is called knowing gratitude.
To further practice another eight dharmas is called repaying gratitude. What are these eight?
First, gain; second, loss; third, defamation;
Fourth, praise; fifth, commendation; sixth, censure;
Seventh is suffering;
eighth is happiness.
Furthermore, practicing four matters is called knowing gratitude and is also called repaying gratitude:
First, upon seeing sentient beings who are evil, one gives rise to compassion in the mind due to the causal conditions of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
second, upon seeing sentient beings who suffer, one does not turn the eyes away for even a moment due to the causal conditions of giving rise to pity (*karuṇā*);
third, upon seeing teachers, parents, and those of virtuous character, the heart and mind are filled with joy due to the causal conditions of giving rise to sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
"Fourth, when seeing sentient beings who are enemies, one’s mind does not give rise to anger, because of cultivating the causes and conditions of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
At that time, Ānanda adjusted his robes, stepped forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"When the Tathāgata first resolved to attain Bodhicitta, he recognized kindness and repaid it by practicing the first four deeds. What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He appeared in the world to instruct those with whom he had a karmic connection."
When his conditions were exhausted, he transferred his spirit into nirvana.
After the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma had perished, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī, where the population was flourishing and the land was abundant and fertile.
That king always governed the country with the True Dharma and did not oppress the people.
In that land there was a mountain named Mount Seers and Sages (*ṛṣi-muni-parvata*).
On that mountain, five hundred pratyekabuddhas constantly resided, and many immortals possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) also dwelt there.
At that time, many birds and beasts came to seek refuge with him.

There was a lion named Dṛḍhapratijña, whose fur was golden in color and who possessed great majesty and prowess; his strength equaled that of a thousand others. When he let out a roar, the flying birds fell to the ground and the running beasts hid themselves away.
While wandering through mountains and marshes, he saw a Pratyekabuddha śramaṇa whose deportment was pure.
Having seen him, his heart rejoiced; he drew near to him day after day and constantly heard him recite the sūtras and preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
At that time, there was a great hunter who, seeing this lion with golden-colored fur, felt joy arise in his heart and thought to himself:
"If I can capture this lion and flay its skin to present to the king, he will surely bestow upon me rank and emolument, so that for seven generations my lineage shall lack for nothing."
Having reflected thus, he spoke again:
"The Lion of Firm Vows, the king among beasts, cannot be reached by bow or arrow, nor can he be restrained by snares or nets."
"I shall now devise another stratagem.
That which the Lion of Firm Vows respects and looks toward is the śramaṇa; I shall now assume the appearance of a śramaṇa and shoot him secretly with my bow."
Covering myself with my *kāṣāya*, I shall observe closely and proceed slowly to the foot of the tree; if he sees me, he will surely come to approach me.
Once he has drawn near, I will draw my bow and shoot him with a poisoned arrow; there is not a one in ten thousand who would escape capture.
Having reflected thus, he immediately returned home and proclaimed these words:
"From the time of our ancestors, through generations of succession, we have always been hunters; yet we have never heard of a beast whose body hair is golden, much less seen one."
"Now I wish to hunt him down.
He then shaved his beard and hair and donned the dharma robes; just as he had contemplated, he returned to the mountains and sat beneath a tree.
At that time, the lion of Firm Vow saw this bhikṣu and felt great joy in his heart; he leaped forward to approach him and licked the bhikṣu’s feet.
Thereupon, the hunter immediately shot at him.
Once struck by the poisoned arrow, he growled and roared, wishing to spring forward and seize him.
As he was about to cause harm, he again thought: "This is a śramaṇa!"
Wearing robes of dyed color is the emblem of the Buddhas, sages, and noble ones of the three periods of time.
If I were to harm him now, it would not be difficult; however, if I were to take his life, I would be robbing the Buddhas, sages, and noble ones of their very insignia.
Having reflected thus, he held his breath and endured the suffering.
After a short while, the poisonous medicine intensified, and the pain became unbearable.
Having reflected again, he desired to bite [the tree] and once more uttered these words:
"It is not difficult to do so.
However, those who would destroy or harm me are censured by all Buddhas, worthies, and sages.
Furthermore, if one cannot distinguish between good and evil in the world, this is a wicked person who harbors poisonous conspiracies, wishing to come and harm me."
If I were not patient, I would be no different from those evil people.
One who cultivates patience is loved and respected by all;
one who lacks patience is detested by the multitude. This increases afflictions (*kleśa*), and because afflictions increase, birth and death (*saṃsāra*) increase.
Because they undergo long-term birth and death, they are born in places of hardship;
because they are born in places of hardship, they distance themselves from virtuous friends;
because they distance themselves from virtuous friends, they do not hear the True Dharma.
Because they do not hear the Dharma, the net of doubt becomes doubly obscured;
because of this net of doubt, they remain far removed from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, I should not now give rise to evil.
Having formed this thought, he immediately spoke in verse:
"May I sacrifice my own body and life, But never give rise to an evil thought toward those clad in dyed robes."
"I vow that even at the cost of my own life, I shall never again give rise to an evil thought toward those who have left the household life.
Having spoken these verses, he immediately passed away.
Heaven and earth shook in six ways, startling all the birds and beasts, who scattered and fled in all directions;
though there were no clouds, it rained blood, and the sun lost its brilliant light.
At that time, the hunter immediately removed his outer garments, took up a knife and flayed [the deer], and carried the load back home.
Having arrived home, he presented it to the king.
The king was filled with joy upon seeing it and asked his ministers:
"Since my birth, I have never heard of a beast possessing golden hair on its body; how is it that today I have seen this with my own eyes?"
"How marvelous!
How strange! he exclaimed, and then slowly questioned the hunter:
"By what means can this hide be obtained?
At that time, the hunter stepped forward and said to the king:
"I only pray that Your Majesty will grant me fearlessness, so that I may relate these matters to Your Majesty."
The king said, "I grant you whatever you wish! Thereupon,
the hunter related all that had occurred to the great king in detail.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was filled with distress, like a person choking who can neither swallow nor spit out.
He immediately went out and issued a proclamation to all his great ministers, minor kings, and the assembled multitude, declaring:
"Gentlemen!..."
You should know that I have heard these words from the wise:
"If there is a beast whose body hair is golden in color, it must be a bodhisattva.
If a single sentient being resolves upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), they cause all sentient beings to obtain great benefit."
"How is it that today this wicked hunter has devised such a stratagem to kill this bodhisattva?

If I were now to bestow upon this evil man official rank, stipends, elephants and horses, the seven treasures, clothing, food and drink, money, or grain and silk, I would be joining him on one path as a companion in his toil."
Having reflected thus, he immediately seized the hunter and took his life.

Taking the lion’s skin, he returned to the mountains and went to the place where the carcass lay. He then gathered a pyre of ox-head sandalwood, cremated the lion’s skin and bones with fire, collected the relics (*śarīra*), and erected a stupa to make offerings to them.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"O sons of good family!
He who was the Lion of Firm Vows is none other than myself, Śākyamuni, at present."
When a bodhisattva thus draws near to a virtuous friend, they will never give rise to evil even at the cost of their own life.
Why is this? It is because they recognize kindness and seek to repay it.

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva, by virtue of being able to draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), is able to swiftly accomplish unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
O son of good family!

A bodhisattva constantly and diligently seeks spiritual friends in order to hear the Buddha-dharma; even from a single phrase, a single verse, or a single meaning, the afflictions of the three realms are entirely withered away.

When a Bodhisattva seeks the Buddha’s words with a sincere heart, their thirst for the Dharma is so profound that they do not begrudge even their own body or life; even if they must tread upon ground of glowing iron and fierce flames, they do not regard it as an affliction.
For the sake of a single verse, a bodhisattva does not even begrudge his life, let alone the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
for the sake of a single verse, he does not even begrudge his body or life, let alone other material wealth.

Because of the benefits of hearing the Dharma, their bodies attain peace and happiness; they develop deep faith, possess a straightforward mind and right view, and upon seeing the teacher of the Dharma, they regard them as their own parents, with no pride or arrogance in their hearts.
For the sake of sentient beings, one listens to the Dharma with a sincere heart, not for the sake of gain or sustenance;
for the sake of sentient beings, one does not seek self-interest;
and for the sake of the True Dharma, one does not fear royal peril, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, or matters such as tigers, wolves, wild beasts, and bandits.
First, one should discipline one's own afflictions and sense faculties, and only then listen to the Dharma; one should not listen at improper times.
One should listen to the Dharma with a sincere mind, showing reverence for the speaker and honoring the Dharma; this is called a bodhisattva knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.
"How does a bodhisattva listen to the Dharma with a sincere mind?
There are four ways of listening to the Dharma;
the first is listening with a sincere mind."
Second is the single-minded;
third is the all-encompassing mind;
fourth is the virtuous mind.
This is called the bodhisattva’s diligent quest for the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Why is this? It is because they mindfully reflect upon the profound kindness of the Buddhas;

because they desire to disseminate the true Dharma of all Buddhas; because they desire to increase the qualities of the Buddhas; because they wish to cause the world to have faith in the Buddha-Dharma; and because they wish to cause all immeasurable sentient beings to fully attain the path of unsurpassed Bodhi. Therefore, out of mindfulness for the immeasurable sentient beings of the ten directions and in order to repay the profound kindness of the Buddhas, it is for these reasons that the bodhisattva diligently seeks the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

"Why does a bodhisattva diligently seek the Buddhist teachings? It is because they wish to cause sentient beings to give rise to faith; therefore, they seek the treatises on causes (*hetu-śāstra*). It is for the sake of knowing all transgressions and faults;

for the sake of refuting the evil and heterodox arguments of non-Buddhists; for the sake of knowing the skillful means to discipline sentient beings; and for the sake of wishing to distinguish the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words from the meaning of worldly speech. For these reasons, the bodhisattva seeks the treatises on causes."
For what reason does a bodhisattva seek the science of grammar?
It is for the sake of purifying and adorning their speech; for impure words cannot clearly proclaim the definitive meaning;
and it is because they desire to understand all meanings.
He does not destroy right speech because of a mind of pride;
he refutes false views in order to know the skillful means for taming sentient beings. For these reasons, the bodhisattva seeks the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*).
For what reason does a bodhisattva seek various medical prescriptions?

It is to cause sentient beings to be free from the four hundred and four types of evil and unwholesome diseases; it is out of compassion for all sentient beings; and it is to cause them to give rise to faith.
Having attained a mind free from affliction, they give rise to joy.

Because they have attained joy, their minds constantly contemplate the great compassion of the Buddhas for the sake of delivering sentient beings; for this reason, the Bodhisattva seeks various medical prescriptions.
For what reason does a bodhisattva seek worldly arts and techniques?
It is to easily obtain wealth for the benefit of sentient beings;
it is to cause sentient beings to give rise to faith.
It is for the sake of knowing worldly affairs and destroying arrogance;
for the sake of taming sentient beings;
and for the sake of knowing all dharmas and subduing the obscuration of darkness.
If there are bodhisattvas who cannot seek these five matters in such a way, they will ultimately be unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi or achieve all-knowledge.
For the sake of attaining unsurpassed bodhi, one seeks five things.
"The Bodhisattva who knows gratitude and repays it speaks for the sake of sentient beings.
What does he speak of?
How is it taught? It is taught by means of the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
what is the subject matter taught? It is the accomplishment of five things for the sake of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
There are two ways of teaching:
first, sequential teaching; second, pure teaching.
Regarding "sequential exposition":
first the *dānapāramitā* is taught, followed by the *śīlapāramitā*, and so on up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
To understand gratitude and repay it, one contemplates their meaning and abides in accordance with the Dharma; this is called sequential exposition.
Regarding pure preaching:
one should not preach to a listener who is seated while the preacher stands;
nor should one preach to a listener who seeks faults in the Dharma or seeks faults in the preacher.
If a listener relies on the person rather than the Dharma, one should not preach for them;
if a listener relies on the letter rather than the meaning, one should not preach for them;
and so on, until: if a listener does not rely on the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), one should not preach for them.
Why is this? It is because such a person is unable to show reverence for the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the pure Dharma.

If the teacher of the Dharma respects the Dharma, and the listener also gives rise to profound respect, listening and receiving it with a sincere mind without conceit or disdain, this is called the pure exposition of the Dharma.
To speak in sequence is to speak of all things.
To speak of all things refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures, down to a single sentence, a single verse, or even half a verse.

Whether regarding the words, the meaning, or the Dharma, when teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening others with respect to that Dharma and its meaning, he may at times reprove them, at times speak the truth, or at times speak through parables, teaching according to what is appropriate;

or he may speak in a shallow manner, or speak in a way that is easy to enter, according to what they wish to hear. This is called the Bodhisattva’s sequential teaching of the Dharma for knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.

Regarding pure preaching: when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) amidst enmity and hatred, and having attained that mind of loving-kindness, he preaches the Dharma to wicked sentient beings and those who are heedless through various skillful means;

he likewise uses skillful means to instruct and preach the Dharma to those who are fond of their own minds, the arrogant and self-indulgent, and the poor. He does not do so for the sake of praising himself, disparaging others, food and drink, gain and support, or fame. This is called the Bodhisattva’s pure preaching of the Dharma through knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.
What is dwelling in accordance with the Dharma?

It is the cultivation of wholesome dharmas through the actions of body, speech, and mind, being fully endowed with purity, recognizing kindness and repaying it, for the sake of adorning *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva recognizes kindness and repays it; he contemplates its meaning, attains mastery through extensive learning, and causes the torch of the Dharma to blaze brightly."
To benefit all sentient beings, one should cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, and extensive learning.
To honor the teacher, one should not seek out faults in the Dharma nor faults in the teacher; being free from malice, one bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings—this is called knowing gratitude.
To receive the joys of humans and devas and to attain the Way and Nirvana—this is called repaying gratitude.

Furthermore, there are four ways in which a bodhisattva cultivates patience (*kṣānti*): destroying impatience, adorning enlightenment (*bodhi*), gathering in sentient beings, and causing them to cultivate patience—whether by practicing patience oneself or inducing others to do so—and thereby remaining far removed from fear; this is called knowing gratitude.
By means of the causal conditions of patience, one is free from anger; one's retinue remains undivided, one does not undergo suffering or affliction, and the mind is without regret.
Having relinquished this body, one enjoys the bliss of humans and devas and swiftly attains the bliss of Nirvana; this is called repaying kindness.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva diligently cultivates vigor, destroys indolence, adorns enlightenment, and gathers in sentient beings.
To cultivate diligence for the sake of the path to enlightenment;
to sleep in peace and awaken in peace, free from all afflictions;
to increase wholesome dharmas and experience physical and mental bliss—this is called self-benefit.
The diligence of a bodhisattva does not afflict sentient beings through beating, throwing, scolding, or reviling; this is called benefiting others.

After relinquishing this body, one enjoys the pleasures of humans and devas, the body attains great strength, and one realizes the path to Bodhi; this is called the great fruit. These are the four matters of a bodhisattva’s diligence.
When a bodhisattva cultivates meditative concentration, they destroy a distracted mind, adorn awakening, and gather in sentient beings.

For the sake of the path to awakening, they cause others to cultivate dhyāna-concentration; experiencing worldly happiness in the present life while their body and mind remain tranquil—this is called knowing gratitude.
Because the body and mind are tranquil, one does not afflict sentient beings; this is called repaying kindness.

After the Bodhisattva has relinquished this body, they receive a pure body, attaining peace, security, and happiness, and realize Great Nirvana; these are called the four matters of the Bodhisattva’s meditative concentration.

"Furthermore, the bodhisattva knows gratitude and repays kindness; he accomplishes wisdom, destroys ignorance, adorns enlightenment, and gathers in sentient beings through the four means of attraction."
To cultivate wisdom for the sake of the path to enlightenment in order to know the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), thereby experiencing physical peace and happiness, is called self-benefit.
To be able to bring forth worldly and world-transcending matters for sentient beings is called benefiting others.
To be able to destroy the two obstacles of afflictions and wisdom is called the great fruit; this is called knowing gratitude, and this is called repaying kindness.
These four matters regarding the Bodhisattva’s wisdom are inconceivable.

"Furthermore, it is not by means of the knowledge of past lives that a bodhisattva knows the events of former existences; rather, he does so in order to observe how sentient beings equally experience the results of their various wholesome and unwholesome karmas."
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through great skillful means, dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven and perfects his lifespan, possessing three superiorities:
first, superiority in lifespan; second, superiority in physical form; [and third, superiority in fame].
Third, his fame is supreme.
At the time of his initial descent, he emits a great radiance that illumines the ten directions;
he knows for himself the moments of his entry into his mother’s womb, his dwelling therein, and his emergence from it.
As he walked seven steps in each of the ten directions without anyone supporting him, he spoke these words:
"This present body of mine is the very last.
Then the devas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas made offerings of various flowers, incense, exquisite music, banners, and canopies.
His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks, such that none could surpass him;
by the power of his kindness and compassion, he destroyed the hosts of Māra’s armies;
and every joint and limb possessed the great strength attained by Nārāyaṇa.
In his childhood and youth, he understood worldly affairs without studying them;
he learned without a teacher and spontaneously attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and at the exhortation of Brahmā, he turned the wheel of the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
While he was in right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), even the thundering roar of a dragon could not cause him to stir;
all wild beasts drew near to him, loving him as if he were their father or mother, for the Buddha knew their hearts and they offered him food;
the cloud-spirits sent down rain to bathe his body, and the trees bent their branches downward to provide shade for his person.
After he had attained the Way, for six years the Māra constantly watched for and sought his weaknesses, but could find no flaw;

[the Bodhisattva] remained constantly in meditative concentration, perfected mindfulness, and was well able to discern the arising and ceasing of applied and sustained thought—this is called the inconceivable co-arising of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding "not arising together": it is for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, like that madman;
by encountering the Tathāgata, they recover their original minds.

The blind regain their sight, those in difficult labor deliver easily, the deaf regain their hearing, and greed, hatred, and delusion are all completely eradicated. This is called the inconceivable "not arising together."
"Furthermore, as for their co-arising, the conduct of the Tathāgata is inconceivable.
He always lies on his right side like a lion king;
whether upon grass or leaves, he remains undisturbed."
The fierce winds of the swirling blue heavens cannot move his robes;
when he sets out and walks, he strides like a lion king or a king of white geese;
and when he wishes to walk, he first extends his right foot.
Wherever they travel, high and low ground alike become level;
their food is never left unfinished, and grains remain in their mouths—this is called the inconceivability of co-arising.
Furthermore, regarding the inconceivability of co-arising:
First, the soles of the feet are level;
second, the soles of the feet bear the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel;
third, the toes are slender and long.
Fourth, the heels are high and full;
fifth, the fingers and toes are webbed;
sixth, the hands and feet are soft and supple.
Seventh, his calves are like those of the king of the eneya deer;
eighth, his ankle bones are not visible;
ninth, standing upright, his hands reach and touch his knees.
Tenth, he has the mark of the concealed male organ, like that of an elephant or a horse king;
eleventh, his body is perfectly rounded and full, like a nyagrodha tree;
twelfth, the hairs on his body point upward.
Thirteenth, each hair curls to the right;
fourteenth, his body is the color of pure gold;
fifteenth, he possesses a constant radiance extending one fathom in every direction.
Sixteenth, his skin is fine and soft, such that dust and grime do not adhere to it;
seventeenth, he has seven parts of his body that are full;
eighteenth, his upper body is like that of a lion.
Nineteenth, his arms and elbows are rounded and well-proportioned;
twentieth, his collarbones are level and full;
twenty-first, he possesses the mark of a well-rounded body.
Twenty-second: he has forty teeth in his mouth;
twenty-third: his teeth are closely set without gaps and are even;
twenty-fourth: the color of his teeth is white.
Twenty-fifth, his jaw is square like that of a lion;
twenty-sixth, he attains the supreme taste among all tastes;
twenty-seventh, he possesses the mark of the fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Twenty-eighth, a broad and long tongue;
twenty-ninth, a Brahma-like voice;
thirtieth, eyes of deep blue color.
Thirty-first, his eyes are like those of a bull king;
thirty-second, there is a white tuft of hair between his eyebrows—such are the eighty kinds of inconceivable marks and secondary characteristics.
Each of these marks and signs of excellence is further endowed with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kinds of subtle and wondrous marks and signs.

Every one of these marks and signs arose because the Bodhisattva, from the first moment he resolved his mind upon enlightenment, remained firm in his bodhi, recognized kindness and repaid it, and cultivated these sublime practices; therefore, he has now attained unsurpassed bodhi.
The Buddha said:
"Because the Tathāgata has for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas sincerely cultivated and maintained the pure precepts, his soles are level.
