Because he made offerings to his parents, upādhyāyas, ācāryas, and virtuous persons, by these causes and conditions, he has obtained the mark of wheels on the soles of his feet."
One does not give rise to thoughts of harm toward sentient beings and harbors no intent to plunder;

if one sees one’s parents, preceptors, teachers, or virtuous persons, one goes out from afar to welcome them, provides them with seats, and pays them respectful homage, thereby subduing arrogance. By these causes and conditions, one obtains long and slender fingers.
By possessing the three aforementioned practices, one obtains full and rounded heels.
By gathering sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), by this causal condition, one obtains webbed fingers and toes.
By anointing and washing one's parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and virtuous persons with fine ghee and oil, through these causes and conditions, one obtains softness in the hands and feet.
Cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas without knowing satiety—by these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of well-rounded calves.

Hearing the Dharma with joy and delighting in explaining it to others, as well as running errands for the sake of the Dharma—by these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of non-protruding anklebones.

With the three karmas purified, by tending to the sick and bestowing medicine, by eliminating arrogance, and by being content with food and drink—for these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of standing upright with his hands reaching his knees.
Seeing those who were separated, he spoke kind words to reconcile them;
he cultivated a sense of shame and remorse within himself and also taught others to do so. By these causes and conditions, he attained the mark of the horse’s sheath.
Having purified the three karmas oneself, one also teaches others to purify them;

if there are sentient beings whose four great elements are unbalanced, one is able to provide medical treatment for them. By these causes and conditions, one attains the mark of the body being perfectly proportioned.
Hearing the Dharma with joy and delighting in explaining it to others, by these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of body hairs that curl upward.
Contemplating the profound meaning of all phenomena, delighting in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas, making offerings to parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and those of virtue;

and while traveling on roads, clearing away bricks, stones, thorns, and impurities from Buddhist stupas and monasteries—by these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of each individual hair curling to the right.
If one gives food, drink, and ornaments to others and thereby eliminates anger, by this causal condition, one obtains two marks:
first, a golden complexion; second, a constant radiance.
By what karmic conditions is the mark of each individual hair obtained?
It is by these very same karmic conditions that one obtains a body that is fine and soft, such that dust and grime do not adhere to it.
By constantly bestowing upon sentient beings whatever things they require, through these causes and conditions, one obtains the mark of the seven parts being full.

Having personally destroyed pride and tempered his own nature, he acts in accordance with the Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings; to eliminate what is unwholesome, he teaches them wholesome dharmas. By these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of the upper body being like that of a lion, the mark of rounded shoulders, and the mark of the collarbones being level and full.
By what karmic conditions does one obtain the mark of slender fingers?
By those very same karmic conditions, one obtains the mark of smooth skin on the body.

By abstaining from double-tongued speech and reconciling those who are at strife, through these causes and conditions, one obtains the mark of forty teeth, the mark of teeth that are closely set without gaps, and the mark of teeth that are even and level.
By practicing loving-kindness toward those in the desire realm, through these causes and conditions, he attained the mark of white teeth.
Seeing those who sought [his help], he welcomed and saw them off with joy; through these causes and conditions, he attained the mark of full and square jaws.
He regards all sentient beings as equal, like an only son; by these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of the supreme flavor.
He constantly bestows upon sentient beings the unsurpassed flavor of the Dharma;
seeing those who have forgotten, he grants them the power of recollection.
Personally upholding the five precepts and further teaching them to others;

cultivating and accumulating a heart of compassion and being able to perform the great gift of Dharma—by these causes and conditions, one attains the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head and the mark of the broad and long tongue.
By speaking truthful words, words of Dharma-joy, and gentle words of Dharma, and by not speaking at improper times, through these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of the Brahma-like voice.
By cultivating and accumulating a heart of compassion and regarding all sentient beings as if they were his own parents, through these causes and conditions, he obtains two marks:
first, eyes of deep blue color; [second, eyelashes like those of a cow].
Second, his eyes are like those of a bull king.
When he sees those with virtue, he praises them truthfully; by this causal condition, he attains the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
Although each of the thirty-two marks has its own specific causes and conditions, the true cause and condition for all of them is the observance of the precepts and diligent effort.

Why is this? If one does not maintain the precepts, even if one is able to practice diligence, one will not even attain a human body, let alone the thirty-two marks, the invisible crown, and the uṣṇīṣa; these are all equally unattainable.
"Furthermore, regarding all actions performed with a concentrated mind and without regret, by these causes and conditions, one attains the mark of level soles.

If one acts with a sincere heart, by these causes and conditions, one attains the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, the second and third marks of webbed fingers and toes, the mark of the seven parts being full, the mark of fine, soft, and rounded shoulders, the mark of a straight body with a complete chest, and the mark of a broad and long tongue."

If one constantly performs [these deeds], by these causes and conditions, one attains the mark of long fingers, the mark of standing upright with hands reaching the knees, the mark of a constant radiance extending one fathom, and the mark of teeth that are closely set without gaps.
If one performs pure deeds, by this causal condition, one obtains other marks.

Furthermore, if one gives rise to a heart of pure goodness toward sentient beings, by this causal condition, one attains soft hands and feet, fine and smooth skin, and the absence of dust or grime adhering to the body.
By practicing and accumulating [merit] in succession and at the proper times, through these causes and conditions, one attains the second, third, and fourth marks.

By joyfully practicing wholesome dharmas and having a mind free from regret or retreat, through these causes and conditions, one attains a golden-colored body, teeth that are always radiant and white, and the tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*).

If, upon hearing praise, one does not give rise to arrogance, but conceals one's wholesome qualities so that others do not know of them, by these causes and conditions, one attains the mark of the horse's sheath.

By dedicating the wholesome dharmas he has cultivated toward bodhi, through these causes and conditions, he attains the mark of a single hair growing from each pore, the mark of body hairs curling upward, the mark of forty teeth in his mouth, and the mark of the supreme sense of taste.
Because of diligent and vigorous effort, through these causes and conditions, he attains the marks of full-jawed cheeks and an upper body like that of a lion.

Because he cherished all sentient beings with a sincere heart as if they were his only son, through these causes and conditions, he attains the marks of even teeth, deep blue eyes, and eyes like those of a bull king.
Cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas without knowing satiety, by these causes and conditions, one obtains the remaining marks.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the stage of natural conduct, they cultivate the karma for the thirty-two marks.
While abiding in the stage of pure conduct, although one possesses these thirty-two marks, they are not yet fully perfected and have not attained clarity or purity.
Only when abiding in the twelve practices do they become clearly manifest and fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
Although there are immeasurable marks, sentient beings differ, being categorized as superior, middling, or inferior, and are inconceivable; for this reason, the Buddha speaks of the thirty-two marks.
If all the merits possessed by all sentient beings were combined and gathered together, they would exactly equal a single pore of the Tathāgata.
All the merits contained within every single pore, when combined and gathered together, constitute one secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*).

When all the merits of these secondary marks are further increased a hundredfold, they constitute one primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*), with the exception of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) and the invisible crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa-śīrṣa*).
Combining all the remaining marks and increasing them a thousandfold, these two marks are formed.

By further aggregating and accumulating all the merits of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, multiplying them by thousands, millions, and billions, one then achieves the Tathāgata’s profound and distant thunderous voice—its sound heard throughout immeasurable and boundless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds as numerous as motes of dust.

"For the sake of sentient beings, he practices great compassion, recognizes kindness and repays it, and cultivates and accumulates these inconceivable, profound, and subtle, inconceivable marks and signs."

Each individual mark and sign is able to benefit immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, as numerous as the dust motes of the great earth, causing them to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind.
By cultivating and accumulating these in succession, one fully attains and perfects the thirty-two marks and signs.

Once they were endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, he caused them all to proceed toward the Bodhi tree, where they would subdue Māra, attain Buddhahood, turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma, benefit sentient beings, cross the ocean of craving and thirst, reach the shore of great wisdom, and accomplish the welfare of all living beings.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
“All you members of the great assembly, all you bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all you sons of good family!

Among you, who is able to constantly keep the Buddha’s kindness in mind, protect and uphold the True Dharma, and transcribe, read, and recite this subtle, profound, and wondrous Sūtra on the Great Expedient Means for Repaying Kindness?”
Who will be able, in the future evil age, to establish great diligence, to receive, uphold, and protect the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Who will be able to protect the Dharma, disseminate this sutra, and bring boundless benefit to all sentient beings?

At that time, within the great assembly, there were eighteen thousand great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who immediately rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the future evil age, we shall be able to receive, uphold, and protect Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; we shall be able to guard the True Dharma and transform sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃha spoke again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I, too, am able to gather in and sustain sentient beings through various skillful means."
The Bodhisattva Vajra said,
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who are about to fall into the three evil realms, I am able to restrain and protect them so that they do not fall.”
Mañjuśrī spoke again: “World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who seek anything whatsoever, I am able to cause them all to be fully provided with it.”
The Bodhisattva Jñānaketu further spoke these words:
"I am able to bestow great wisdom upon sentient beings.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Dharmaketu spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
I am able to universally bestow the Dharma upon all sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha.
“World-Honored One!
I vow to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Candraprabha.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to transform and guide all sentient beings, causing them to cultivate merit and virtue.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Suvārakṣita.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to teach and transform all sentient beings, causing them to be free from negligence.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to transform and guide all sentient beings, causing them all to perceive the meaning of the inexhaustible realm.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Candrottara.
“World-Honored One!
I am able to bestow unsurpassed peace and happiness upon all sentient beings.

In this manner, each of these bodhisattvas made their own extraordinary and wondrous vows to adorn enlightenment and benefit all sentient beings. Out of mindfulness of the Buddha’s kindness and in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness, they immediately rose from their seats, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May this sutra be entrusted to us, the assembly of bodhisattvas.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be practiced?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is titled 'The Compendium of All Roots of Goodness,' and it is also titled 'Great Skillful Means,' and also titled 'Subtle and Secret Practice,' and also titled 'Requiting the Buddha's Kindness.'"
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the assembly of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:
"You all should practice according to what has been taught!
When this Chapter on the Entrustment was spoken, seventy-two thousand śrāvakas gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi.

Together with all other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra on the Buddha’s Requital of Kindness through Great Expedient Means, Scroll Seven.
